label: Chapter 5
title: The Rationalist Proof
tagline: Everything has an explanation — so something must explain itself
oneSentence: Since everything has an explanation — a principle no one can reject without sawing off the branch their own reasoning sits on — the existence of contingent things must finally be explained by an absolutely necessary being, and anything necessary in the strictest sense must be purely actual, simple, subsistent existence itself, one, and the cause of all else: that is, God.
bigPicture:
The first four proofs each started from a metaphysical feature of ordinary things: change (the Aristotelian proof), composition (the Neo-Platonic proof), abstract truths (the Augustinian proof), and the distinction between essence and existence (the Thomistic proof). The rationalist proof starts from something even more general — the fact that things are **intelligible**, that there is always a reason why they exist and are as they are. Its engine is the **principle of sufficient reason (PSR)**, the thesis that everything has an explanation, whether or not we ever find it.

Feser spends most of Stage 1 not on God but on defending PSR. He grants it strong inductive support, but insists it is far more certain than any empirical generalization: denying it wrecks our trust in perception, then our trust in reasoning itself, and makes nonsense of the scientific practice of explaining things by laws of nature. Borrowing and extending arguments from Alexander Pruss, Robert Koons, and Michael Della Rocca, he argues that even PSR’s critics quietly rely on it every time they argue. With PSR in hand, he divides everything into the **contingent** (explained by something outside itself) and the **necessary** (explained by its own nature), and shows that no series of contingent things — not even an infinite one — can explain why there are contingent things at all, or why any one of them exists right now.

Stage 2 then does something the classic rationalists (Leibniz, Clarke) did not do in quite this way: it ties necessity to the Aristotelian-Thomistic metaphysics of the earlier chapters. Anything that is necessary in the strictest sense cannot have unactualized potentials, parts, or an essence distinct from its existence — so the necessary being is the same purely actual, simple, self-subsistent reality the other proofs reached, with all the divine attributes that follow.

What makes this chapter distinctive is its terrain: it fights on the ground of explanation itself. That makes it the natural proof for people who think the universe might just be a “brute fact,” and it shows why Feser’s Thomistic construal of PSR — explanation as *making intelligible*, not as logical entailment, and no demand to explain abstract propositions — dodges the most famous objections to Leibniz-style arguments.
objectives: State the principle of sufficient reason precisely and explain two ways it differs from the principle of causality (a sufficient reason need not be distinct from what it explains; PSR, unlike the causal principle, applies to absolutely everything).

Reconstruct Feser’s three-layer defense of PSR — the inductive case, the reductio from perception and from reasoning itself, and Della Rocca’s explicability-argument dilemma — and explain why denying PSR is self-undermining.
Explain, using the book-and-shelf example, why a chain of laws of nature ending in a brute fact explains nothing at all.
Define contingent and necessary being and show why PSR leaves no third option.

Explain why an infinite series of contingent causes — taken as a whole (Leibniz/Clarke) or as a series of simultaneous sustaining causes — cannot be the ultimate explanation, answering Hume and the fallacy-of-composition charge.
Derive pure actuality, absolute simplicity, and subsistent existence from necessity in the strictest sense, and explain why there can be only one necessary being, which causes everything else.
Answer the ‘big conjunction of contingent truths’ (modal-collapse) objection using the Thomist understanding of propositions and of explanation.
Explain why the universe cannot be the necessary being and why ‘What caused God?’ fails against this proof (self-explanatory is not self-caused).
Compare Feser’s version of the argument with Leibniz’s and Clarke’s, identifying at least three differences.

summary.heading: Stage 1: Explanations everywhere, and the principle they suggest (pp. 147–148)
summary.body:
Feser opens with ordinary detective work. A strange pair of sunglasses on your sofa turns out to have been left by a visiting friend. A rash on your arm is traced to poison oak brushed on a hike. Scratching on the roof proves to be a cat or a family of raccoons. Science does the same thing at a higher level: biologists explain new life forms by mutation and natural selection, physicists explain water’s temperature by mean molecular kinetic energy and planetary orbits by Kepler’s laws.

Even when we fail to find an explanation, we do not conclude there is none — and we often have an explanation of *why* we lack one. An unsolved murder stays unsolved because the killer avoided fingerprints and witnesses and hid the body well.

This raises the question: does absolutely everything have an explanation, including ones we will never discover? The thesis that it does is the **principle of sufficient reason (PSR)**. Leibniz made it famous, but thinkers of many schools have held it. Feser cites Thomist formulations: whatever exists has a sufficient reason for existing; “everything is intelligible”; and (Wuellner) there is an adequate objective explanation for the being of whatever exists and for all of its attributes.

Notice two features of how Feser introduces the principle. First, he starts from practice rather than theory. PSR is presented as a statement of something we already rely on in every inquiry, from finding a lost item to doing physics. Second, the principle concerns the explanation of *existence and attributes*, not only of events. It asks why a thing is there at all and why it is as it is, which is why it can later be applied to the existence of contingent things as such. And whether PSR is true is a different question from whether we can find particular explanations: PSR concerns what there *is*, not what we *know*.
summary.takeaway: PSR — everything has an explanation, whether or not we find it — simply states what our everyday and scientific practice of explaining already takes for granted.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest thing to see in this opening section is the difference between two claims that sound almost the same:

- **The epistemic claim:** we can (or eventually will) find an explanation for everything.
- **The ontological claim:** there *is* an explanation for everything, whether or not anyone ever finds it.

PSR is the second claim. Feser makes the point by stressing that the principle covers explanations ‘we haven’t discovered and never will discover.’ This matters because the easiest way to dismiss PSR is to point to things we can’t explain — the origin of life, the fine details of consciousness, a crime that is never solved. None of these counts against PSR, because PSR makes no promise about our success.

The **unsolved murder** is carefully chosen. It shows that when our explanatory efforts fail, we not only keep believing an explanation exists but can often *explain the failure itself*: the killer wore gloves, avoided witnesses, and hid the body. Our failures are intelligible too. Try a small thought experiment. You lose a sock in the laundry. You search everywhere and never find it. Do you ever conclude that the sock ceased to exist for no reason at all? No. You conclude it is behind the machine, or went out with the towels, or was taken by the dog. The sock case and the murder case have the same structure: the explanation is unknown, not absent.

Note the scope of the Thomist formulations Feser cites. Wuellner’s version speaks of a sufficient reason for *the being of whatever is* and for *all attributes of any being*. So PSR applies not only to events (why the roof scratched) but to existence (why the cat exists) and to features (why water has the temperature it has). That breadth is what later lets Feser ask why contingent things exist at all (steps 11–14) and why a particular thing exists now (steps 15–17).

People often think PSR is a claim about *causes of events*, or that it demands we be able to answer every ‘why?’ question. Both are mistakes. It is a claim that reality is intelligible through and through, which is exactly step 1 of the formal argument. The ordinary examples in this section also prepare steps 2–3: they are the data that make PSR look inductively secure.

checks.q: What does Feser’s unsolved-murder example chiefly illustrate?
options: That some events have no explanation
That when we fail to find an explanation we still assume one exists, and can often explain the failure itself
That detectives rely on PSR more than scientists do
That PSR is false for free human actions
checks.explanation: The murder remains unsolved *because* the killer was careful. Even our failures to explain are explained, which shows we never infer ‘no explanation exists’ from ‘none found.’

checks.q: As formulated in this section, PSR is a claim about…
options: what there is: every existing thing and every attribute has an explanation, whether or not we discover it
what we will eventually come to know
only events that occur in time
only the laws of physics
checks.explanation: PSR is ontological, not epistemic, and it covers existence and attributes, not just events.

summary.plain: We explain things all the time — a forgotten pair of sunglasses, a rash, a noise on the roof — and science does the same on a bigger scale. Even when we can’t find the explanation, we assume there is one. The chapter’s starting idea, called the principle of sufficient reason, is that absolutely everything has an explanation, whether or not we ever find it.

summary.heading: PSR is not the principle of causality (p. 148)
summary.body:
PSR resembles the principle of causality from earlier chapters, but the two are distinct, and the difference matters for the whole chapter.

- **A cause must be distinct from its effect; a sufficient reason need not be.** Nothing can cause itself, but something could in principle be *self-explanatory* — its reason for existing could lie in what it is. (Whether anything actually is self-explanatory is what the argument will settle.)
- **The causal principle does not say everything has a cause; PSR does say everything has a sufficient reason.** Whatever has a cause has its sufficient reason in something else; whatever lacks a cause (if anything does) must have its sufficient reason in itself.

So every cause is a reason — it makes its effect intelligible — but not every reason is a cause. Keep this in mind: it is why the proof never has to make an ‘exception’ for God.

Why does Feser insist on this so early? Because the chapter will conclude that something exists whose sufficient reason is *internal* to it. If PSR were just the principle of causality stretched to cover everything, that conclusion would be incoherent, since it would require something to cause itself. With the two principles distinguished, the conclusion is consistent. There is a structural point too. The principle of causality, properly stated, applies only to things with potentials that get actualized; PSR applies to absolutely everything, including anything with no potentials at all. PSR is the more general principle, and in chapter 7 Feser notes that the principle of causality can be seen as following from it.
summary.takeaway: A cause must be distinct from its effect, but a sufficient reason can be a thing’s own nature — so PSR, unlike the causal principle, covers everything without implying that anything is self-caused.
summary.deepDive:
Everything in this chapter depends on keeping two ideas apart: **cause** and **sufficient reason**.

A cause, in the Aristotelian sense used in earlier chapters, is something that actualizes a potential in something *else*. The hand moves the stick, and the air cools the coffee. Because causing means bringing some potential into actuality, nothing can cause itself; it would have to be already actual, in order to do the causing, and not yet actual, in order to be caused.

A sufficient reason is broader. It is whatever makes a thing *intelligible*. Sometimes that is a cause, as with the rash explained by the poison oak. But sometimes the reason lies in the thing’s own nature. Consider a mathematical example. Why do the interior angles of a Euclidean triangle add up to two right angles? Nothing *causes* them to — no force or agent brings it about. The explanation lies in what a triangle is. That is a sufficient reason that is not a cause. (The example illustrates internal explanation of an *attribute*; the chapter will argue that in one unique case, the *existence* of a thing can be explained by its nature.)

Now run a thought experiment. Suppose some being X exists. PSR says there is an explanation. There are two places it could be:

1. Outside X, in which case X is caused and its reason is distinct from it.
2. Inside X, in its own nature, in which case X is uncaused but *not* unexplained.

The principle of causality speaks only to case 1. PSR covers both. That is why Feser can say that ‘all causes are reasons, but not all reasons are causes.’ It also sets up step 9, the dichotomy between contingent and necessary, and the final reply to ‘What caused God?’ (see the last objections section).

The usual confusion runs like this: ‘Theists say everything needs an explanation, then exempt God.’ This merges the two principles. The argument never says everything has a *cause*, and it never exempts God from having a *reason*. Chapter 7 traces the confusion historically: Descartes and Spinoza spoke of God as ‘cause of himself’ when they meant something like ‘sufficient reason of himself,’ and Hume and his successors took the rationalist claim to be ‘everything has an efficient cause,’ a claim no serious defender of the cosmological argument made. Keeping the distinction clear dissolves the charge of special pleading before it arises.

checks.q: Which statement captures the relation between causes and sufficient reasons?
options: All reasons are causes, but not all causes are reasons
Causes and reasons are the same thing
All causes are reasons, but not all reasons are causes
Neither is ever a kind of the other
checks.explanation: Every cause makes its effect intelligible, so it is a reason. But a thing’s own nature can be its reason without causing it.

checks.q: If something had no cause at all, where would PSR locate its sufficient reason?
options: Nowhere, since PSR allows uncaused things to be unexplained
In an earlier member of a temporal series
In the minds that think about it
In itself, in its own nature
checks.explanation: Feser says that whatever lacks a cause would have to have its sufficient reason in itself. PSR never allows ‘no reason at all.’

checks.q: Why is the cause/reason distinction essential to the chapter’s conclusion?
options: Because the conclusion is a being whose reason is internal to it, and if reasons were always causes that would require self-causation
Because it shows PSR is merely empirical
Because it allows Feser to deny that God has any explanation
Because it proves the universe had a beginning
checks.explanation: The necessary being is self-explanatory. If every reason were a cause, a self-explanatory being would be a self-caused one, which is incoherent.

summary.plain: An explanation is not always a cause. A cause is some other thing that brings something about, and nothing can bring itself about. But something can be explained by what it is in itself, the way a triangle’s three sides are explained by what a triangle is. That leaves room for something that explains its own existence without causing itself.

summary.heading: The inductive case for PSR (pp. 148–149)
summary.body:
One argument for PSR mirrors chapter 1’s empirical argument for the principle of causality. Treated as an inductive generalization, PSR is as well supported as any. First, we generally find explanations when we look, and when we don’t, we usually have reason to think one exists but is out of reach (missing evidence, for example). Second, following Pruss, the world does not behave as it would if PSR were false. Unexplained events would be happening constantly, and the world would lack the intelligibility that makes both science and common sense work so well. That the world is as orderly and intelligible as it is would be a miracle if PSR were false.

The argument has two parts. The first is familiar: explanations keep turning up. The second, from Pruss, is subtler. Consider what the world *would* look like if PSR were false. If things could arise or occur for no reason, there would be nothing to make such brute events rare, and nothing to confine them to the unobservable or the microscopic. So the absence of a constant stream of inexplicable events is itself evidence. Feser models this on chapter 1’s empirical argument for the principle of causality, where W. Norris Clarke observed that if causality failed, nothing would stop an elephant or a hotel from appearing on your lawn. In both cases, an empiricist who doubts the principle is doubting something experience supports as well as it supports anything. But Feser treats the inductive argument as a supplement. It shows PSR is at least as secure as any scientific generalization, and the next sections argue that it is far more secure.
summary.takeaway: Even judged merely as an inductive generalization, PSR is as well supported as anything, and the world’s lack of constant brute events would be a miracle if it were false.
summary.deepDive:
Why should the *absence* of brute events count as evidence for PSR? It helps to think in terms of expectations. Ask: if hypothesis H were true, what would we expect to observe? Then compare with what we do observe.

- **If PSR is true**, every event and every thing has an explanation. We should expect a world where investigation tends to succeed, surprises turn out to have sources, and science steadily uncovers deeper regularities.
- **If PSR is false**, some things happen for no reason at all. And here is the key point: *nothing* would govern how often, where, or at what scale such brute events occur. A reason-less event is, by definition, not constrained by anything. So there is no reason to expect them to be rare, tiny, or hidden. Bowling balls could materialize in kitchens, and your coffee could turn to lead mid-sip.

What we observe fits the first picture overwhelmingly and the second not at all. That is why Feser, following Pruss, says the world’s orderliness would be ‘a miracle’ if PSR were false.

A thought experiment makes this concrete. Imagine a detector that beeps whenever something happens with no explanation whatsoever. Every lab and household has one. In a PSR-false world they would presumably be beeping constantly. In our world, whenever a ‘beep’ seems to occur — a strange noise, an unexpected lab result — patient investigation finds a source. The detector has, as far as we can tell, never truly gone off.

There is a nuance, though. Feser does not rest PSR on induction. Inductive support can make a principle highly probable, but he holds that PSR is *more certain* than any empirical hypothesis. The inductive case comes first because it meets the empiricist on his own ground. It shows that an empiricist has no business singling PSR out for doubt, since it is as well confirmed as any law of science.

This section is what grounds steps 2 and 3: if PSR were false, unexplained things would be extremely common (2), and common sense and science find the opposite (3). Together they give PSR by modus tollens.

A common confusion is to think that because *this* argument is inductive, PSR is ‘just induction’ and might fail at the cosmic scale. Feser agrees that induction alone wouldn’t settle the matter. That is why the next sections turn to the reductio, which shows that the denial of PSR is self-undermining wherever it is applied.

checks.q: What is the second prong of the inductive case, drawn from Pruss?
options: That PSR is self-evident to everyone
That the world does not behave as we would expect if PSR were false, since brute events would then be common
That quantum mechanics confirms PSR
That every scientist believes PSR
checks.explanation: Beyond ‘we find explanations,’ the argument notes what a PSR-false world would look like: nothing would keep brute occurrences rare.

checks.q: Which formal steps does this section chiefly support?
options: Steps 19–21
Steps 11–12
Steps 15–16
Steps 2–3
checks.explanation: Step 2 says brute events would be common if PSR were false, and step 3 says common sense and science find the opposite.

summary.plain: One reason to believe everything has an explanation is plain experience: we keep finding explanations when we look. And if things could happen for no reason, we’d expect weird, unexplained events all the time. We don’t see that, so the principle looks very well supported.

summary.heading: More certain than a hypothesis: the reductio from perception (p. 149)
summary.body:
Feser insists PSR is *far more* certain than any empirical hypothesis. If it seems hard to prove, that is because it is more evident than anything we could say for or against it. Following Garrigou-Lagrange, it cannot be demonstrated directly but can be defended indirectly by **reductio ad absurdum** — showing that its denial leads to absurdity.

The first reductio comes from Pruss, developing a point from Koons: **denying PSR leads to radical skepticism about perception.** If PSR is false, our perceptual experiences might occur for no reason at all, with no connection to the external objects we take to cause them. Worse, we could not even say such a disconnect is *improbable*, because objective probabilities depend on the objective tendencies of things — and if PSR fails, events might happen in ways that have nothing to do with any tendencies. So no one can consistently deny PSR while trusting the senses or the empirical science built on them.

It helps to be clear about what the argument does *not* claim. It does not claim that if PSR is false, our perceptions actually are disconnected from reality. It claims that we would have no grounds for thinking they are not, and no grounds even for thinking a disconnect unlikely. That second part blocks the easy escape. A critic might say: ‘A brute disconnect is possible, but surely improbable.’ The reply is that probability judgments are not free-floating. Objective probabilities reflect the tendencies of things; a die lands six about a sixth of the time because of how dice are made. If PSR is false, events need not follow any tendency, so there is no basis for the probability judgment the critic needs. That is why the Pruss/Koons argument yields radical, not merely modest, skepticism.
summary.takeaway: If PSR is false, nothing connects our experiences to their supposed objects and we can’t even call a disconnect improbable, so denying PSR forfeits trust in perception and empirical science.
summary.deepDive:
Begin with why Feser reaches for a *reductio* at all. Following Garrigou-Lagrange, he says PSR cannot be demonstrated directly, not because it is doubtful but because it is *more evident* than anything we could use to prove it. First principles are often like this. Consider the law of non-contradiction: you cannot derive it from anything more certain, but you can show that anyone who denies it ends up unable to say anything definite. A reductio proves a principle by showing that its denial is ruinous, not by deriving it from deeper premises.

Now walk through the perceptual case slowly. You look at a red apple and have a visual experience of redness and roundness. Ordinarily we explain the experience like this: light reflects off the apple, enters your eyes, and your visual system processes it. The apple is part of the *explanation* of your experience, and that is exactly why the experience counts as evidence that an apple is there.

Suppose PSR is false. Then your experience might occur *for no reason*: no apple, no light, no processing. It might just happen. And you could not tell the difference from the inside, since a brute experience of an apple would feel exactly like a caused one.

The critic’s natural fallback is probability: ‘Sure, a brute apple experience is possible, but it’s wildly unlikely.’ Feser, following Pruss, blocks this. Objective probabilities depend on the objective tendencies of things. We can say a fair coin lands heads half the time because of the coin’s physical make-up. But brute events, by definition, are not produced by any tendency, so there is no fact about how probable they are. The critic has cut the very branch the probability judgment would sit on.

The result is that someone who denies PSR cannot consistently claim to be justified in trusting perception, or the empirical science built on it. This is what supports step 4 (without PSR we couldn’t trust our cognitive faculties) and step 5 (but we can), from which PSR follows.

Two clarifications. First, Feser presents this as one way the reductio ‘might go,’ developing remarks by Pruss, who was himself developing a point from Koons. Second, the argument concerns *justification*, not truth. People often think it claims that denying PSR makes our perceptions false. It doesn’t; it shows that the denier loses the right to think they are true. The next section shows that retreating from perception to pure reason doesn’t help.

checks.q: Why can’t someone who denies PSR say a disconnect between perception and reality is merely improbable?
options: Because improbable events never happen
Because perception is infallible
Because objective probabilities depend on things’ objective tendencies, which events could ignore if PSR were false
Because Garrigou-Lagrange ruled it out
checks.explanation: Probability judgments presuppose that events flow from the natures and tendencies of things. Brute events have no such source, so there is no basis for calling them improbable.

checks.q: According to Garrigou-Lagrange, as Feser cites him, PSR…
options: can be demonstrated directly from more basic axioms
is merely a useful working assumption
is known only by revelation
cannot be demonstrated directly but can be demonstrated indirectly, by reductio
checks.explanation: PSR is too basic to be derived from anything more evident, so it is defended by showing that its denial leads to absurdity.

summary.plain: Feser argues the principle is more than a good bet, because denying it leads to absurdity. If things could happen for no reason, your experiences might have nothing to do with the world around you, and you couldn’t even say that was unlikely. So denying the principle means you can no longer trust your senses.

summary.heading: Pushing further: denying PSR undermines reasoning itself (pp. 149–150)
summary.body:
A stubborn critic might accept perceptual skepticism and retreat to a priori knowledge (logic, mathematics). Feser argues that this retreat offers no shelter.

Whenever we accept a claim as rationally justified, we assume two things: that we *have* a good reason for it (a justification), and that this reason is *why* we accept it (the cause of our assent). We think we are moved to believe precisely because the considerations are good. We also assume that our cognitive faculties track truth and the standards of logic.

If PSR is false, we have no grounds for any of these assumptions. What causes our assent might be unrelated to what our faculties deliver; what they deliver might be unrelated to truth or logic. We might believe everything we believe for no reason, while it merely *seems* — also for no reason — that we believe on good grounds. And this applies to any grounds for doubting PSR too. So **rejecting PSR is self-undermining**: it removes the possibility of rational inquiry, including the inquiry that led to rejecting PSR.

Feser’s extension can be set out as a chain. (1) Being rationally justified in a belief involves not only *having* a good reason but believing *because of* it. (2) It also assumes that our faculties deliver their verdicts because of truth and logical relations, not at random. (3) Both of these ‘because’ claims are explanatory claims. (4) If PSR is false, there is no guarantee that such explanatory connections hold in any given case, and no way to tell from the inside, since the feeling of having good grounds could itself arise for no reason. (5) So nobody who denies PSR can be justified in any belief, including the belief that PSR is false. That is what it means to call the denial self-undermining.
summary.takeaway: Rational belief assumes that our reasons actually cause our assent and that our faculties track truth — explanatory connections someone who denies PSR can no longer count on, even for the denial itself.
summary.deepDive:
The English word ‘reason’ does double duty, and Feser’s argument exploits that. When we ask for ‘the reason’ someone believes something, we might mean:

- **the justification**: the evidence or argument that supports the belief; or
- **the cause**: what actually produced the belief in the person’s mind.

In a rational belief, these coincide. The justification *is* the cause: you believe the bridge is safe *because* you read the engineer’s report, and the report is also what makes the belief reasonable. Now imagine someone who believes the bridge is safe because a coin flip told him so, and who happens to be right. He has a true belief, but it is not rationally held, because what caused it has nothing to do with what would justify it.

Here is the thought experiment at the heart of the section. Suppose beliefs could arise **for no reason at all**, uncaused by any evidence or faculty. And suppose, also for no reason, they came with a vivid sense of conviction: ‘I see clearly that this follows.’ From the inside, a brute belief with brute conviction would be indistinguishable from a well-reasoned one. If PSR is false, nothing rules this out. You could never be sure your belief is caused by your reasons rather than merely *accompanied* by a feeling that it is.

This is why retreating to a priori knowledge offers no refuge. Logic and mathematics are known by reasoning, and reasoning is exactly what has been compromised. The deliverances of our faculties might have ‘nothing to do with truth or standards of logic’ (to paraphrase Feser), and we couldn’t tell.

Then comes the turn that makes the position **self-undermining** rather than just uncomfortable. The critic’s own case against PSR is a set of beliefs held for reasons. If PSR is false, those beliefs too might be caused by nothing related to their merits. So the critic has no justified way to hold his conclusion. This is not a claim that denying PSR is *self-contradictory*. It is a claim that no one could ever be *justified* in denying it.

This section completes the support for steps 4–5. A frequent confusion is to think the critic can restrict PSR to the mind: ‘explanations hold in my reasoning, just not for the existence of the universe.’ But what principled line separates the two? That question is exactly what Della Rocca presses in the next sections.

checks.q: What two things does Feser say we suppose whenever we accept a claim as rationally justified?
options: That we have a reason for it, and that this reason is what causes us to accept it
That the claim is necessarily true and self-evident
That others agree with it and experts endorse it
That it is observable and repeatable
checks.explanation: A reason functions as both justification and cause. We also assume our faculties track truth and logic. PSR’s denial threatens both assumptions.

checks.q: Why doesn’t retreating to a priori knowledge rescue someone who denies PSR?
options: Because a priori knowledge doesn’t exist
Because mathematics depends on perception
Because logic is merely conventional
Because without PSR even a priori beliefs might be caused by factors unconnected to our reasons or to truth
checks.explanation: The problem is not specific to the senses. It concerns the connection between any belief and its grounds, which PSR’s denial leaves unsecured.

checks.q: A friend says: ‘I deny PSR, but I’m confident my arguments are sound.’ What is Feser’s point against him?
options: His confidence is unjustified, since on his own view the sense of having good grounds might itself arise for no reason
His arguments must be formally invalid
He must secretly be a theist
PSR applies only to physical events, so his confidence is fine
checks.explanation: The denial is self-undermining. It removes any assurance that the friend’s conviction is produced by his arguments’ merits.

summary.plain: It gets worse for the denier: you couldn’t trust your own thinking either. Believing something for good reasons means those reasons are what actually produce your belief. If things can happen for no reason, your beliefs — including the belief that the principle is false — might have popped up for no reason while merely feeling justified.

summary.heading: Science presupposes PSR: why brute-fact laws explain nothing (pp. 150–151)
summary.body:
J. L. Mackie and Bertrand Russell held that we can have real explanations, including scientific ones, without PSR. We explain phenomena by laws, those laws by deeper laws, and perhaps reach a most fundamental level of laws that is simply a **brute fact** — true, but with no explanation at all.

Feser calls this incoherent. Suppose I say a book stays off the floor because it rests on a shelf, but the shelf’s staying up has no explanation whatsoever. Have I explained the book’s position? The shelf, by hypothesis, has no tendency of its own to stay aloft — it just does, brutely — so it has no such tendency to pass on to the book. The ‘explanation’ is an illusion. Giving the book a brute tendency of its own does not help; that merely moves the illusion somewhere else.

Likewise, if law C is explained by law B, and B by law A, but A is a brute fact, then nothing about A or beyond A accounts for its operation, so A has nothing to impart to B or C. A regress of laws ending in a brute fact is as incoherent as an instrument that is not the instrument of anything. A series of ever-deeper laws works like the **hierarchical causal series** of the earlier chapters: the lower members only transmit what they derive from above.

The point generalizes beyond shelves and laws. Whenever something explains only by passing along what it has received — a borrowed tendency, a borrowed power, a borrowed explanatory force — the chain as a whole explains nothing unless it ends in something that has what it passes along *in its own right*. That is the logic of the hierarchical series in chapters 1, 2, and 4, now applied to explanation itself.
summary.takeaway: If the most fundamental laws are brute facts, they have nothing to impart to the laws they supposedly explain, so explanation by a hierarchy of laws ending in a brute fact is an illusion.
summary.deepDive:
The key word in this section is **impart**. When a higher-level law is explained by a deeper one, what exactly does the deeper law contribute?

Take a real-world chain. Kepler’s laws say planets move in ellipses. Newton’s law of gravitation explains *why* they do: the ellipses are what gravity produces in a two-body system. General relativity, in turn, explains why Newton’s law holds as well as it does. At each step the deeper law does not just *describe* more; it accounts for the shallower one. The explanatory force flows downward: the shallower law holds *because* the deeper one does.

Now suppose the chain stops at a law A that is a brute fact: there is nothing about A, and nothing beyond A, in virtue of which A holds. What does A have to pass down? Nothing. It has no explanatory force of its own to give. Everything below A inherits exactly what A has, which is no explanation. So the apparent explanations of B and C were never real explanations of why things happen. They were a set of conditionals — *if* A holds, then B, *if* B, then C — hanging from nothing.

Feser’s book and shelf is the vivid version. The book is ‘explained’ by the shelf only if the shelf really has a tendency to stay up. A shelf floating brutely has no such tendency, so the book’s position is not explained either. His parenthetical point is subtle and worth noticing: you can’t fix this by giving the *book* a brute tendency of its own, because then the book’s position rests on a brute fact, and the illusion has merely moved.

A course illustration: a train of carriages rolling along a track. Each carriage is pulled by the one in front. Lengthen the train as much as you like; without an engine, no carriage moves. A regress of laws is like this, and it is the same structure as the **hierarchical (per se) series** of earlier chapters: stick, stone, and hand. Hence Feser’s image of an effect produced by an instrument that is not the instrument of anything.

This section supports step 6, that there is no principled way to deny PSR while accepting genuine explanations in science, and step 7, that there are such explanations.

The usual confusion is to think ‘at least the higher levels are explained relative to the lower ones; only the bottom is unexplained.’ But an explanation that ultimately rests on nothing does not explain *why* anything happens. And note the fair comparison: the theist also thinks the regress ends. The question is whether it ends in something that explains itself or something that explains nothing.

checks.q: Which thinkers does Feser cite for the view that explanation can bottom out in brute-fact laws?
options: Leibniz and Clarke
Pruss and Koons
J. L. Mackie and Bertrand Russell
Ross and van Inwagen
checks.explanation: Mackie (The Miracle of Theism) and Russell (the Copleston debate) are cited. Pruss and Koons supply the perceptual-skepticism argument.

checks.q: Why does giving the book its own brute tendency to stay aloft not help?
options: Books cannot have tendencies
It violates the conservation of energy
Tendencies are unobservable
It only relocates the illusion rather than eliminating it
checks.explanation: A brute tendency in the book is just as unexplained as a brute shelf, so the problem has moved, not been solved.

checks.q: To what does Feser compare a regress of laws that ends in a brute fact?
options: A linear series of ancestors
An effect produced by an instrument that is not the instrument of anything
A proposition entailed by a necessary truth
A fallacy of composition
checks.explanation: A regress of laws is like a hierarchical causal series, in which lower members only transmit what they receive. Without a source there is nothing to transmit.

summary.plain: Some people say science explains things by laws of nature, and the deepest laws are just there, with no explanation. Feser says that doesn’t work. A shelf floating in midair for no reason wouldn’t explain why the book on it stays up, and in the same way, unexplained laws at the bottom can’t really explain anything built on top of them.

summary.heading: Della Rocca’s explicability arguments — and Feser’s extension (pp. 151–153)
summary.body:
Michael Della Rocca notes that even PSR’s critics routinely use **explicability arguments (EAs)**: arguments that we should deny some state of affairs obtains because, if it did, it would be inexplicable. Materialists defend reductive theories of consciousness on the grounds that consciousness would otherwise be inexplicable. Early modern thinkers rejected (a caricature of) substantial forms as insufficiently explanatory. Inductive reasoning rejects the idea that the future and unobserved will differ from the past and observed, because that would leave them inexplicable.

Using an EA does not by itself commit you to PSR. But apply the EA method to the question of why things *exist*, and you are committed to PSR, since PSR just is the claim that existence must be explained. Della Rocca gives the critic three options:

1. Some EAs are legitimate, but not EAs about the sheer existence of things.
2. No EAs are legitimate.
3. All EAs are legitimate, including those about existence.

Option 3 simply is accepting PSR. Option 2 is unavailable to anyone who uses EAs elsewhere — and EAs are standard in philosophy and science. Option 1 has no non-question-begging defense. Why allow EAs everywhere except existence? Saying it is a brute fact that some EAs work begs the question against PSR, which denies brute facts. Appealing to intuition fails too, since the critic’s own reliance on EAs elsewhere undercuts that particular intuition. Conclusion: we have no good reason to think anything is explicable unless everything is.

Feser pushes further. Della Rocca concedes that option 2, though deeply problematic, might not be strictly incoherent. Feser disagrees. Even a critic who rejects Della Rocca’s specific examples still accepts valid and inductively strong patterns of reasoning and rejects fallacies — precisely because logic embodies standards of intelligibility and explanatory adequacy. Many arguments *are* explanations: Aristotelian ‘explanatory demonstrations’ (all rational animals can use language; all men are rational animals; so all men can use language), arguments to the best explanation, and inductive reasoning generally. Giving up all EAs means giving up argument itself, which is incoherent for anyone who argues against PSR. And accepting argument in general while rejecting particular EAs is really option 1 again — which is arbitrary.
summary.takeaway: You cannot consistently demand explanations everywhere else yet exempt the existence of things, and giving up explanatory reasoning altogether means giving up argument itself.
summary.deepDive:
Della Rocca’s argument is a trap built from the critic’s own habits. Let’s examine its weakest-looking joint, option 1, and see why it doesn’t hold.

Option 1 says: explicability arguments (EAs) are fine in general, but not when the question is why things exist at all. To make this reasonable, the critic needs a *reason* for the exemption. What could it be?

- **‘It’s just a brute fact that EAs work in some domains and not others.’** But whether there are brute facts is the very point in dispute. PSR says there are none, so invoking one to defend the exemption assumes the critic’s conclusion. That is question-begging.
- **‘It’s intuitively obvious that existence needs no explanation.’** Della Rocca’s reply is ingenious. The critic trusts EAs elsewhere — about consciousness, about induction, about substantial forms. That practice reflects a strong, general intuition that inexplicability counts against a hypothesis. So the critic’s particular intuition that existence is exempt conflicts with the intuitions he relies on everywhere else, and his own practice gives reason to distrust it.

A course analogy: a detective who rules out every theory of a crime that would leave clues unexplained — then, when the last clue points somewhere inconvenient, declares that it ‘just happened.’ We would not call this caution; we would call it special pleading.

Now **Feser’s extension**, which targets option 2 (reject all EAs). Della Rocca allowed it might be coherent though problematic. Feser argues it is incoherent for anyone who argues. Why? Because logic itself embodies standards of intelligibility. Consider:

- An **explanatory demonstration**: all rational animals can use language; all men are rational animals; so all men can use language. The premises don’t just establish the conclusion; they show *why* it holds.
- **Inference to the best explanation**, which accepts hypotheses precisely because they explain.
- **Induction**, which, as Della Rocca notes, presupposes that things have explanations.

Strip all of these away and very little of argument remains. And if the critic keeps argument in general while rejecting only Della Rocca’s specific EAs, he has not taken option 2 at all; he is back in option 1, which is arbitrary.

This section grounds step 6 (no principled way to deny PSR while crediting genuine explanations) and step 7 (there are genuine explanations). The usual confusions: (a) thinking Della Rocca proves PSR from nothing, when it actually shows that the critic’s position is unstable given what he already accepts; (b) thinking EAs are a peculiarly philosophical move, when they are routine in science and ordinary inference.

checks.q: Why can’t the critic of PSR take Della Rocca’s option 3?
options: Because it is logically contradictory
Because accepting all explicability arguments, including those about existence, amounts to accepting PSR
Because no philosopher uses explicability arguments
Because it would require believing in substantial forms
checks.explanation: PSR just is the claim that existence must be explicable, so option 3 is PSR.

checks.q: Which of these is one of Della Rocca’s examples of an explicability argument?
options: Inductive reasoning’s rejection of the idea that the future will be unlike the past, since that would make the future inexplicable
Anselm’s ontological argument
Kant’s antinomies of pure reason
Hume’s fork
checks.explanation: Della Rocca’s examples include induction, reductive accounts of consciousness, and the early modern rejection of substantial forms.

checks.q: Feser holds that option 2 (reject all explicability arguments) is incoherent because…
options: Della Rocca proved it is
it contradicts quantum mechanics
it entails theism directly
rejecting all explanatory reasoning means rejecting argument itself, since logic embodies standards of intelligibility
checks.explanation: Explanatory demonstrations, inference to the best explanation, and induction are all explanatory. Giving them up leaves the critic unable to argue against PSR.

terms: Inference to (argument to) the best explanation
summary.plain: The philosopher Michael Della Rocca notices that everyone, including critics of the principle, argues that things must have explanations — in science, in everyday reasoning, in philosophy. It’s arbitrary to demand explanations everywhere except for why things exist at all. And refusing to reason this way altogether would mean giving up arguing, which the critic can’t do while arguing.

summary.heading: Contingent and necessary: no third option (p. 154)
summary.body:
With PSR established, Feser draws a basic division. A thing’s explanation lies either **in something outside it** or **in its own nature**.

- If outside, the thing is **contingent**: it depends on outside circumstances and would not exist if they failed to obtain.
- If in its own nature, the thing is **necessary**: something about what it is makes it impossible for it not to exist, so it depends on nothing else.

There is no third option. A thing explained neither by its nature nor by anything else would be explained by nothing, and PSR rules that out. And contingent things obviously exist: stones, trees, dogs, people.

Three clarifications make the division sharper. First, ‘contingent’ is defined by *where the explanation lies*, not by how long a thing lasts. An everlasting thing, such as a beginningless universe, would still be contingent if its existence were explained by something outside it. Second, ‘necessary’ does not mean ‘true by definition.’ It means that something about what the thing is excludes its not existing, and Stage 2 will spell out what such a nature must be. Third, the argument for ‘no third option’ is short but carries a lot of weight. An explanation lies inside the thing or outside it, and ‘neither’ just means ‘no explanation,’ which PSR has already ruled out. That is why the long defense of PSR matters. Without PSR, a third option, the brute fact, would be available, and the rest of the argument could never get started. With PSR, every real thing is either explained by another or self-explanatory. The remaining question is only whether *everything* could be of the first kind.
summary.takeaway: Given PSR, everything is either contingent (explained by another) or necessary (explained by its own nature); the brute-fact ‘third option’ is exactly what PSR excludes.
summary.deepDive:
This short section does more work than its length suggests, because it converts PSR into the tool the rest of the argument uses.

Start with the definitions and a worked example. A **candle flame** is contingent in Feser’s sense. Its existence is explained by things outside it: the wick, the wax, the oxygen in the room, the match that lit it, and the laws of combustion operating right now. Remove any of these and the flame is gone. That dependence on outside circumstances is what ‘contingent’ means here.

What would a **necessary** being be? Something whose existence is explained by what it is, so that its nature excludes its failing to exist. We have no everyday example of a thing like that, which is exactly why the chapter must argue for one. But we do have everyday examples of *attributes* explained by a nature. A triangle’s angles sum to two right angles because of what a triangle is. The necessary being would be the unique case where not just an attribute but *existence itself* follows from the nature.

Now the heart of the section: why there is **no third option**. Picture every existing thing sorted into bins by where its explanation is found:

1. Bin A: explanation outside it (contingent).
2. Bin B: explanation in its own nature (necessary).
3. Bin C: explanation nowhere (brute).

PSR, established in steps 1–8, says Bin C is empty. So step 9 can say that every existing thing is in A or B. Everything later is an elimination argument. Steps 11–13 and 15–16 show that Bin A cannot explain itself as a whole or explain any member’s present existence, so steps 14 and 17 conclude that Bin B is not empty.

Two nuances are worth noting. First, **contingent is not the same as temporary.** A beginningless, endless universe would still be in Bin A if it depended on anything outside itself. Second, **necessary is not the same as logically necessary.** Feser’s necessity is grounded in the nature of a thing (Stage 2: pure act, simplicity, essence = existence), not in the meanings of words.

Finally, step 10, that contingent things exist, is the most modest premise in the book. Stones, trees, dogs, and people plainly depend on outside conditions.

People often think ‘contingent’ means ‘I can imagine it not existing.’ But Feser’s definition is about real dependence, not imagination. As chapter 6 argues against Schrader, what we can picture is a poor guide to what is really possible.

checks.q: On Feser’s definition, what makes a thing contingent?
options: That it will someday cease to exist
That we can imagine it not existing
That its explanation lies in something outside it
That it is made of matter
checks.explanation: Contingency concerns where a thing’s explanation lies, not its duration, imaginability, or materiality.

checks.q: By this chapter’s definitions, could a universe with no beginning still be contingent?
options: No, because anything beginningless is necessary
Only if it will also end
Only if it is finite in size
Yes, because contingency concerns whether its explanation lies outside it, not how long it lasts
checks.explanation: A beginningless universe that depends on outside conditions is still contingent. That is why Feser can grant an infinite past.

summary.plain: Once we accept that everything has an explanation, there are only two options for any thing. Either it is explained by something else (Feser calls this ‘contingent’), or it is explained by its own nature (he calls this ‘necessary’). ‘Explained by nothing at all’ is exactly what the principle rules out.

summary.heading: Could it be contingent all the way down? (pp. 154–155)
summary.body:
Suppose every contingent thing is caused by an earlier contingent thing, back to infinity. The details can vary: a beginningless universe in which A was caused by B, B by C, and so on forever; or an endless cycle of universes, each beginning with a Big Bang produced by the Big Crunch of the one before; or a beginningless **multiverse** in which universes branch off from other universes. The details don’t matter. Each version is an infinite series of contingent things, and Feser grants for argument’s sake that such a series is possible.

It can then seem that everything is explained without any necessary being, since each member is explained by the one before it. Hume draws exactly this conclusion in his *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion*. Feser replies that this is an illusion: some things that need explaining remain unexplained.

Why does Feser grant the infinite regress instead of arguing, as the kalam argument does, that an infinite past is impossible? Partly because he doesn’t need to deny it: the rationalist proof, like the Aristotelian and Thomistic proofs, never rested on a claim that the world had a beginning. And partly because granting it makes the argument stronger. If a necessary being is required *even on the assumption* of a beginningless universe, a cyclic cosmos, or an eternal multiverse, then no future discovery about the age or shape of the universe can touch the conclusion. The scenarios are deliberately varied to show that the argument doesn’t care about the physical details. All that matters is that each is some variation on an infinite series of contingent things.
summary.takeaway: Feser grants, for argument’s sake, any beginningless series of contingent things — one universe, endless cycles, or a multiverse — and then argues that Hume is wrong to think such a series leaves nothing to explain.
summary.deepDive:
This section sets up the opponent’s best case, so it pays to state that case as strongly as Hume did.

In his *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion* (Part IX), Hume suggests something like this. Suppose I show you the particular cause of each of twenty particles of matter. It would be unreasonable for you then to ask what caused the whole twenty, since the ‘whole’ is just the twenty particles grouped together by an act of the mind. Explain each, and you have explained all. Apply this to an infinite series: each state of the universe is caused by the one before, so each is explained, and nothing is left over. On this view a necessary being is an unneeded extra.

Notice how much Feser concedes. He does not say an infinite past is impossible. He lays out three versions:

- **A single beginningless universe**, in which A is caused by B, B by C, and so on forever back.
- **An endless cycle**, in which our universe began with a Big Bang, but that Big Bang came from the Big Crunch of an earlier universe, which had its own Big Bang, and so on without a first.
- **A beginningless multiverse**, in which universes branch off from other universes, with no first universe.

Then he adds that exactly how the details go doesn’t matter. The point is structural: each is an infinite series of contingent things.

A thought experiment helps. Imagine a physicist announces tomorrow that our universe is one link in an infinite chain of cycles. Does the rationalist proof lose anything? No. Feser has already granted that. Compare the **kalam argument**, which would be in trouble, because it needs a beginning. This is one of the most practically important features of Feser’s approach: its conclusion is insulated from cosmology.

How does this feed the formal argument? Step 11 begins with a concession: *even if* each contingent thing were explained by an earlier one, back to infinity. This section supplies that ‘even if.’ The next sections supply the ‘still unexplained’ part.

People often think any argument for a first cause is about a *first moment in time*, so an infinite past refutes it. That is the most common confusion about cosmological arguments generally. Feser’s arguments concern dependence (why there are contingent things, and what keeps each one existing now), which an infinite past leaves untouched. In Scholastic terms, a series going back in time is a *per accidens* series and could be infinite. What cannot be infinite without a first member is the series of present dependence, the kind the next sections examine.

checks.q: Why does Feser grant that an infinite series of contingent things is possible?
options: Because he believes the universe is infinitely old
Because the argument doesn’t depend on a beginning, and granting one shows the conclusion survives any cosmology
Because Aquinas proved the past is infinite
Because PSR requires infinite regresses
checks.explanation: The concession costs nothing and makes the argument immune to discoveries about the universe’s age.

checks.q: Which philosopher concluded that an infinite series of contingent causes needs no necessary being?
options: Samuel Clarke
G. W. Leibniz
David Hume
Robert Koons
checks.explanation: Hume draws this conclusion in the Dialogues. Leibniz and Clarke are the ones who reply that the series itself needs explaining.

summary.plain: Could everything be explained by something else, in a chain going back forever — an infinitely old universe, or endless cycles of universes? Feser allows this for the sake of argument. The philosopher David Hume thought such a chain would explain everything with no need for God, and Feser sets out to show that Hume was wrong.

summary.heading: The Leibniz–Clarke point: why does the series exist at all? — and the composition charge (pp. 155–156)
summary.body:
The first reply comes from Leibniz and Samuel Clarke. Even if every member is caused by an earlier member, we can still ask why the **series itself** exists, because the series is just as contingent as its members. It could have failed to exist, so why doesn’t it?

(In a footnote Feser warns against the famous framing ‘why is there something rather than nothing?’ It can suggest that there *could* have been nothing at all, and the arguments of this book imply otherwise: what is purely actual, simple, subsistent existence itself, and absolutely necessary could not have failed to exist. The better question is **why there are any contingent things at all**.)

Critics say the question commits the **fallacy of composition**. Each stone in a pile may weigh less than an ounce without the whole pile weighing less than an ounce, so perhaps a series of contingent members need not itself be contingent. As Feser noted in chapter 4, reasoning from parts to whole is only sometimes fallacious; it depends on the feature involved. It fails for weight, but works for color: if every Lego block is red, whatever you build from them is red. Contingency behaves like color. Three stones are no less contingent than one, and three million no less than three. In fact, collections are **doubly contingent**: each stone depends on things like the laws of physics keeping its atoms together, and the collection depends on that *plus* the stones being gathered as they are. It is silly to think the collection of all contingent things would suddenly become non-contingent.
summary.takeaway: The whole series of contingent things is itself contingent — contingency, like color and unlike weight, carries from parts to whole — so its existence still needs explaining.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is that **part-to-whole reasoning is valid for some properties and invalid for others**, and that contingency is on the valid side.

Take the two stock examples slowly.

- **Weight:** each pebble weighs less than an ounce; the pile weighs ten pounds. The inference ‘each part is light, so the whole is light’ fails, because weight *adds up*: the whole’s weight is the sum of the parts’ weights, and sums can exceed any part.
- **Color:** each Lego brick is red; the wall is red. The inference succeeds, because the wall’s color just is the color of its bricks. Combining red things doesn’t produce some new, non-red color.

So what kind of property is **contingency**? Contingency is *dependence on outside conditions*. What happens when you combine dependent things? You don’t cancel their dependence; you add to it. Feser’s stones make this vivid. One stone depends on physical laws keeping its atoms together. A collection of three depends on that for each stone, *and* on the three being gathered in just this way. The collection is **doubly contingent**. Scaling up to three million, or to all contingent things there are, only multiplies the dependencies. At no point does independence suddenly appear.

A course test for spotting the difference: ask whether combining the parts could *remove* the feature. Adding pebbles removes lightness; adding red bricks can’t remove redness; adding dependent things can’t remove dependence.

Two further nuances. First, Feser reuses this reply from chapter 4 (the red Lego wall). There he also noted that the Thomistic proof never needed a claim about the universe as a whole, and the same will be true of this chapter’s second route. Second, his footnote reframes the famous question. ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’ suggests that nothing at all was a real possibility, while the arguments of the book imply that a purely actual, necessary being could not have failed to exist. The better question is **why there are any contingent things at all**.

This section secures the core of step 11: even granting an infinite chain of immediate causes, the series’ existence remains to be explained, because the series is as contingent as its members, if not more so.

People often think Feser claims that *every* part-to-whole inference is valid. He doesn’t. He claims only that this one is, because of the kind of property contingency is. Others think the ‘series’ is a mere mental grouping, as Hume suggested. But the question ‘why are there any contingent things?’ is not about an arbitrary grouping. It is about the real fact that dependent things exist at all.

checks.q: Why is contingency ‘more like color than weight’?
options: Because a collection of contingent things is no less dependent than its members, and in fact more so
Because contingency can be observed, like color
Because color and contingency are both subjective
Because weight is itself contingent
checks.explanation: Combining dependent things adds dependencies rather than removing them. Weight, by contrast, sums and so doesn’t transfer from parts to whole.

checks.q: What question does Feser suggest in place of ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’
options: Why is there a universe rather than a multiverse?
Why did the Big Bang happen?
Why are there any contingent things at all?
Why is there anything we can know?
checks.explanation: The ‘nothing’ framing implies nothingness was possible, which the arguments deny. The real question concerns contingent things.

checks.q: Someone says, ‘Asking why the whole exists is illegitimate, since only the parts need explaining.’ Which reply fits Feser?
options: Wholes never need explaining, so the objector is right
The whole is just as contingent as its parts (doubly so) and could have failed to exist, so its existence needs explaining
Only necessary beings have parts
The whole is identical to God
checks.explanation: The Leibniz–Clarke point: the series could have failed to exist, so its existence calls for explanation.

summary.plain: Even an endless chain of dependent things is itself dependent: it could have failed to exist, so why does it exist? Critics say you can’t reason from parts to whole, and sometimes that’s true (light pebbles can make a heavy pile). But it works for some features, like color, and dependence is one of them: a pile of dependent things is, if anything, more dependent.

summary.heading: The geometry books, and why a contingent ‘outside cause’ only passes the buck (pp. 156–158)
summary.body:
Against Hume, Feser denies that finding an immediate cause for each member explains everything. He borrows Leibniz’s example of an infinite series of geometry books, each copied from an earlier one. Every book has an immediate cause, yet obvious questions remain. Why does the series have this content? Why geometry, rather than Shakespeare, a coloring book, or a car-repair manual copied forever?

Similarly, even a beginningless series of contingent things leaves us asking why it consists of these kinds of things — stones, trees, dogs, people, planets, stars, galaxies — rather than others, and why the universe, the cycle of universes, or the multiverse is governed by these laws and not different ones. Answering such questions requires something beyond the series.

Could that ‘something beyond’ be itself contingent? Then it needs a cause too, and so does any further contingent cause. Positing an infinite higher-order series of contingent causes only relocates the problem, since everything that pushed us beyond the first series applies equally to the second, a third, a fourth — and even to an infinite series of infinite series. Each move just **passes the explanatory buck**. So, as Leibniz and Clarke concluded, given PSR there must be a cause outside the contingent series which is **necessary**: something that by its nature could not fail to exist and depends on nothing. Only this can end the regress of explanation.

The two replies in this section do different jobs. The geometry-books point shows that a regress of immediate causes leaves specific facts unexplained — content, kinds, laws — so something beyond the series is needed. The buck-passing point shows that this ‘something beyond’ cannot itself be contingent, since any contingent explainer just restarts the regress one level up. Together they force the conclusion: a necessary being.
summary.takeaway: Immediate causes for every member leave the series’ content, kinds, and laws unexplained, and any contingent explainer outside the series just restarts the regress, so only a necessary being ends it.
summary.deepDive:
Let’s build the buck-passing argument step by step, since it is the engine of steps 11–14.

**Level 1.** Call the infinite series of contingent things S1: stars, stones, dogs, universes, whatever. Why does S1 exist, with these kinds of things and these laws? Leibniz’s geometry books show that citing each member’s immediate cause doesn’t answer this. Each copy was copied from an earlier copy, but why is the series about *geometry* — and not Shakespeare, a coloring book, or an auto-repair manual? The same question applies to our universe: why stones, trees, dogs, planets, and galaxies, and why these laws rather than others?

**Level 2.** Suppose someone answers: ‘S1 is caused by C1, something outside it — a universe-generator, say — which is itself contingent.’ Being contingent, C1 has its explanation outside itself, in some C2, and so on. Now we have a new series S2 = {C1, C2, C3, …}. Every reason we had for asking about S1 applies to S2: it could have failed to exist, and it has a specific character. We have not answered the question; we have moved it.

**Level n.** Keep going: S3 explains S2, S4 explains S3. Even take the ultimate move: an infinite series of infinite series. Gather the whole thing up. It is still made entirely of contingent members, and so, by the reasoning of the previous section, it is still contingent. The question returns with full force.

A course analogy fixes the idea: an endless line of people, each borrowing a dollar from the next. The line can be infinitely long, and you can add a second line of ‘higher’ lenders; no dollar ever turns up unless someone has one that isn’t borrowed. Borrowed existence, like borrowed money, cannot explain itself.

So, as Leibniz and Clarke concluded, the only way to end the regress is a cause that is **not contingent**: something that by its nature could not fail to exist and depends on nothing. This is steps 12–14. Step 12 states the buck-passing problem, step 13 concludes that no contingent thing or series can explain why there are contingent things, and step 14 infers, by PSR and the dichotomy of step 9, that a necessary being is the cause.

People often think this argument claims that ‘infinite regresses are impossible.’ It doesn’t. It grants infinite regresses and argues that a regress made *entirely of contingent members*, however long or however nested, leaves contingent existence unexplained. Others think the necessary being is posited to explain the *first* event in time. It is posited to explain why the whole series, of whatever length, exists at all.

checks.q: What question does the infinite library of geometry books leave unanswered?
options: Who printed the first copy
How many copies there are
Whether paper is contingent
Why the series contains geometry rather than some other content
checks.explanation: There is no first copy in the scenario. The point is that immediate causes don’t explain the series’ specific content.

checks.q: Why doesn’t an infinite series of infinite series of contingent causes finally explain contingent existence?
options: Because it is too large to exist
Because the same reasons that made the first series insufficient apply to it, since it is still contingent
Because PSR forbids infinite series
Because such series must have a beginning in time
checks.explanation: Nesting contingent series doesn’t produce independence. The reasons that pushed us beyond the first series apply at every level.

summary.plain: Picture an endless chain of books, each copied from an earlier one. Every copy has a cause, but that doesn’t explain why the books are about geometry rather than anything else. And pointing to some other dependent thing outside the chain just starts the same question over, so only something that depends on nothing can end it.

summary.heading: A second route: what keeps a thing in existence right now? (p. 158)
summary.body:
Feser stresses that we need not argue, as Leibniz and Clarke did, from the collection of contingent things as a whole. Grant again an infinite past. We can still ask of **any particular contingent thing why it continues to exist at this moment** rather than being annihilated. Pointing to whatever produced it in the past does not answer this. Because it is contingent, nothing in its nature guarantees its existence — and that is as true now, and at every moment, as it was when it first came to be.

So PSR requires something that causes it to exist here and now. If that cause is contingent, the same question arises about it, producing a regress of **simultaneous** causes with the same problems as the temporal regress: the simultaneous series taken as a whole needs an outside explanation just as much as the thing we started with. Only a cause that exists necessarily, by its own nature, can end this regress. This route reaches a necessary being without any talk of ‘the universe as a whole’ or the multiverse — just from the present existence of one ordinary contingent thing.

The phrase ‘rather than being annihilated’ is doing real work. Ordinarily we think of things perishing by being broken down into other things: a log burns to ash. Annihilation would be more radical — the thing simply ceasing to be, with nothing left over. The here-and-now question is why a contingent thing’s existence is *preserved* from moment to moment at all, and that question arises for anything whose nature doesn’t include its existence. In chapter 6 Feser develops the corresponding doctrine of divine conservation.
summary.takeaway: Whatever produced a contingent thing in the past, its existence right now needs a present, simultaneous cause, and a regress of contingent sustainers ends only in a necessary being.
summary.deepDive:
The key to this route is separating two questions we usually run together:

1. **How did this thing come to be?** (the cause of its *becoming*)
2. **Why does it exist right now?** (the cause of its *being*)

For a house, the first answer is the builders. But the builders can leave, retire, or die, and the house stands. Its present existence depends on other things acting *now*: the strength of its materials, the forces holding its molecules together, and whatever keeps those in existence. Feser’s point is that for any contingent thing, question 2 has to be answered separately, because its nature doesn’t guarantee its existence at this moment any more than it did at its first moment. Being contingent is not something a thing grows out of.

Try a thought experiment with chapter 4’s dog, Fido. Fido’s parents explain how Fido came to be. But Fido exists *now*, and nothing in what a dog is guarantees that dogs exist. So what accounts for Fido’s existence at this instant? Something acting simultaneously: his cells, their molecules, the physical conditions sustaining them, and so on. If each of these is contingent, then each needs its own present sustainer, and we have a regress of **simultaneous** causes.

Feser says this regress has the same problem as the temporal one. Taken as a whole, the series of present sustainers is contingent and needs an explanation outside itself. It is also a *hierarchical* series, like the hand, stick, and stone, in which lower members have their power only from higher ones. So it must terminate in something that exists **of its own nature**. That is what steps 15–17 formalize: step 15 says persistence needs a simultaneous cause, step 16 that an infinite chain of contingent sustainers is still an unexplained contingent series, and step 17 that the only remaining explanation is a necessary being as simultaneous cause.

Why is this route important? Because it never mentions the universe as a whole, the multiverse, or the Big Bang, so the fallacy-of-composition charge has nothing to attack, and it is indifferent to whether time had a beginning.

People often reply that things just keep existing ‘by default’ unless something destroys them, perhaps citing inertia or conservation laws. But that default is exactly what needs explaining for something whose nature doesn’t include existence. Laws that describe how things persist presuppose that the things exist; they are themselves contingent (see chapter 1 on inertia). Feser’s question goes deeper: why is there, at this moment, anything for such laws to describe?

checks.q: Why doesn’t a contingent thing’s past cause explain its present existence?
options: Because past causes no longer exist
Because time is unreal
Because nothing in its contingent nature entails its existence now, any more than at its first moment
Because causes must always be larger than their effects
checks.explanation: Its contingency persists at every moment, so its present existence needs a present explanation.

checks.q: What advantage does the here-and-now route have over the Leibniz–Clarke route?
options: It needs no claim about the universe or the series of contingent things as a whole
It proves that the universe began
It doesn’t depend on PSR
It makes Stage 2 unnecessary
checks.explanation: It starts from one particular thing existing now, so composition worries don’t arise. It still depends on PSR and still needs Stage 2.

summary.plain: There’s a second way in that doesn’t mention the whole universe at all. Take any ordinary thing, like a mug. Whatever made it in the past, something has to account for its existing right now, and if that something is also dependent, the question repeats. The chain of present support has to end in something that exists on its own.

summary.heading: How the rationalist proof complements the earlier proofs (p. 159)
summary.body:
This second route echoes the Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, and Thomistic proofs, and Feser presents the proofs as complementing one another. The *deep reason* things are contingent — needing outside causes both to come into being and to go on existing — is that they are mixtures of actuality and potentiality, are made of parts, and have an essence distinct from their existence. The *deep reason* such things require causes at all is that otherwise they would be unintelligible, and PSR tells us everything is intelligible.

So the basic idea can be developed in several ways: (1) argue that the collection of contingent things needs an outside cause; (2) argue that any particular contingent thing needs a cause at every moment; or (3), borrowing from the other proofs, argue that anything with potentiality, parts, or a real essence–existence distinction needs a cause at every moment. Whichever route we take, the rationalist proof starts by defending PSR and ends, inescapably, at an **absolutely necessary being** — God.

This claim of complementarity is unusual. Critics often treat the classic arguments for God as rivals, as if a defender must choose one and stake everything on it. Feser presents them as illuminating one another. The Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, and Thomistic proofs identify the metaphysical *structure* that makes ordinary things dependent: potency, parts, and an essence distinct from existence. The rationalist proof identifies the *principle* that makes dependence demand an explanation: intelligibility. Someone who resists one argument’s starting point may find another’s more compelling, and each argument’s conclusion reinforces the others’.
summary.takeaway: The earlier proofs show why things are contingent (potency, parts, essence ≠ existence), and PSR shows why contingent things must have causes, so the proofs reinforce one another.
summary.deepDive:
Feser offers three ways to develop the rationalist proof. To see them clearly, apply all three to one ordinary object, a cat sitting on a windowsill.

**Route 1 (Leibniz–Clarke, collection):** The cat is one member of the vast collection of contingent things — cats, stars, galaxies, universes. Why does this collection exist at all, with these kinds and these laws? No contingent member or series can answer. So there must be a necessary cause of the whole. (Steps 11–14.)

**Route 2 (here-and-now, particular thing):** Forget the collection. Why does *this cat* exist at this moment? Its birth doesn’t explain its present existence, and a chain of contingent present sustainers only raises the same question again. So there must be a necessary sustaining cause. (Steps 15–17.)

**Route 3 (hybrid, borrowing from the earlier proofs):** The cat is a mixture of actuality and potentiality: it is actually on the windowsill and potentially on the floor. It is composite, made of organs, cells, and molecules, and of form and matter. And its essence (what a cat is) is distinct from its existence (that this cat is). Each of these features means it needs a cause at every moment.

Now the deeper point. Why are things contingent in the first place? Feser answers with the earlier chapters: because they are act–potency mixtures, composite, and essence–existence composites. That is the *metaphysical anatomy* of dependence. And why must dependent things have causes at all, rather than simply existing brutely? Because otherwise they would be unintelligible, and PSR says everything is intelligible. That is the *principle* behind the demand. The two halves need each other: the earlier proofs show what contingency consists in, and the rationalist proof shows why contingency requires an explanation.

This also previews Stage 2 (step 19). If contingency comes from potency, composition, and a distinction of essence and existence, then a necessary being must lack all three. In the other direction, whatever lacks all three is necessary.
