keyTerms.origin: Related to the ancient charge of self-refutation, as in Plato’s critique of Protagoras’ relativism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simply false: a self-undermining view might conceivably be true, but no one could be justified in believing it.

keyTerms.definition: Della Rocca’s term for arguing that some state of affairs does not obtain because, if it did, it would be inexplicable.
keyTerms.example: Materialists argue that consciousness must be physical because otherwise it would be inexplicable.
keyTerms.origin: Coined by Michael Della Rocca in ‘PSR’ (Philosophers’ Imprint, 2010).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inference to the best explanation: an EA rejects a scenario because it would be inexplicable, while IBE accepts the hypothesis that explains best.

keyTerms.definition: (1) Some EAs are legitimate, but not those about the sheer existence of things; (2) no EAs are legitimate; (3) all EAs are legitimate. Option 3 amounts to accepting PSR, option 2 is self-defeating, and option 1 is arbitrary or question-begging.
keyTerms.example: A critic who uses inductive reasoning cannot take option 2.
keyTerms.origin: Della Rocca (2010). Feser extends it by arguing that option 2 is incoherent, not merely problematic.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A simple dilemma: this is a trilemma, and the critic is pushed into the one option (1) that is arbitrary.

keyTerms.definition: Aristotelian term for a deductive argument whose premises give the reason why its conclusion is true, so that the argument is also an explanation.
keyTerms.example: All rational animals can use language; all humans are rational animals; so all humans can use language.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s Posterior Analytics: demonstration of the reasoned fact (why something is so), in Scholastic terms demonstratio propter quid.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Demonstration quia (that something is so): it proves a fact from its effects or signs without giving the reason why.

keyTerms.definition: A chain of explanations by ever more fundamental laws of nature. Feser argues it must end in something self-explanatory, not a brute fact, or none of it explains anything.
keyTerms.example: Law C explained by B, B by A — if A is brute, B and C are explained by nothing.
keyTerms.origin: Greek nomos, ‘law,’ plus logos, ‘account’: a regress of laws explaining laws.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Temporal causal regress: a nomological regress is hierarchical (laws operating now through deeper laws), not a chain of past events.

keyTerms.definition: Wrongly inferring that a whole has a property because its parts do. Whether such an inference is fallacious depends on the property.
keyTerms.example: Stones under an ounce each don’t make a pile under an ounce (fallacious), but red Lego bricks do make a red wall (valid).
keyTerms.origin: A traditional informal fallacy, catalogued since Aristotle’s Sophistical Refutations.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Fallacy of division (whole to parts). Also contrast valid part-to-whole reasoning about color-like properties.

keyTerms.definition: Feser’s point that a collection of contingent things depends both on each member’s existence and on the members being arranged or gathered as they are.
keyTerms.example: A pile of stones depends on each stone’s atoms holding together and on the stones being gathered in one place.
keyTerms.origin: Feser’s own description of collections in chapter 5.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Merely contingent: an individual stone depends on one set of conditions, a collection on those conditions plus its assembly.

keyTerms.definition: The hypothesis, granted for argument’s sake, that each contingent thing was caused by an earlier one without beginning — a beginningless universe, endless Big Bang/Big Crunch cycles, or a beginningless multiverse.
keyTerms.example: Hume’s view in the Dialogues that such a series needs no further explanation.
keyTerms.origin: Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, Part IX; echoed by modern cyclic and multiverse cosmologies.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The kalam argument’s claim that an actual infinite is impossible: Feser grants the infinite series for argument’s sake.

keyTerms.definition: Answering a request for explanation by pointing to something that needs the same kind of explanation, which relocates the problem without solving it.
keyTerms.example: Explaining one infinite contingent series by a second, higher-order contingent series.
keyTerms.origin: From the English idiom ‘pass the buck’ (originally a marker passed between players in poker). The phrase is Feser’s.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Explaining: passing the buck postpones the explanation to something needing the same kind of explanation.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that keeps something in existence here and now, as distinct from a cause that produced it in the past.
keyTerms.example: Feser’s second route: what keeps this stone existing at this moment, rather than being annihilated?
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic causa essendi (cause of being), as opposed to causa fiendi (cause of becoming). Linked to the doctrine of divine conservation.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Cause of becoming: what produced a thing in the past, not what keeps it existing now.

keyTerms.definition: Existing with no unactualized potential whatsoever. Required of a necessary being, since having potentials would make it depend on an actualizer. Also called ‘pure act’; the adjective is ‘purely actual.’
keyTerms.example: The Unmoved Mover of chapter 1.
keyTerms.origin: Latin actus purus; Aristotle’s energeia (actuality). Chapter 1’s Unmoved Mover.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Maximal activity or busyness: pure act means lacking any unrealized potential, not doing a great many things.

keyTerms.definition: Having no parts of any kind — physical, metaphysical, or logical. Required of a necessary being, since a composite would depend on whatever combines its parts. The adjectives are ‘simple’ and ‘noncomposite.’
keyTerms.example: The One of chapter 2.
keyTerms.origin: Latin simplex, ‘without fold’; Plotinus’ One. Chapter 2’s conclusion.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being easy to understand: divine simplicity means having no composition of any kind, not conceptual ease.

keyTerms.definition: That whose essence just is existence, rather than an essence that merely receives existence. Required of a necessary being.
keyTerms.example: The first cause of chapter 4.
keyTerms.origin: Aquinas’ ipsum esse subsistens, ‘subsistent being itself.’ Chapter 4’s conclusion.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A being that merely has existence permanently: God does not have existence, he is existence.

keyTerms.definition: The explanans is what does the explaining; the explanandum is what gets explained.
keyTerms.example: Explanandum: the ground is wet this morning. Explanans: it rained last night.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘that which explains’ and ‘that which is to be explained’; standard in philosophy of science since Hempel and Oppenheim.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Premise / conclusion: not every argument is an explanation. Explanans and explanandum concern why something is so, not merely that it is.

keyTerms.definition: The single proposition formed by conjoining every true contingent proposition. It is the basis of the objection (Ross, van Inwagen, Rowe) that PSR cannot be satisfied or leads to modal collapse.
keyTerms.example: ‘Grass is green and Paris is in France and…’ for every contingent truth.
keyTerms.origin: James Ross (1969), Peter van Inwagen (1983), William Rowe (1997). Often abbreviated BCCF, for ‘big conjunctive contingent fact.’
keyTerms.confuseWith: The collection of contingent things: that is concrete and is treated by Feser’s series argument, while the objection targets an abstract proposition.

keyTerms.definition: The Thomist view that an explanation must make its explanandum intelligible but need not logically entail it.
keyTerms.example: The sun’s gravity explains elliptical orbits, though other gravitational influences could have prevented them.
keyTerms.origin: Thomist understanding of PSR, backed by Pruss’ observation that scientific causal explanations generally do not entail their explananda.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The deductive-nomological model: it requires the explanandum to be deducible from laws plus conditions.

keyTerms.definition: The view, defended in chapter 3, that universals and propositions are real but exist only in the minds that entertain them, not in a Platonic realm.
keyTerms.example: Once concrete triangles and the minds that think of triangularity are explained, there is nothing left over to explain.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian-Thomistic ‘moderate realism’; defended in chapter 3.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Platonic realism: the view that universals and propositions exist in a third realm independent of all minds.

keyTerms.definition: Nothing more than commitment to PSR — the view that reality is intelligible through and through. It does not include innate ideas or the claim that all knowledge rests on a priori truths.
keyTerms.example: The proof is ‘rationalist’ in the way it treats brute facts, not in its epistemology.
keyTerms.origin: Latin ratio, ‘reason.’ Historically the early modern school of Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Rationalism as a theory of knowledge (innate ideas, a priori foundationalism): Feser adopts only the metaphysical commitment to PSR.

keyTerms.definition: The early modern cosmological argument, developed by Leibniz and Samuel Clarke, that even an infinite series of contingent things needs an explanation beyond itself, which can only be a necessary being.
keyTerms.example: Leibniz asks why an infinite series of copied geometry books contains geometry at all. Feser adopts this as his first route (steps 11–14).
keyTerms.origin: Leibniz, ‘On the Ultimate Origination of Things’ (1697); Clarke, A Demonstration of the Being and Attributes of God (1705).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The kalam argument: kalam argues from the universe’s beginning, while the Leibniz–Clarke argument works even with an infinite past.

keyTerms.definition: The claim that if every member of an infinite series is explained by its predecessor, the whole series is thereby explained, so nothing more is needed.
keyTerms.example: ‘Each universe in the cycle came from the Big Crunch of the one before, so everything is accounted for.’
keyTerms.origin: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part IX.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The fallacy-of-composition charge: that says the whole need not share the parts’ contingency, while Hume says the parts’ explanations exhaust the whole’s.

keyTerms.definition: A conclusion about all cases of a kind drawn from many observed cases. Feser grants PSR is as well supported inductively as anything, but says it is far more certain than any induction.
keyTerms.example: Every time we investigated a strange noise, it had a source, so strange noises have sources.
keyTerms.origin: Latin inductio, ‘a leading in’; Aristotle’s epagōgē.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Deductive proof: induction makes a conclusion probable, while deduction guarantees it if the premises are true.

keyTerms.definition: Probability grounded in the real tendencies and dispositions of things, not in our feelings of confidence. Pruss and Koons argue that without PSR it would have no basis.
keyTerms.example: A fair die’s one-in-six chance of a six comes from its shape and weighting.
keyTerms.origin: Modern philosophy of probability (propensity theories); used by Pruss.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Subjective probability (credence): how confident a person happens to be, which may not track anything real.

keyTerms.definition: Knowledge that does not depend on sense experience for its justification, such as logic and mathematics. It is where a PSR-denier might retreat after giving up perception.
keyTerms.example: Knowing that 7 + 5 = 12 without counting objects.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘from what comes before’ (experience); standardized by Kant.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Innate ideas: a priori knowledge need not be inborn. Feser accepts a priori reasoning while rejecting rationalist innatism.

keyTerms.term: Inference to (argument to) the best explanation
keyTerms.definition: Reasoning that accepts a hypothesis because it explains the evidence better than its rivals. Feser notes that such arguments obviously presuppose that things have explanations.
keyTerms.example: The detective concludes the butler did it because that best explains the muddy boots and the missing key.
keyTerms.origin: Named by Gilbert Harman (1965); C. S. Peirce’s ‘abduction.’
keyTerms.confuseWith: Explicability argument: IBE picks the best explanation, while an EA rejects scenarios that would leave things inexplicable.

keyTerms.definition: In Aristotelian philosophy, the principle that makes a thing the kind of substance it is and grounds its characteristic powers. Early moderns rejected (a caricature of) it as insufficiently explanatory, which is one of Della Rocca’s EA examples.
keyTerms.example: What makes this animal a dog, with a dog’s powers and tendencies, rather than a heap of particles.
keyTerms.origin: Latin forma substantialis; Aristotle’s morphē / eidos, as developed by the Scholastics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Shape: substantial form is not geometric shape but the organizing nature of a substance.

keyTerms.definition: The view that consciousness is nothing but physical processes. Its defenders often argue that consciousness would otherwise be inexplicable, which is an explicability argument.
keyTerms.example: ‘Pain just is a certain kind of neural firing, otherwise how could it fit into physics?’
keyTerms.origin: Twentieth-century philosophy of mind (identity theory, functionalism).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Eliminativism: reductionists say consciousness is real but physical, while eliminativists deny that some mental states exist at all.

keyTerms.definition: A cosmological scenario in which each universe begins with a Big Bang produced by the collapse (Big Crunch) of a previous one, with no first universe. Feser grants it for argument’s sake.
keyTerms.example: Universe 3 arises from the crunch of universe 2, which arose from universe 1’s crunch, and so on forever backward.
keyTerms.origin: Oscillating-universe models in twentieth-century cosmology.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A multiverse: a cyclic model has a succession of universes, while a multiverse has universes branching and coexisting.

keyTerms.definition: The hypothesis of many universes, with some branching off from others, possibly with no beginning. For Feser it is just one more variation on an infinite series of contingent things.
keyTerms.example: Universes bud off from a parent universe during its lifetime and carry on after it collapses.
keyTerms.origin: Contemporary cosmology and interpretations of quantum mechanics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A necessary being: however large or old, a multiverse is composite and changing, and so contingent.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which each member’s causal power at this moment depends on the member above it, so the series needs a first member with power of its own. Feser compares a regress of laws to such a series.
keyTerms.example: A hand moves a stick that moves a stone. Remove the hand and nothing moves, however many sticks there are.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic distinction between causes ordered per se (essentially) and per accidens (accidentally); chapter 1.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A linear (per accidens) series, such as a chain of ancestors, whose earlier members need not still exist or act.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that produces its effect only by virtue of power derived from another cause. An ‘instrument that is not the instrument of anything’ is Feser’s picture of incoherence.
keyTerms.example: The stick that moves the stone only because the hand moves it.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic causa instrumentalis; Aristotle’s examples of tools.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Principal cause: the source of the power, which acts through the instrument.

keyTerms.definition: The consequence that every truth is necessary, so that nothing could have been otherwise. Critics say PSR leads to it if explanations must entail what they explain.
keyTerms.example: If God’s necessary nature entailed that you are reading this now, you could not have been doing anything else.
keyTerms.origin: Contemporary analytic philosophy; the BCCF argument of Ross, van Inwagen, and Rowe.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Determinism: determinism says the past plus the laws fix the future, while modal collapse says every truth is absolutely necessary.

keyTerms.definition: Aristotle’s distinction between what a thing actually is and what it can become. Things that mix the two are contingent, according to chapter 5’s account of why things need causes. ‘Potential’ and ‘potentiality’ name the capacities; a ‘mixture of act and potency’ is anything that has both.
keyTerms.example: Water is actually liquid and potentially ice or steam.
keyTerms.origin: Greek energeia/entelecheia and dynamis; Latin actus and potentia.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Possibility in general: potency is a real capacity in a thing, not merely something one can imagine.

keyTerms.definition: Having parts of any kind, whether physical parts, form and matter, or essence and existence. A composite depends on whatever combines its parts, so it cannot be strictly necessary.
keyTerms.example: A tree has cells, which are made of molecules, which are held together by physical forces.
keyTerms.origin: Latin compositus, ‘put together’; Neo-Platonic proof, chapter 2.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Complicated: even a very simple-looking material thing is composite, and ‘simple’ here means ‘without parts,’ not ‘easy.’

keyTerms.definition: The Thomist thesis that, in everything but God, what a thing is (its essence) is really distinct from the fact that it is (its existence), so existence must be given to it by a cause.
keyTerms.example: Knowing what a T. rex is tells you nothing about whether any exist today.
keyTerms.origin: Aquinas, De ente et essentia; chapter 4.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The concept versus the object: the distinction is real in the thing, not just a difference between our idea and the thing.

keyTerms.definition: Something like a number, universal, or proposition that is not a concrete physical thing. For the Scholastic realist, it exists only in the minds that think it.
keyTerms.example: The number 2, triangularity, and the proposition that snow is white.
keyTerms.origin: Latin abstrahere, ‘to draw away’: what the intellect draws from concrete particulars.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Fictional object: abstract objects are real and grounded in minds, while fictional objects don’t exist.

keyTerms.definition: What a declarative sentence expresses: the content that can be true or false. The BCCF objection treats propositions as things needing explanation, and Thomists do not.
keyTerms.example: ‘Snow is white’ and ‘Schnee ist weiss’ express one proposition.
keyTerms.origin: Latin propositio, ‘a setting forth.’
keyTerms.confuseWith: Sentence: a sentence is a linguistic item in a particular language, while a proposition is what it means.

keyTerms.definition: A feature that many particular things can share. For Feser’s Scholastic realism, universals exist in particular things and in minds, not in a separate realm.
keyTerms.example: Triangularity, shared by every triangle drawn on every chalkboard.
keyTerms.origin: Latin universalis, ‘pertaining to all’; the medieval ‘problem of universals.’
keyTerms.confuseWith: A collection: triangularity is not the set of all triangles but what each triangle has.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas’ argument from possibility and necessity (Summa Theologiae I, q. 2, a. 3). Feser cites it for the distinction between things necessary through another, like angels, and a being necessary of itself.
keyTerms.example: Angels cannot die, yet they receive their existence, so they are necessary only through another.
keyTerms.origin: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae (1265–1274).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The rationalist proof: both reach a necessary being, but the Third Way reasons from things that can come to be and pass away, and is not framed around PSR.

keyTerms.definition: The idea of a thing that causes its own existence. It is incoherent in the efficient-cause sense, and Feser’s God is not a causa sui but self-explanatory.
keyTerms.example: Descartes and Spinoza spoke of God as causa sui, which, per ch7a, blurred cause and sufficient reason.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘cause of itself’; Descartes, Spinoza.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Self-explanatory: explanation by one’s own nature involves no potential being actualized.

keyTerms.definition: Applying a general rule to everything except the case one favors, without a principled reason. Critics accuse theists of it with ‘everything needs an explanation except God.’
keyTerms.example: ‘All players must follow the rules, except my team.’
keyTerms.origin: Originally a legal term for introducing new matter to avoid the force of an argument.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A principled distinction: God’s self-explanation rests on independently motivated contrasts (act/potency, simple/composite), not on exemption.

keyTerms.definition: Hume’s argument that because we can conceive of something beginning without a cause (or explanation), this is possible. Feser says conceiving A without conceiving its cause is not conceiving A as uncaused.
keyTerms.example: Picturing a coffee cup suddenly appearing on an empty table.
keyTerms.origin: Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40), I.iii.3; answered in chapter 1 with Anscombe.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Genuine conceivability of absence: imagining without the cause is not imagining that there is no cause, just as thinking of a trilateral isn’t denying it is a triangle.

keyTerms.definition: The obligation to support one’s position. Feser argues it lies on PSR’s critic to show how PSR can coherently be rejected, not on PSR’s defender, though the defender can meet a burden too.
keyTerms.example: Raising a puzzle about the big conjunction doesn’t discharge the critic’s burden of answering the reductio arguments.
keyTerms.origin: Latin onus probandi, from legal practice.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Refutation: shifting the burden of proof doesn’t refute a view. Feser both shifts the burden and gives positive arguments.

keyTerms.definition: An explanation that makes an outcome intelligible by showing it was probable given the laws and conditions, without entailing it. It is the obvious case of explanation without entailment.
keyTerms.example: Smoking explains a patient’s lung cancer even though not all smokers get cancer.
keyTerms.origin: Philosophy of science (Hempel’s inductive-statistical model).
keyTerms.confuseWith: No explanation: an event that is merely probable, not certain, is still explained.

keyTerms.definition: The conception of God shared by the major monotheistic traditions and philosophers like Aquinas: one, simple, immutable, eternal, purely actual, subsistent existence, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good, cause of all. It is the conclusion of step 26.
keyTerms.example: The God described at the end of every one of Feser’s five proofs.
keyTerms.origin: Term used by recent philosophers for the theism of Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, Maimonides, and Avicenna.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theistic personalism: the view of God as a very great person who changes and has parts, which Feser rejects.

keyTerms.definition: The view that God and the world are identical. Chapter 7 notes that if the universe really were self-explanatory and necessary, the result would be pantheism, not atheism.
keyTerms.example: ‘Nature itself is divine.’
keyTerms.origin: Greek pan, ‘all,’ plus theos, ‘god’; associated with Spinoza.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Classical theism: God sustains everything at every moment but is distinct from the world, as simple from composite and pure act from potency.

keyTerms.definition: The property of being understandable in principle, of having something that accounts for why a thing is and is as it is. ‘Intelligible’ is the adjective. The Thomist formula ‘everything is intelligible’ is one way of stating PSR.
keyTerms.example: The tides are intelligible once we know about the moon’s gravity, even to people who have never studied physics.
keyTerms.origin: Latin intelligibilis, ‘able to be understood’ (from intellegere, ‘to understand,’ literally ‘to read between’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being understood by us: something can be intelligible in itself even if no human has yet understood it, like the unsolved murder.

keyTerms.definition: A series of explanations or causes in which each member depends on a further one, without end. Feser grants such regresses for argument’s sake but argues that a regress of contingent explainers leaves something unexplained.
keyTerms.example: A beginningless chain of universes, each arising from the Big Crunch of the one before.
keyTerms.origin: Latin regressus, ‘a going back.’
keyTerms.confuseWith: Vicious circle: a regress goes on without end, while a circle loops back to its starting point. Both fail to explain, for different reasons.

keyTerms.definition: The necessity of a proposition whose denial is self-contradictory, or which is true simply because of the meanings of its terms. This is not the sense in which Feser calls God necessary. Statements true by definition are called ‘analytic.’
keyTerms.example: ‘All bachelors are unmarried’ is true by definition.
keyTerms.origin: Modern analytic philosophy’s ‘analytic’ or ‘conceptual’ necessity; discussed in chapters 6 and 7 in connection with Kant and the ontological argument.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphysical necessity: grounded in what a thing is (pure act, simplicity, essence = existence), not in the meanings of words.

keyTerms.definition: The necessity of a thing that cannot fail to exist because of what it is, here grounded in pure actuality, absolute simplicity, and the identity of essence and existence. It is stronger than merely conditional necessity but is not logical necessity.
keyTerms.example: God cannot fail to exist, not because ‘God exists’ is true by definition, but because there is no potential, part, or received existence in him that could fail.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian-Thomistic metaphysics; defended against Grayling’s false dichotomy in chapter 7.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conditional necessity: being a necessary condition for something else (as oxygen is for fire) does not by itself mean being unable to fail to exist.

keyTerms.definition: The valid argument form: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P. Steps 2–3, 4–5, and 6–7 each yield PSR by an argument of this shape.
keyTerms.example: If PSR were false, brute events would be common; brute events are not common; so PSR is not false.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘the mode that removes’ (it removes the antecedent by removing the consequent); Stoic and medieval logic.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Denying the antecedent (if P then Q; not P; so not Q), which is invalid.

keyTerms.definition: A deductively valid argument’s conclusion must be true if its premises are. An inductively strong argument’s premises make its conclusion probable. Feser says the critic of PSR still relies on both standards, which embody norms of intelligibility.
keyTerms.example: Valid: all men are rational animals, rational animals can use language, so men can use language. Strong: every observed raven is black, so the next raven will be black.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s logic (deduction); Bacon and Hume (induction).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Soundness: a sound argument is valid and also has true premises.

keyTerms.definition: A fundamental regularity or principle governing how physical things behave. Feser argues that a chain of laws explaining laws cannot end in a brute fact, and chapter 7 notes that on any account laws cannot be ultimate explanations.
keyTerms.example: Kepler’s laws of planetary motion, explained in turn by Newtonian gravitation.
keyTerms.origin: Early modern science (Descartes, Newton). Aristotelians treat laws as summaries of how substances behave given their natures.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A cause: a law describes or summarizes how things act and does not by itself make anything exist.

keyTerms.definition: Determinism: every event is fixed by prior conditions and laws. Indeterminism: some events, such as certain quantum events on many interpretations, are not so fixed. Feser argues that indeterminism is not unintelligibility, so it poses no threat to PSR.
keyTerms.example: The exact moment a radioactive atom decays is not fixed by prior conditions on standard interpretations, yet quantum theory explains why decays occur with the rate they do.
keyTerms.origin: Modern philosophy of science; debates over the interpretation of quantum mechanics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Uncaused or unexplained: an indeterministic event can still have a cause and an explanation.

keyTerms.definition: Unable to change. Immutability is the attribute of being changeless. What is purely actual cannot change, since change is the actualization of a potential.
keyTerms.example: Unlike water, which can freeze or boil, pure act has no potential to become anything it is not already.
keyTerms.origin: Latin immutabilis, ‘unchangeable’; chapters 1 and 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inert or lifeless: divine immutability means fullness of actuality, not frozen inactivity.

keyTerms.definition: Existing without beginning, end, or temporal succession. Eternity is the attribute. In the classical sense it follows from immutability, since time is the measure of change.
keyTerms.example: God does not live through a series of moments the way we pass from breakfast to lunch.
keyTerms.origin: Latin aeternus; Boethius’ definition: the complete possession all at once of unending life.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Everlasting: an everlasting thing lasts through all time, while an eternal being is outside temporal succession altogether.

keyTerms.definition: Not made of matter (immaterial) and not a body (incorporeal). The first cause must be both, since matter involves potentiality and bodies are composite.
keyTerms.example: A number or a mind’s act of understanding is not a physical object with a size and a location.
keyTerms.origin: Latin in- (‘not’) + materia (‘matter’) / corpus (‘body’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Invisible: air is invisible but material. Immaterial means not made of matter at all.

keyTerms.definition: Complete, lacking nothing. Perfection is the attribute. In Thomist usage, what is purely actual is perfect because imperfection is a lack of some actuality a thing could have.
keyTerms.example: A sketch is imperfect because it lacks the detail it could have; pure act lacks no actuality at all.
keyTerms.origin: Latin perfectus, ‘thoroughly made, completed’; chapters 1 and 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Morally flawless in a human sense: divine perfection is metaphysical fullness of being, from which goodness follows.

keyTerms.definition: All-powerful: able to do or produce anything that is intrinsically possible. Omnipotence is the attribute. It follows from being the purely actual source of all actualization.
keyTerms.example: The cause of the existence of everything other than itself can produce any intrinsically possible thing; it cannot make a square circle, which isn’t a ‘thing’ at all.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis (‘all’) + potens (‘powerful’); chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Able to do the logically impossible: omnipotence concerns what is possible, not contradictions.

keyTerms.definition: All-knowing: knowing everything that is knowable. Omniscience is the attribute. It follows from the first cause being an intellect that grounds all things and all possibilities.
keyTerms.example: The cause of everything knows every creature, since it knows itself as their cause.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis (‘all’) + sciens (‘knowing’); chapters 3 and 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Merely very well informed: omniscience is knowledge of all that can be known, not just an enormous store of facts.

keyTerms.definition: Good without any defect. In Thomist terms, goodness is being or actuality considered as desirable, so what is purely actual is supremely good.
keyTerms.example: A good knife fully realizes what a knife is for; pure act lacks no realization at all.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian-Thomistic ‘convertibility’ of being and goodness; chapters 1 and 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Morally well-behaved like a virtuous person: divine goodness is not compliance with moral obligations but fullness of being.

keyTerms.definition: Possessing intellect, the power to grasp concepts, truths, and possibilities. Chapter 3 argues that the ground of all necessity and possibility is a necessarily existing intellect, identical with pure act.
keyTerms.example: Abstract truths like 2 + 2 = 4 exist in an eternal, divine intellect.
keyTerms.origin: Latin intellectus; the Augustinian proof, chapter 3.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Clever or calculating: divine intelligence is not reasoning step by step but simple, eternal understanding.

keyTerms.definition: A cosmological argument that the universe began to exist and so has a cause. Feser’s rationalist proof does not depend on any claim about a beginning; it grants an infinite past.
keyTerms.example: ‘Whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; so it has a cause.’
keyTerms.origin: Arabic kalām (‘speech,’ medieval Islamic theology), e.g., al-Ghazali; defended today by William Lane Craig.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The argument from contingency (Leibniz–Clarke, Feser), which works even if the universe had no beginning.

keyTerms.definition: Invoking God to fill a gap in current scientific knowledge, which a future scientific theory might close. Feser denies that his arguments are of this kind: they are metaphysical demonstrations about what any empirical theory presupposes.
keyTerms.example: ‘Science can’t yet explain X, so God did it.’
keyTerms.origin: Phrase associated with twentieth-century debates (e.g., Charles Coulson); discussed in chapter 7.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphysical demonstration: it claims there is no possible non-divine explanation, not merely that none has been found yet.

keyTerms.definition: An argument that God exists from the very concept of God, for example that a supremely perfect being must exist because existence is a perfection. Feser, like Aquinas, does not rely on it.
keyTerms.example: Descartes: a supremely perfect being lacking existence would be a contradiction.
keyTerms.origin: Named by Kant (German ontologischer Beweis); Anselm, Descartes.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Cosmological argument: it reasons from the existence of contingent or changing things, not from a definition.

keyTerms.definition: Conservation is God’s continual sustaining of creatures in existence at every moment. Annihilation would be a thing’s ceasing to exist altogether, not merely being transformed into something else. The here-and-now route asks why contingent things are conserved rather than annihilated.
keyTerms.example: A burning log isn’t annihilated; it is changed into ash and smoke. What keeps the log, ash, and smoke existing at all is the question of conservation.
keyTerms.origin: Latin conservare (‘to preserve’) and nihil (‘nothing’); chapter 6 treats conservation and concurrence.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Creation at the beginning of time: conservation is ongoing sustaining, relevant even if the world had no beginning.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that causes other things without itself being caused. In a hierarchical series it is ‘first’ in the order of dependence, not necessarily in time. Feser adds that it is self-explanatory, not unexplained.
keyTerms.example: The hand that moves the stick that moves the stone is first in that series right now.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover; Aquinas’ Five Ways.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The first event in time: a first cause in Feser’s sense is first in the order of present dependence, whether or not time had a beginning.

keyTerms.definition: The view that knowledge comes from, or is justified by, sense experience. Humean empiricism doubts principles like causality and PSR. Feser notes the irony that PSR is as well supported by experience as anything.
keyTerms.example: Hume holds that we never observe causal necessity, only one event regularly following another.
keyTerms.origin: Greek empeiria, ‘experience’; Locke, Berkeley, Hume.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Aristotelian ‘empiricism’: Thomists also hold that knowledge begins in the senses but reject Hume’s skeptical conclusions.

keyTerms.definition: The philosophical tradition following Thomas Aquinas. A Thomist is an adherent. Feser writes as a Thomist, and his construal of PSR is the Thomist one.
keyTerms.example: Garrigou-Lagrange and Wuellner, whose formulations of PSR Feser cites, are Thomists.
keyTerms.origin: From Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Rationalism: Thomism is Aristotelian and grounds knowledge in experience, though it shares PSR with the rationalists.

keyTerms.definition: The view that abstract objects such as universals, numbers, and propositions exist in a realm of their own, independent of all minds and material things. Feser rejects it in favor of Scholastic realism.
keyTerms.example: A Platonist says triangularity would exist even if there were no triangles and no minds at all.
keyTerms.origin: From Plato’s theory of Forms.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Scholastic (moderate) realism: universals are real but exist only in things and in the minds that abstract them.

keyTerms.definition: God’s will is free in that nothing external or internal compels him to create or to create one world rather than another. Chapter 6 defends it against the charge that simplicity rules it out.
keyTerms.example: Nothing in the concepts of lion or unicorn forced God to create lions rather than unicorns.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic doctrine of the divine will; chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Arbitrariness: free choice is intelligible in light of the chooser’s goodness and wisdom without being necessitated.

keyTerms.definition: The view that all necessity is a matter of linguistic convention, so that no extra-linguistic thing can be necessary. Feser rejects it because it confuses sentences with propositions and because mathematical and logical necessity isn’t conventional.
keyTerms.example: The claim that ‘2 + 2 = 4’ is necessary only because of how we use the symbols.
keyTerms.origin: Twentieth-century logical positivism; raised against God by J. N. Findlay; chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Logical necessity itself: one can accept that some truths are necessary without holding that necessity is merely conventional.

keyTerms.definition: The argument (from chapters 1, 2, and 4) that there cannot be more than one purely actual, absolutely simple, self-subsistent being, because anything that distinguished two such beings would be a potential, part, or limitation.
keyTerms.example: Two drops of water differ in their matter or location; two purely actual beings would have nothing by which to differ.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle, Plotinus, and Aquinas each give versions.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Monotheism by assumption: uniqueness is argued for, not assumed.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which earlier causes need not continue to exist or act for later ones to act, such as a chain of ancestors. Such a series could in principle go back infinitely, which is why Feser can grant an infinite past.
keyTerms.example: Your grandfather produced your father, who produced you, and you can go on existing and acting after your grandfather is gone.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic distinction between causes ordered per accidens (‘accidentally’) and per se (‘essentially’); chapter 1.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Per se (hierarchical) series: every member depends on higher members acting right now.

keyTerms.definition: The purely actual cause of all change reached by the Aristotelian proof (chapter 1). Stage 2 of the rationalist proof identifies the necessary being with it.
keyTerms.example: The first member of the hierarchy that actualizes the potentials of everything that changes, here and now.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle, Physics VIII and Metaphysics XII (Greek to proton kinoun akinēton).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A first mover in time: the Unmoved Mover is first in the order of present dependence.

keyTerms.definition: The absolutely simple, noncomposite first principle reached by the Neo-Platonic proof (chapter 2). Stage 2 identifies the necessary being with it.
keyTerms.example: Just as a composite like a tree needs something holding its parts together at every moment, the One needs nothing, having no parts.
keyTerms.origin: Plotinus, Enneads (Greek to hen).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A numerical ‘one’ among many: the One is unique because it is simple, not merely because there happens to be one of it.

keyTerms.definition: Assuming, in an argument, the very point in dispute. Feser says a critic who defends restricted PSR by calling the restriction a brute fact begs the question, since brute facts are what PSR denies.
keyTerms.example: Arguing ‘brute facts exist because the universe is a brute fact’ assumes what needed proving.
keyTerms.origin: Latin petitio principii, ‘assuming the starting point’; Aristotle’s Prior Analytics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Raising the question: in logic, ‘begging the question’ means assuming the conclusion, not prompting a question.

keyTerms.definition: Adopted solely to avoid an unwelcome conclusion, without independent motivation. Chapter 7 calls the brute-fact view of fundamental laws ad hoc.
keyTerms.example: Declaring the laws of physics a brute fact only because otherwise one would have to accept an argument for God.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘for this (purpose).’
keyTerms.confuseWith: Special pleading: that exempts a favored case from a general rule, while ‘ad hoc’ means unmotivated except by the need to escape an argument. The two often overlap.

keyTerms.definition: The view that nature, the world of physical things studied by science, is all there is, with nothing beyond it such as God. A naturalist holds this view. Brute-fact naturalism treats the universe or its basic laws as unexplained.
keyTerms.example: ‘The laws of physics are the bottom level of reality, and they just hold.’
keyTerms.origin: Latin natura, ‘nature’; a dominant stance in modern analytic philosophy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Science: naturalism is a philosophical claim about what exists, not a finding of any scientific experiment.

keyTerms.definition: The view that God does not exist. An atheist holds it. Feser argues that if the five proofs succeed, atheism is false, though which form of theism is true remains a further question.
keyTerms.example: Russell’s position in his debate with Copleston.
keyTerms.origin: Greek a- (‘without’) + theos (‘god’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Agnosticism: the agnostic suspends judgment about God’s existence, while the atheist denies it.

keyTerms.definition: The part of philosophy that studies the most general features of reality: being, existence, causation, necessity, possibility, change. ‘Metaphysical’ is the adjective. Feser’s proofs are metaphysical rather than scientific arguments.
keyTerms.example: Asking why anything contingent exists at all is a metaphysical question; asking how old the universe is is a scientific one.
keyTerms.origin: Greek ta meta ta physika, ‘the things after the physics,’ the title given to Aristotle’s treatise on first philosophy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Physics or cosmology: these study how the physical world behaves, while metaphysics studies what any physical theory takes for granted.

keyTerms.definition: The part of philosophy that studies knowledge and justified belief. ‘Epistemic’ describes what concerns knowledge. PSR is an ontological claim (about what there is), not an epistemic one (about what we can know).
keyTerms.example: Asking ‘can we ever be justified in trusting perception?’ is an epistemological question.
keyTerms.origin: Greek epistēmē, ‘knowledge,’ + logos, ‘account.’
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphysics: metaphysics asks what there is, epistemology asks how we know it.

keyTerms.definition: An argument claiming to show with certainty, from premises about the most general features of reality, that something must be so. Feser presents his proofs this way, not as probabilistic hypotheses competing with scientific theories.
keyTerms.example: Showing that any contingent thing requires a necessary cause, whatever the scientific facts turn out to be.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian-Scholastic notion of demonstration (Greek apodeixis); chapter 7’s reply to the ‘god of the gaps’ charge.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An inference to the best explanation: that claims only that a hypothesis is more probable than its rivals.

keyTerms.term: Kant’s objection (cosmological argument presupposes the ontological)
keyTerms.definition: Kant claimed that arguing from contingent things to a necessary being secretly relies on the ontological argument, which he thought unsound. Feser answers (chapter 7) that the necessity in question is metaphysical, not definitional, so no such reliance exists.
keyTerms.example: Aquinas rejected the ontological argument yet endorsed cosmological arguments, which shows the two can come apart.
keyTerms.origin: Immanuel Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (1781); repeated by A. C. Grayling.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Kant’s other objection, that causal principles cannot be extended beyond experience, which chapter 1 answers with the geometry comparison.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that nothing can both be and not be in the same respect at the same time. Like PSR, it is a first principle that cannot be proved from anything more evident but can be defended by showing that denying it is absurd.
keyTerms.example: Anyone who argues that the law is false must assume that his claim is true and not also false.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle, Metaphysics IV. ‘First principle’ translates Greek archē and Latin principium.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A conclusion: a first principle is a starting point of reasoning, not something derived.

keyTerms.definition: A complete way reality could have been. Contemporary philosophers often analyze necessity as truth in all possible worlds. Feser thinks this gets the order of explanation backward: what is possible depends on the natures of things.
keyTerms.example: ‘There is a possible world in which you never became a reader of philosophy.’
keyTerms.origin: Leibniz; formalized in twentieth-century modal logic (Kripke, Lewis, Plantinga).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Imaginable scenario: what we can picture is a poor guide to what is really possible, as chapter 6 argues against Schrader.

keyTerms.definition: God’s causing things to exist, and a creature is anything so caused. In the classical view creation includes God’s conserving things in existence at every moment, not just starting them off.
keyTerms.example: Every stone, dog, star, and angel is a creature, dependent on God for its existence right now.
keyTerms.origin: Latin creare, ‘to make, bring forth.’
keyTerms.confuseWith: A first event in time: even a beginningless world would be created, in the sense of depending on God for its existence.

distinctions.name: Cause vs. sufficient reason

left.label: Cause
left.desc: Something distinct from its effect that actualizes a potential in it. Nothing causes itself, and the principle of causality does not say that everything has a cause.

right.label: Sufficient reason
right.desc: Whatever makes a thing intelligible. It can be distinct from the thing (when the thing is caused) or identical with the thing’s own nature (when the thing is self-explanatory). PSR says everything has one.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This distinction dissolves ‘What caused God?’ and ‘Why can’t the universe be unexplained if God is?’ God has a sufficient reason — his own nature — but no cause. Every cause is a reason, but not every reason is a cause. Hume’s tradition blurred the two (see ch7a).

distinctions.name: Contingent vs. necessary being

left.label: Contingent
left.desc: Explained by something outside itself; depends on outside circumstances; could fail to exist. Examples: stones, trees, dogs, people, universes, multiverses.

right.label: Necessary
right.desc: Explained by its own nature; cannot fail to exist; depends on nothing. In the strictest sense, it must be purely actual, simple, and subsistent existence.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Given PSR, this division is exhaustive: ‘explained by nothing’ is excluded. The whole argument is an elimination — contingent things cannot ultimately explain contingent existence, so a necessary being must.

distinctions.name: Strict (absolute) vs. broad (derivative) necessity

left.label: Broad or derivative necessity
left.desc: Aquinas’ looser sense: having no natural tendency to corrupt. Angels, being immortal, qualify, but they are still caused.

right.label: Strict or absolute necessity
right.desc: Depending on nothing at all for existence. This requires pure actuality, simplicity, and identity of essence and existence.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Stage 2 works only with strict necessity. It also answers the suggestion that numbers or propositions are non-divine necessary beings: their necessity, like the angels’, is derivative, flowing from the infinite mind that thinks them.

distinctions.name: Weight-like vs. color-like properties (part-to-whole reasoning)

left.label: Weight-like (inference fails)
left.desc: Properties that do not carry over from parts to whole. Each stone weighing under an ounce does not make the pile weigh under an ounce.

right.label: Color-like (inference holds)
right.desc: Properties that do carry over. If each Lego brick is red, the wall built from them is red.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Contingency is color-like — indeed, collections are *more* contingent than their members. This defuses the fallacy-of-composition charge against asking why the whole series of contingent things exists.

distinctions.name: The series route vs. the here-and-now route

left.label: Series route (Leibniz, Clarke)
left.desc: Asks why the whole series of contingent things (universe, cycle of universes, or multiverse) exists at all, and what explains its specific kinds and laws.

right.label: Here-and-now route (Feser’s addition)
right.desc: Asks what keeps one particular contingent thing in existence at this very moment. The answer is a regress of simultaneous sustaining causes, which must end in a necessary being.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The second route never makes a claim about the universe as a whole, so the composition charge has nothing to attack. It also ties the rationalist proof to the hierarchical-series reasoning of chapters 1, 2, and 4.

distinctions.name: Explanation as entailment vs. explanation as intelligibility

left.label: Entailment model (some rationalists and contemporary PSR formulations)
left.desc: The explanans must logically entail the explanandum, and propositions themselves need explaining. This invites the big-conjunction (modal-collapse) objection.

right.label: Intelligibility model (Thomist PSR)
right.desc: The explanans must make the explanandum intelligible, which scientific explanations routinely do without entailment. Only concrete things and their attributes need explaining.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This is the main way Feser’s PSR differs from Leibniz-style versions, and it is why the most famous objection to PSR does not touch his argument.

distinctions.name: Brute fact vs. self-explanatory terminus

left.label: Brute-fact terminus
left.desc: The regress ends in something with no explanation at all (Mackie, Russell). By hypothesis it has nothing to pass down, so nothing below it is truly explained.

right.label: Self-explanatory terminus
right.desc: The regress ends in something whose own nature explains it. It can therefore give explanatory power without borrowing any.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The atheist and the theist both end the regress somewhere. The question is whether the stopping point is intelligible. Only a self-explanatory stopping point makes the rest of the chain explanatory, just as only a shelf that is really supported can hold up the book.

illustrations.title: Sunglasses, a rash, and raccoons on the roof
illustrations.body:
Feser starts with the small detective stories of daily life. There are unfamiliar sunglasses on the couch (a friend forgot them), a rash on your arm (poison oak on Saturday’s hike), scratching overhead (a cat or raccoons). Science extends the same habit to evolution, temperature, and planetary orbits.

The telling detail is the **unsolved murder**. We don’t conclude that the victim died for no reason. We explain even our failure to explain: the killer wore gloves, left no witnesses, and hid the body. Use this to show that *we already live by PSR*, and that ‘no explanation found’ never slides into ‘no explanation exists.’

illustrations.title: The book on the shelf that holds itself up for no reason
illustrations.body:
A book is off the floor because it rests on a shelf. Now suppose the shelf’s staying up has *no explanation at all* — no brackets, no wall, nothing. It just hangs there, brutely. Have we explained why the book stays up? No. The shelf has no real tendency to stay aloft, so it has none to lend the book. Saying the book has its own brute tendency just moves the mystery.

Feser applies this to laws of nature. If law C is explained by B and B by A, but A is a brute fact, then C and B are not really explained either; the ‘explanation’ is a trompe-l’oeil. In ch7b Feser extends the image: it is like resting the shelf on brackets and then letting go of the brackets in midair.

illustrations.title: Stones versus red Lego bricks
illustrations.body:
Critics say that asking why the whole series of contingent things exists commits the fallacy of composition: pebbles each under an ounce don’t make a pile under an ounce. Feser agrees that part-to-whole reasoning *sometimes* fails — for weight, for example. But it works for color: build anything out of red Lego bricks and it will be red.

Contingency is like color. One stone is contingent. Three stones are no less so, and three million no less than three. In fact a collection is **doubly contingent**: it needs each stone to go on existing *and* needs the stones to be gathered together as they are. The collection of *all* contingent things doesn’t suddenly become necessary.

illustrations.title: Leibniz’s infinite library of geometry books
illustrations.body:
Imagine a geometry textbook copied from an earlier copy, that one from a still earlier one, and so on with no first copy. Each book has a perfectly good immediate cause. Yet the important questions are untouched. Why does the series contain *this* content? Why geometry, and not Shakespeare, a coloring book, or an auto-repair manual copied forever?

The universe is the same. Even an infinitely old chain of stars, dogs, and galaxies leaves open why it is made of *these* kinds of things, governed by *these* laws. This is Leibniz’s answer to Hume’s claim that explaining each member explains everything.

illustrations.title: The instrument that is the instrument of nothing
illustrations.body: In earlier chapters, a stone is moved by a stick, which is moved by a hand. The stick has causal power only as an instrument; take away the hand and it moves nothing, no matter how long the chain of sticks. Feser says a chain of ever-deeper laws of nature is like this kind of hierarchical series. Each law ‘transmits’ explanatory power from the one above it. A chain ending in a brute fact is like a stick moving a stone with no hand anywhere — an instrument that is not the instrument of anything.

illustrations.title: The calculator or the slot machine?
illustrations.body:
Imagine a device whose screen shows ‘4’ when you type ‘2+2.’ If its circuitry really computes, the display is reliable. But suppose displays could appear *for no reason at all*, unconnected to the circuitry, and occasionally match the right answer by coincidence. You could never know whether you were holding a calculator or a slot machine that sometimes pays out.

That is your mind if PSR is false. Your beliefs might arise with no connection to your evidence, and your sense that ‘this follows logically’ might itself occur for no reason. Every argument — including arguments against PSR — would then be a slot-machine readout. Use this to make the self-undermining point concrete.

illustrations.title: The endless chain of IOUs
illustrations.body:
You ask a friend for $100. He says he’ll borrow it from his cousin, who will borrow it from her coworker, and so on forever. Does anyone ever get the money? Only if someone in the chain *has* money that isn’t borrowed. Lengthening the chain — even to infinity — just multiplies debts. Adding a second infinite chain of lenders ‘outside’ the first changes nothing.

Contingent things have their existence ‘on loan.’ A series of borrowers, however long, cannot explain why there is any existence to pass around. Only something that owns its existence by its very nature — a necessary being — can explain it. This makes the ‘passing the explanatory buck’ point vivid.

illustrations.title: The lamp that is on right now
illustrations.body:
Why is the lamp shining at this moment? ‘Because someone flipped the switch yesterday’ is part of its history, but it doesn’t explain the light *now*. Cut the current and the light is gone instantly, whatever happened yesterday. What explains the present light is something acting *simultaneously*: current from the wiring, from the grid, from the generator.

Feser’s second route asks this question about existence itself. Whatever produced a tree long ago, nothing in the tree’s nature guarantees that it exists at this instant. So something must be sustaining it now — and a chain of contingent sustainers is another ‘current’ that must come from somewhere. (Like all physical analogies, this one is imperfect: the generator is itself contingent. That is exactly the point — the chain has to end in what is not contingent.)

illustrations.title: The selective detective
illustrations.body:
Picture a detective who insists on explaining every clue — the muddy boots, the missing key, the torn letter — until the last clue points to something inconvenient. Then he announces, ‘That one has no explanation. It just happened.’ We would call this arbitrary, not rigorous.

This is Della Rocca’s point. PSR’s critics demand explanations everywhere in science and philosophy, then declare the existence of things off-limits. Unless they can give a *non-arbitrary* reason for drawing the line there, and not one that itself relies on a brute fact or a question-begging intuition, their stance is special pleading.

objections.title: Explain each member and you’ve explained the whole
objections.whoRaises: David Hume (Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion); many modern skeptics
objections.objection: Suppose the universe has an infinite past, each state caused by the one before. Then every contingent thing has an explanation — its predecessor. PSR is fully satisfied without any necessary being. Asking for an explanation of ‘the whole series’ in addition is asking for something extra that doesn’t exist.
objections.reply:
Feser grants the infinite series for argument’s sake and then shows that something is still unexplained.

1. **The series is itself contingent.** It could have failed to exist, so why does it exist? (Leibniz, Clarke.)
2. **Its specific character is unexplained.** In Leibniz’s infinite chain of copied geometry books, each copy has a cause, but nothing explains why the series is about geometry rather than Shakespeare. Similarly, nothing in an infinite regress explains why the world consists of *these* kinds of things under *these* laws.
3. **The present is unexplained.** Even granting the past chain, what keeps any one thing in existence *now*? Its past producer doesn’t, since nothing in the thing’s nature guarantees its existence at this moment.

So the regress leaves the most important questions untouched.
objections.pushback: If the skeptic says the whole is ‘just the sum of its parts, explained when the parts are,’ ask whether the infinite geometry library really leaves nothing to explain. If the skeptic still resists, switch to the here-and-now route, which makes no claim about wholes at all: *this* stone exists now; what explains that, right now?

objections.title: The fallacy of composition
objections.objection: Each member of the series is contingent, but it doesn’t follow that the series as a whole is contingent — just as each brick weighing a pound doesn’t make the wall weigh a pound. Asking for a cause of ‘the whole’ commits the fallacy of composition.
objections.reply:
Part-to-whole reasoning is fallacious only for *some* properties. It fails for weight, but not for color: a wall of red Lego bricks is red. Contingency is color-like. A collection of three contingent stones is no less contingent than one stone, and a collection of millions no less than three. In fact, collections are **doubly contingent**: they depend on each member existing *and* on the members being assembled as they are. Nothing about piling up contingent things makes them necessary.

In addition, the here-and-now route does not reason from parts to whole at all. It starts from the continued existence of one particular thing.
objections.pushback: If the critic says, ‘But maybe the totality is different in kind,’ ask what feature of adding more contingent items would remove their dependence. Each addition adds dependence, not independence. You can also turn the charge around, as Feser does in ch7a: it is Hume who reasons fallaciously when he infers that explaining each member explains why there is anything in the series at all.

objections.title: A contingent cause outside the series
objections.whoRaises: Typical skeptic seeking to avoid a necessary being
objections.objection: Grant that the series of contingent things needs a cause beyond itself. Why must that cause be *necessary*? Perhaps it is some further contingent thing — a meta-universe, a universe-generating mechanism, or a higher-level series.
objections.reply: Then that contingent cause needs a cause of its own, and so does the next. Positing a second infinite series of higher-order contingent causes merely **relocates** the problem, because every reason that forced us beyond the first series applies equally to the second. We would then need a third series, a fourth, and so on — even an infinite series of infinite series — and each move just passes the explanatory buck. Only something whose existence is explained by its own nature can end the regress, so, given PSR, the cause must be necessary.
objections.pushback: If the skeptic asks, ‘Why not an infinite hierarchy of generators, forever?’ point out that the whole hierarchy is contingent too and is itself one more thing needing explanation. Infinity doesn’t turn borrowed existence into owned existence; think of the endless chain of IOUs.

objections.title: The fundamental laws are just brute facts
objections.whoRaises: J. L. Mackie; Bertrand Russell (in the Copleston debate); many scientific naturalists
objections.objection: Science explains phenomena by laws, and laws by deeper laws. At the bottom lie the most fundamental laws, which simply hold. That is a perfectly respectable place for explanation to stop. We have real explanations without PSR.
objections.reply: This is incoherent. If the deepest law A is a brute fact — nothing in A and nothing beyond A accounts for its operation — then A has nothing to pass on to the laws it supposedly explains. It is like saying a book stays up because of a shelf that stays up for no reason. The shelf has no real tendency to stay aloft, so it can give none to the book. A regress of laws is a **hierarchical series**, and a hierarchical series whose first member has no power of its own is like an instrument that is the instrument of nothing. So if the base is brute, *none* of the higher explanations is genuine, which undercuts the very science the objector is relying on.
objections.pushback: If the objector says, ‘The higher laws are still explained relative to the lower ones,’ grant that this is a *conditional* explanation, then ask whether a chain of conditionals whose first antecedent has no ground actually explains why anything happens. Also note, with ch7b, that this position is ad hoc: its only motive seems to be avoiding arguments like this one.

objections.title: PSR is just a useful empirical generalization
objections.whoRaises: Empiricist skeptics; those who say PSR holds ‘within the universe’ but not for the universe
objections.objection: Sure, we usually find explanations. But that is an inductive generalization from local cases. It may simply break down at the level of existence itself or of the cosmos as a whole. PSR is a helpful rule of thumb, not a law of reality.
objections.reply: Feser grants that PSR has *at least* the inductive support any generalization can have: we find explanations when we look, and the world lacks the constant brute events we would expect if PSR were false. But he insists it is far more certain than any empirical hypothesis, because it can be defended by **reductio**. Denying it undermines trust in perception (Pruss/Koons), then reasoning itself, since beliefs could arise with no connection to reasons or truth, and it makes scientific explanation illusory. Induction itself presupposes that things have explanations (Della Rocca). So PSR is not one generalization among others; it is a precondition of forming generalizations at all. As for ‘not for the cosmos,’ that is Della Rocca’s option 1, which cannot be defended without arbitrariness.
objections.pushback: If the skeptic insists that a rule can hold locally and fail globally, ask what *principled* feature of existence exempts it. As chapter 1 argued against Kant, we learn a principle from experience without its scope being limited to experience — just as geometry learned from black-ink diagrams applies to figures of any color.

objections.title: Bite the bullet: accept perceptual skepticism
objections.objection: Fine — without PSR, I can’t justify trusting my senses. I’ll accept that and retreat to a priori knowledge: logic and mathematics, which don’t depend on perception. I can still reject PSR from there.
objections.reply: There is no refuge in the a priori. Any justified belief assumes two things: that we have a good reason for it, and that this reason is *why* we hold it. We also assume our faculties track truth and logic. Without PSR, none of this is secure. Our assent might be caused by something unrelated to our reasons, our faculties might produce outputs unrelated to truth, and it might merely seem — for no reason — that we reason well. That covers a priori reasoning too, and in particular it covers the reasoning behind rejecting PSR. So denying PSR is **self-undermining**: it removes the possibility of rational inquiry altogether.
objections.pushback: If the critic says, ‘I’m not claiming my beliefs *are* uncaused, only that they *could* be,’ reply that this is enough. If PSR is false, there is no principled reason to think any belief is connected to its grounds, so the critic has lost any right to confidence in his own argument.

objections.title: Explicability arguments are fine — just not about existence
objections.whoRaises: Contemporary critics of PSR (Della Rocca’s option 1)
objections.objection: I happily argue that things must have explanations in science and philosophy. But the sheer existence of things is a special case where demanding an explanation is inappropriate. That’s just where explanation stops.
objections.reply: Following Della Rocca: why draw the line exactly there? The critic cannot say it is a brute fact that some explicability arguments work and others don’t, since that begs the question against PSR, which denies brute facts. Nor can he appeal to intuition, because his own reliance on explicability arguments everywhere else undermines trust in this one exempting intuition. Without a non-question-begging rationale, the exemption is special pleading. The upshot: we have no good reason to think *anything* is explicable unless *everything* is.
objections.pushback: If the critic says, ‘Existence isn’t a property, so there’s nothing to explain,’ note that the question is not about an abstract property but about why these concrete, dependent things exist and continue to exist. That is exactly what the here-and-now route asks of each individual thing.

objections.title: Then I reject all explicability arguments
objections.objection: To avoid inconsistency, I’ll give up explicability arguments entirely. I won’t argue that anything must have an explanation. Della Rocca himself concedes this may not be strictly incoherent.
objections.reply: Feser thinks Della Rocca is too generous. Even someone who gives up the specific examples still accepts valid and inductively strong patterns of reasoning and rejects fallacies, *because* logic embodies standards of intelligibility and explanatory adequacy. Many arguments are themselves explanations: explanatory demonstrations (all rational animals can use language; humans are rational animals; so humans can use language), inference to the best explanation, and induction. Abandoning all of these means abandoning argument itself, which is incoherent for anyone who argues against PSR. And if the critic keeps argument in general while rejecting particular explicability arguments, he is really back at option 1, which is arbitrary.
objections.pushback: If the critic says he can use deduction without explanation, ask why he trusts modus ponens: because the premises make the conclusion’s truth *intelligible*. And ask whether he ever uses induction or inference to the best explanation. Almost everyone does, many times a day.

objections.title: It’s ‘rationalism’ — innate ideas and armchair a priori knowledge
objections.whoRaises: Empiricists; readers wary of Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz
objections.objection: Rationalism is a discredited school that believed in innate ideas and thought all knowledge rests on truths known independently of experience. An argument built on it inherits its flaws.
objections.reply: The argument assumes none of those doctrines. It is ‘rationalist’ only in one respect: it denies that there are, or could be, inexplicable brute facts, and holds that reality is intelligible through and through. Its rationalism is simply PSR. Feser, a Thomist, takes knowledge to begin with experience. Moreover, the argument does not accept everything defended in PSR’s name: it does not require explaining propositions, and it does not demand that explanations entail what they explain.
objections.pushback: If the objector says PSR itself is an ‘a priori prejudice,’ point out that it has inductive support *and* a reductio defense, and that the objector presupposes it whenever he reasons from evidence.

objections.title: The big conjunction of contingent truths (the ‘modal collapse’ argument)
objections.whoRaises: James Ross, Peter van Inwagen, William Rowe
objections.objection: Conjoin every true contingent proposition into one Big Conjunction. It is contingent. It can’t be explained by a necessary proposition, because whatever a necessary truth entails is necessary — which would make everything necessary (modal collapse). It can’t be explained by a contingent proposition, because any such proposition is already a conjunct, so the Big Conjunction would explain itself, and nothing contingent explains itself. So something has no explanation, and PSR is false.
objections.reply:
Feser’s Thomist version of PSR escapes both horns.

1. **Propositions aren’t Platonic objects that need explaining.** The objection has force only if propositions exist ‘out there’ like stones and dogs. For the Scholastic realist (ch3), abstract objects exist only in the minds that think them. What needs explaining are concrete things and their attributes. Once concrete triangles and the minds (including God’s) that grasp triangularity are explained, there is nothing left over. The same goes for propositions: explain the concrete states of affairs and the minds that entertain them, and everything is explained.
2. **Explanation isn’t entailment.** The argument needs the premise that an explanans must *logically entail* the explanandum. Few real explanations work that way. As Pruss notes, scientific causal explanations generally don’t. The sun’s gravity explains elliptical orbits, yet other gravitational influences could have interfered. PSR requires only that the explanans make the explanandum **intelligible**. So a necessary being can explain contingent reality without making it necessary.
objections.pushback: If the critic reformulates in terms of concrete things (‘the aggregate of all contingent beings’), you are back to the series argument, which Feser answers directly. If the critic insists that a ‘full’ explanation must rule out every alternative, ask whether he thinks science has *never* explained anything. If entailment were required, almost no scientific explanation would count.

objections.title: We can conceive of something happening for no reason
objections.objection: I can imagine a coffee cup popping into existence with no explanation. Whatever is conceivable is possible, so PSR is not necessarily true.
objections.reply: This recycles the Humean objection to the principle of causality answered in chapter 1. Imagining a cup appearing *without also imagining its explanation* is not imagining it *as having no explanation*. We can think of a trilateral without thinking of it as a triangle, but no trilateral could fail to be a triangle. Also (Anscombe), to tell a cup’s coming into existence apart from its merely being moved from elsewhere, Hume must bring causes back into the story. And PSR is additionally backed by the reductio: a world where things can happen for no reason is one where we couldn’t trust our minds.
objections.pushback: If the objector presses ‘conceivability implies possibility,’ point out that what we can picture (mental images) is a poor guide to what is metaphysically possible, as ch6a argues. Picturing an empty scene tells us nothing about whether anything could exist unexplained.

objections.title: Quantum mechanics shows events happen for no reason
objections.whoRaises: Popular science writers (e.g., Stenger, Krauss, Rosenberg); typical skeptic
objections.objection: Radioactive decay and other quantum events are indeterministic. Nothing determines when a particular atom decays, so some events have no explanation. PSR is empirically refuted.
objections.reply: This objection is even weaker against PSR than against the principle of causality. Whether or not odd quantum phenomena have a *cause*, they plainly have an *explanation*: they presuppose, and are made intelligible by, the laws of quantum mechanics. Indeterminism is not unintelligibility, and PSR does not require deterministic entailment (recall the sun and the orbits). And, as Della Rocca notes, the critic who appeals to quantum mechanics still owes an answer: where exactly is the line between legitimate and illegitimate explicability arguments, and why there?
objections.pushback: If the critic says, ‘The specific timing of this decay is unexplained,’ answer that the statistical laws and the nature of the system make it intelligible that such an event happens with such a probability. PSR asks for intelligibility, not entailment. The interpretation of quantum mechanics is also disputed; some interpretations are deterministic (ch1). It can’t bear the weight of refuting a principle presupposed by all inquiry.

objections.title: Puzzles about PSR show it’s false, so the burden is on its defenders
objections.objection: PSR generates paradoxes — the Big Conjunction, quantum cases, and so on. Until its defenders resolve every puzzle, we should reject it.
objections.reply: Raising puzzles for *some* formulation of PSR doesn’t refute PSR as such. Some formulations, like the Thomist one, lack the assumptions that generate the puzzles. More importantly, there are *positive arguments* that PSR is true and that even its critics presuppose it, and puzzles don’t answer those arguments. So the burden of proof lies on the critic, who must show how PSR can be **coherently rejected**. (The defender can meet a burden too, and Feser thinks he has.)
objections.pushback: If the critic says the burden always lies on the one making a universal claim, ask whether he places the same burden on the laws of logic. Principles presupposed by all inquiry are not treated like ordinary hypotheses.

objections.title: Why not say the universe itself is the necessary being?
objections.whoRaises: Hume (Cleanthes in the Dialogues, Part IX); New Atheists such as Dawkins and Krauss (see ch7a)
objections.objection: Grant PSR and grant that something exists necessarily. Why think it’s God? Maybe the universe itself — or matter-energy, or the multiverse — is the necessary being.
objections.reply: Whatever exists necessarily must be purely actual and simple (Stage 2). The universe changes, so it has potentials being actualized and is not purely actual. It has many diverse parts, so it isn’t simple. It is as contingent as its parts. Therefore it cannot be a necessary being. The same holds for the multiverse, the Big Bang, or the laws of physics, each of which involves potency, composition, or an essence distinct from existence. Stage 2 has also shown why the necessary being must have the other divine attributes.
objections.pushback: If the critic suggests ‘the fundamental stuff’ (energy, the quantum field) is necessary, ask whether it has potentials (it changes state) and structure (it has parts or components). If it does, it isn’t necessary in the strict sense. As ch7a notes, if something really were purely actual, simple, and self-existent, it would have divine attributes, and the view would be pantheism, not atheism.

objections.title: Numbers and propositions are necessary beings that aren’t God
objections.objection: Mathematical objects and propositions exist necessarily, yet no one calls them God. So ‘necessary being’ doesn’t get you to God.
objections.reply: As chapter 3 argued, on independent grounds, abstract objects cannot exist apart from minds that entertain them. So if they are necessary — and there is reason to think they are — their necessity is **derivative**, depending on an infinite mind that thinks them. They are not absolutely necessary in the strict sense Stage 2 uses, which is necessity that depends on nothing.
objections.pushback: If the Platonist insists abstracta exist mind-independently, you are in chapter 3 territory: press the Augustinian argument that universals, propositions, and possibilities must exist in an intellect, and ultimately in a divine one.

objections.title: ‘What caused God?’ / ‘If God can be unexplained, so can the universe’
objections.objection: If everything needs an explanation, what explains God? And if you say God needs no explanation, why can’t I say the universe needs none?
objections.reply: This fails twice over. First, the proof never says everything has a *cause*; it says everything has an *explanation*. Second, it makes **no exception for God**. God’s existence is explained by his own nature as purely actual, simple, and subsistent existence itself.
