The universe cannot be explained by its own nature, since it has potentials and parts and is as contingent as its components. So the contrast is not ‘explained vs. unexplained’ but **self-explanatory vs. not self-explanatory**. The line is drawn by independently motivated distinctions (act/potency, simple/composite, essence/existence), not by special pleading. And self-explanatory is not self-caused: having a cause means having a potential actualized, and having an explanation does not.
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘self-explanatory’ is just a label, ask him to state what feature of the universe could make its existence follow from its nature. If none can be named, the asymmetry is real, not stipulated.

objections.title: ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’ — couldn’t there just have been nothing?
objections.whoRaises: Popular framing of cosmological arguments; physicists writing on ‘universes from nothing’
objections.objection: The rationalist argument answers the question ‘why is there something rather than nothing?’ But that question assumes there *could* have been nothing at all. If total nothingness was possible, perhaps our universe is just the lucky alternative.
objections.reply: Feser warns against this framing. It suggests that absolute nothingness was a genuine possibility, and the proofs imply otherwise: what is purely actual, simple, the ground of all possibility, subsistent existence, and absolutely necessary could not have failed to exist. So the correct question is: **why are there any contingent things at all?** Framed this way, the proof asks nothing about ‘nothing’; it asks what explains dependent things.
objections.pushback: If the critic asks how we know there couldn’t have been nothing, reply that this is a *conclusion* of the argument, not a premise. And if someone offers a physical ‘nothing’ (a quantum vacuum governed by laws), note that such a ‘nothing’ is a contingent something that needs explaining (ch7a on Krauss).

objections.title: PSR collapses modality even for God: creation would be necessary and God unfree
objections.whoRaises: Contemporary analytic critics of PSR and of classical theism (a modern variant; not discussed in ch5)
objections.objection: If God’s necessary nature fully explains why this world exists, then this world follows necessarily from God, and nothing could have been otherwise. That is modal collapse and it removes divine freedom. If instead God’s choice is not fully explained, PSR fails.
objections.reply: Use the chapter’s own resources. PSR, as Feser construes it, requires that the explanans make the explanandum **intelligible**, not that it **entail** it. The sun explains the orbits without necessitating them, and a free agent’s reasons explain a choice without forcing it. The world is intelligible in light of God’s nature, knowledge, goodness, and will, without being logically deducible from God’s nature alone. As ch6b argues, nothing internal or external compels God to create lions rather than unicorns, so his will is free. His free choice is the explanation, and it makes creation intelligible without making it necessary.
objections.pushback: If the critic insists that an explanation leaving alternatives open is ‘not sufficient,’ ask whether he accepts any explanation of human free action or any scientific explanation. By his standard almost nothing is ever explained. Grant that divine freedom is mysterious; ch6b notes our own freedom is too. Mystery is not contradiction.

objections.title: A ‘necessary being’ is incoherent
objections.whoRaises: Hume, Kant, J. N. Findlay; also Russell in the Copleston debate (a modern variant answered in ch6a and ch7a)
objections.objection: Necessity belongs to propositions (such as ‘bachelors are unmarried’), not to things. Whatever we can conceive as existing we can conceive as not existing, so no being exists necessarily. And appealing to a necessary being secretly relies on the ontological argument.
objections.reply: The necessity at issue is not logical or definitional necessity — God does not exist ‘by definition’ the way bachelors are unmarried. It is **metaphysical** necessity grounded in what the being is: something with no potentials that could fail to be actualized, no parts that could come apart, and no essence that must receive existence from outside. That is neither logical necessity nor mere conditional necessity (ch7a). Nor is imagining an empty scene a real test of possibility, since God is not an object we could picture present or absent (ch6a). And Aquinas rejected the ontological argument while endorsing arguments like this one, which shows there is no hidden dependence.
objections.pushback: If the critic insists that all necessity is conventional, note that the truths of logic and mathematics are necessary without being mere conventions (ch3, ch6a). Also note that the argument *derives* the existence of a necessary being from contingent things plus PSR, so rejecting its possibility at the outset begs the question.

misconceptions.myth: PSR is just another way of saying ‘everything has a cause.’
misconceptions.correction: PSR says everything has a *sufficient reason*, which may be an outside cause or the thing’s own nature. The principle of causality, by contrast, applies only to potentials being actualized and never says that everything has a cause. Every cause is a reason, but not every reason is a cause.

misconceptions.myth: The argument needs the universe to have had a beginning.
misconceptions.correction: Feser explicitly grants an infinite past — a beginningless universe, endless Big Bang/Big Crunch cycles, or a beginningless multiverse — and argues that a necessary being is still required.

misconceptions.myth: The argument stands or falls with claims about ‘the universe as a whole,’ so the fallacy of composition sinks it.
misconceptions.correction: The composition charge fails anyway, since contingency is color-like, not weight-like. And Feser’s here-and-now route starts from one contingent thing’s present existence, with no premise about the whole.

misconceptions.myth: Feser’s PSR requires every explanation to logically entail what it explains, which makes everything necessary.
misconceptions.correction: The Thomist PSR requires only that explanations make things *intelligible*. Most scientific explanations, like gravity explaining orbits, do not entail their explananda. This is why the big-conjunction (modal-collapse) objection misses.

misconceptions.myth: The argument says God is self-caused (causa sui).
misconceptions.correction: God is *self-explanatory*, not self-caused. To be caused is to have a potential actualized, which is impossible for pure act. Explanation by one’s own nature involves no such actualization.

misconceptions.myth: Calling it ‘rationalist’ means it relies on innate ideas and armchair knowledge of the world.
misconceptions.correction: Its only ‘rationalism’ is PSR — the denial of brute facts. It assumes no doctrine of innate ideas or a priori foundationalism.

misconceptions.myth: PSR is merely an inductive rule of thumb that might fail at the cosmic scale.
misconceptions.correction: PSR has inductive support, but Feser’s main defense is a reductio: denying it undermines perception, reasoning, and scientific explanation, including the reasoning used to deny it.

misconceptions.myth: A ‘necessary being’ means a being that exists by definition, so the argument presupposes the ontological argument.
misconceptions.correction: The necessity is metaphysical, grounded in pure actuality, simplicity, and identity of essence and existence, not in the definition of a word. Aquinas rejected the ontological argument while accepting arguments like this one.

misconceptions.myth: Once you have ‘a necessary being,’ it could be the universe, the laws of physics, or numbers.
misconceptions.correction: Stage 2 shows that a strictly necessary being must be purely actual and simple, which rules out anything that changes or has parts. Abstract objects have only derivative necessity, dependent on an infinite mind.

misconceptions.myth: The proof is basically Leibniz’s argument restated.
misconceptions.correction: Feser adds a Thomist PSR (intelligibility, not entailment; no Platonic propositions), a stronger reductio defense of PSR, the here-and-now route alongside the whole-series route, and a Stage 2 that grounds necessity in act/potency, simplicity, and essence/existence.

misconceptions.myth: Denying PSR just means humbly admitting there are mysteries.
misconceptions.correction: A mystery is a fact whose explanation we don’t know. A brute fact is one that *has* no explanation. PSR is fully compatible with mystery, as in the unsolved murder. What it denies is brute facts.

misconceptions.myth: The rationalist proof is a ‘God of the gaps’ argument that science might someday close.
misconceptions.correction: It doesn’t fill a gap in scientific knowledge. It asks why anything contingent exists and persists at all, whatever the scientific facts turn out to be. As chapter 7 stresses, it aims at metaphysical demonstration, not a probabilistic hypothesis competing with physics.

explain.tweet: Everything has an explanation — deny it and you can’t trust your own reasoning. Stones, stars, and universes owe their existence to something else, and no chain of borrowers explains why anything exists. So something exists by its own nature: pure act, one, cause of all. God.
explain.elevator: Everything has an explanation. We assume this in science and in daily life, and if we denied it, we couldn’t trust our own reasoning. Now, most things are explained by something outside them. Their existence is on loan. A chain of borrowers, even an infinite one, never explains why there is any existence to lend. So something must exist by its own nature. And anything like that can’t change or have parts, which rules out the universe. There can be only one such thing. That’s God.
explain.twoMinute:
Here’s the idea. Everything has an explanation — philosophers call this the **principle of sufficient reason**. That doesn’t mean we always *find* the explanation. It means there always *is* one. You already believe this. If your car won’t start, you never think, ‘Maybe it’s failing for no reason at all.’

Could it be false? Think about what that would mean. If things can happen for no reason, then your beliefs could pop into your head for no reason too, including the belief that everything has an explanation, or that it doesn’t. You couldn’t trust your senses or your logic. And science would be hollow: if the deepest laws of physics were brute facts with no explanation, they couldn’t really explain anything built on top of them. That’s like saying a book stays up because it sits on a shelf that floats for no reason.

So accept the principle. Now notice that some things are explained by something *else*. A tree depends on soil, sun, and the laws of physics, and on its atoms holding together right now. Call those things **contingent**. Other things might be explained by their *own nature*. Call those **necessary**.

Could everything be contingent? Suppose an infinite chain, each thing caused by an earlier one. You still haven’t explained why the chain exists, or why it has these laws rather than others, or what keeps this tree existing *this second*. A chain of borrowed existence, however long, is like an infinite line of people borrowing money from each other: nobody ever actually has any money. So something must exist by its own nature.

What would that be like? It couldn’t have unrealized potentials, because then it would depend on whatever realizes them. It couldn’t have parts, because then it would depend on what holds them together. Its very essence would have to be *to exist*. That rules out the universe, which changes and has parts. There can be only one such being, and it’s the cause of everything else. That’s what classical theists have always meant by God.

And God isn’t an exception to the principle. God has an explanation, his own nature. Everything else is explained by him.
explain.eli12:
Imagine you find a cookie on your desk. You’d wonder who put it there, right? You’d never think, ‘It’s just there for no reason.’ That’s the big rule of this chapter: **everything has a reason why it’s there**.

Now, most things are there because of *something else*. The cookie is there because your friend left it. Your friend exists because of her parents. A tree needs sun, soil, and water. Things like that are **borrowers**: they borrow their existence from other things.

Here’s a puzzle. Suppose everybody in a line borrows a dollar from the next person, and the line goes on forever. Does anyone actually get a dollar? No! Somebody has to *have* a dollar that isn’t borrowed. It’s the same with existence. If everything borrowed its existence, there would be no existence to borrow.

So there must be something that doesn’t borrow its existence — something that exists just because of what it is. That thing can’t be made of parts, because parts need to be put together. It can’t change, because changing means depending on something to change you. The universe is made of parts and changes all the time, so it isn’t that thing.

There can only be one thing like that, and everything else gets its existence from it. That’s what people mean by God. And God isn’t cheating the rule. God has a reason for existing too: his reason is just what he is.
whiteboard: Write ‘PSR: Everything has an explanation.’ Beneath it draw two arrows: ‘in something else’ → CONTINGENT, and ‘in its own nature’ → NECESSARY. Cross out a third arrow labeled ‘in nothing’ and say that PSR rules it out.

Box: ‘Why believe PSR?’ List three supports: (1) we always find explanations or know why we can’t; (2) deny it and you can’t trust perception or reasoning — self-undermining; (3) you can’t use explanatory arguments everywhere else and exempt existence without arbitrariness (Della Rocca).
Draw a book on a shelf floating in air with a ‘?’ under the shelf. Write ‘brute-fact law’ on the shelf. Say: if the bottom is unexplained, nothing above it is explained either.

Draw a long chain of circles running off to the left, labeled ‘…C ← B ← A’ with ‘∞’ at the end. Circle the whole chain and write ‘still contingent — why this chain? why these laws?’ Add a little stack of geometry books.
Next to it, draw a pebble and a pile of pebbles. Write ‘weight: ✗ parts→whole; color: ✓ parts→whole; contingency is like color (doubly contingent).’
Draw a second, higher chain above the first labeled ‘contingent cause of the chain’ with an arrow pointing to ‘same problem again → passing the buck.’

Switch to a vertical diagram: a single tree at the bottom, with arrows pointing up to ‘what sustains it NOW?’ → contingent sustainer → contingent sustainer … → NECESSARY BEING at the top. Say: this route needs no claim about the universe as a whole.
Stage 2: write ‘Necessary ⇒ no potentials (pure act), no parts (simple), essence = existence.’ Draw arrows from these back to ‘Ch1 Unmoved Mover, Ch2 the One, Ch4 Subsistent Existence.’
Write ‘Only one possible → cause of everything else → immutable, eternal, immaterial, omnipotent, omniscient, good = GOD.’
Finish with a two-column box: ‘God — self-explanatory (not self-caused)’ vs. ‘Universe — explained by another.’ Say that no exception has been made: everything has an explanation.
explain.keyAnalogy: **Borrowed existence: the endless chain of IOUs.** Ask your listener to imagine needing $100. You borrow it from A, who borrows it from B, who borrows it from C, forever. Does money ever actually arrive? Only if someone in the chain *has* money without borrowing it. Now map it: contingent things have their existence on loan, from their causes and from whatever sustains them right now. Lengthening the chain, even to infinity, only multiplies debts. Adding a second infinite chain of ‘higher’ lenders changes nothing, because they are borrowers too. Only something that *owns* its existence by its very nature can explain why there is any existence to go around. That is a necessary being. Two tips: (1) stress the *here and now*: the loans are being made at this moment, not just in the distant past, so ‘the chain goes back forever’ is no answer; (2) use it to defuse ‘What caused God?’: the rich lender doesn’t need a loan, and that isn’t an exception to how money works but the only way anyone gets paid. Limit: the analogy doesn’t by itself show the necessary being is simple or unique. That takes Stage 2.

persuade.coreInsight:
The idea that makes the argument click is that **the demand for explanation is not a theist’s optional extra; it is the price of reasoning at all**, and the argument never exempts God from it. Once someone sees that (a) they rely on PSR every time they trust evidence, infer, or explain anything, and (b) the conclusion is not an unexplained God but a *self-explanatory* one whose nature is existence itself, the ‘special pleading’ charge disappears and the only question left is whether anything else could explain itself.

The argument usually fails to click for two reasons. First, people hear ‘everything has a cause’ instead of ‘everything has an explanation,’ and then ‘What caused God?’ looks devastating. Second, people picture a chain of events stretching back in time to a first moment, so an infinite past seems to defeat the argument. Correct both at the start: explanation, not causation; and dependence *now*, not a starting point in time.

audiences.startingPoint: Science explains everything that can be explained. Explanation bottoms out in the fundamental laws of physics, which just are what they are. Appeals to God look like a ‘god of the gaps.’
audiences.approach: Start *inside* scientific practice. Point out that the whole enterprise assumes there are explanations to find, and that the world’s intelligibility would be a miracle without PSR. Then press the book-and-shelf point: if the fundamental laws are brute, the higher-level explanations physics is proud of are illusory. Present the argument as a question about the *preconditions* of science, not a rival hypothesis. It is not a gap-filler; it asks what makes any law explanatory at all. On quantum mechanics: quantum events are made intelligible by quantum laws, and indeterminism is not unintelligibility.
audiences.openingQuestion: When a physicist explains a phenomenon by a law, and that law by a deeper law, what makes the deepest one explanatory — and if it’s a brute fact, what is it passing up the chain?
audiences.avoid: Don’t frame God as a better physical hypothesis or pin the argument to the Big Bang. Don’t suggest science is unreliable; the argument is that science is *more* reliable than brute-fact naturalism can account for.

audiences.who: Philosophy student who knows the literature
audiences.startingPoint: Knows van Inwagen’s modal-collapse argument, the Hume–Edwards ‘explain the parts and you’ve explained the whole’ reply, and thinks PSR is a dubious rationalist dogma.
audiences.approach: Be precise about *which* PSR you defend. Present the Thomist construal: explanation as intelligibility, not entailment, and only concrete things and their attributes as explananda. Show how this defuses the big-conjunction argument. Lead with Della Rocca’s line-drawing dilemma and Feser’s extension (giving up all explicability arguments means giving up argument). Use the here-and-now route to sidestep composition worries. Distinguish strict from derivative necessity, and self-explanatory from self-caused.
audiences.openingQuestion: Which version of PSR are you rejecting — one that requires entailment and treats propositions as explananda, or one that only requires intelligibility of concrete beings? And where exactly do you draw Della Rocca’s line?
audiences.avoid: Don’t wave away the big-conjunction argument as ‘just a puzzle’ without giving the two-part reply. Don’t overstate: say the burden is on the critic to show PSR can be *coherently* denied, and don’t claim PSR is provable by direct demonstration.

audiences.who: Brute-fact atheist (‘the universe is just there, and that’s all’)
audiences.startingPoint: Explanations have to stop somewhere. Stopping at the universe is no worse, and more economical, than stopping at God.
audiences.approach: Agree that explanation must stop somewhere, then focus on the *kind* of stopping point: brute (explaining nothing) versus self-explanatory (able to ground everything else). Show that brute-fact stopping is either arbitrary (why only there?) or self-undermining (if brute facts are allowed, your beliefs could be brute too). Then show why the universe can’t be a self-explanatory stopping point: it changes, has parts, and is doubly contingent. Emphasize that God is not an unexplained stopping point; that is the asymmetry.
audiences.openingQuestion: Do you allow brute facts anywhere other than at the very bottom of reality? If not, what’s special about the bottom?
audiences.avoid: Don’t claim the brute-fact view is stupid; it is a serious position held by Russell and Mackie. Don’t slide into ‘everything has a cause,’ which hands them the ‘What caused God?’ reply.

audiences.who: Believer who knows popular apologetics (e.g., the kalam argument)
audiences.startingPoint: Thinks the argument is about the universe having a beginning, and uses ‘What caused God? — nothing, God is eternal’ as a quick answer.
audiences.approach: Show that this proof is *stronger* for granting an infinite past, and that its key question is dependence right now. Teach the difference between causes and reasons so they stop saying ‘everything that begins has a cause’ when they mean something else. Walk through Stage 2, since the step from ‘necessary being’ to God is where most amateur versions stop. Model honesty about what the argument does *not* show, such as the truth of any specific revelation.
audiences.openingQuestion: Would your argument still work if the universe turned out to be infinitely old? This one does — want to see why?
audiences.avoid: Avoid triumphalism and overclaiming. Don’t treat ‘necessary being’ as meaning ‘exists by definition’ (the ontological argument), and don’t skip the defense of PSR as if it were obvious to everyone.

audiences.startingPoint: Feels there is an ultimate reality but identifies it with the universe, nature, or ‘energy,’ and is wary of a personal God.
audiences.approach: Affirm the intuition that there is an ultimate, self-sufficient ground of things; the argument agrees. Then ask what such a ground must be like. It can’t change or have parts, because anything that does depends on something else. The universe and ‘energy’ change and have structure, so they depend on something deeper. Show how necessity leads to simplicity, unity, and intellect, and why the ultimate ground is distinct from the world while sustaining it at every moment.
audiences.openingQuestion: If there is something that everything else depends on, could it be something that itself changes and is made of parts?
audiences.avoid: Don’t dismiss their spiritual sense as confused. Don’t lead with doctrinal specifics. Keep it to what the argument shows: one, simple, necessary, intelligent cause of all.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I know the contingency argument: ‘everything needs an explanation, therefore God.’ But why should *everything* need an explanation? Maybe some things are just brute facts.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Fair question. When you find a puddle under your car, do you ever seriously consider that it’s there for no reason at all?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: No, but that’s because puddles have always had causes in my experience. That’s induction, not a law of reality.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Induction supports it, agreed. But try this. If things can happen for no reason, could your belief that some things happen for no reason have popped into your head for no reason?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: In principle, I suppose. But I believe it because of arguments.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Exactly — you assume the arguments are *why* you believe it, and that your mind tracks logic and truth. Those are claims about explanation. Once you allow things to happen for no reason, you lose the right to be confident of either, including about your case against the principle.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That feels like a trick. I can accept that *some* things lack explanations without thinking everything is random.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Then where is the line? You accept explanatory reasoning in physics, in induction, in philosophy of mind. Why exempt the existence of things? ‘It’s just a brute fact that the line falls there’ assumes the very thing in dispute.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Say explanation stops at the fundamental laws of physics. Everything else is explained by them, and they just hold.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Picture a book resting on a shelf, and the shelf floating in midair for no reason at all. Is the book’s position explained?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Not really. But laws aren’t shelves.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The structure is the same. If the deepest law has nothing in it or beyond it that accounts for its holding, it has nothing to pass up the chain. The higher ‘explanations’ are borrowed from a lender who has no money.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: All right, suppose I grant the principle. The universe could be infinitely old, each state caused by the one before. Then everything is explained.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Leibniz asked you to imagine an infinite series of geometry books, each copied from an earlier one. Every copy has a cause, but why geometry? Why these laws, these kinds of things? And the series itself could have failed to exist.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That’s the fallacy of composition. Parts being contingent doesn’t make the whole contingent.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It depends on the property. Weight doesn’t transfer from parts to whole; color does — a wall of red bricks is red. Is a pile of three stones *less* dependent than one stone? It depends on each stone *and* on their arrangement. But I don’t even need the whole. Take your coffee mug. What explains its existing right now, this second?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Its atoms, and the forces holding them together.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Which are contingent too. So what keeps *them* in existence now? You get a chain of present dependencies. Finite or infinite, it’s all borrowed existence, and it needs something that exists by its own nature.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine: something necessary. Why not the universe itself, or the quantum field?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Ask what it takes to exist by your own nature. You can’t have potentials waiting to be actualized, or parts that must be held together, or existence you merely receive, because any of those makes you dependent. The universe changes and has parts, so it can’t be the necessary thing.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then what explains God? If you let God go unexplained, let the universe go unexplained.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: I don’t let God go unexplained. God’s existence is explained by his nature, which just is existence, pure actuality with nothing borrowed. The universe’s nature can’t do that. The contrast isn’t explained versus unexplained; it’s self-explanatory versus explained by another. And self-explanatory isn’t self-caused.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Van Inwagen’s objection, then. Take the conjunction of all contingent truths. If a necessary truth explains it, it’s entailed, so it’s necessary. Modal collapse.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That assumes explanation means entailment. Gravity explains elliptical orbits without entailing them, since other forces could interfere. The principle only asks that things be made intelligible. And propositions aren’t Platonic objects floating around needing their own explanation. Explain the concrete things and the minds that think about them, and nothing is left over.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Even if all this works, you’ve reached a necessary being, not the God of any religion.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: You’ve reached one, purely actual, simple, eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing, good cause of everything — the God of classical theism. Which religion, if any, has the fuller story is a further question. But if this works, atheism doesn’t.

socratic: When you can’t find the explanation for something, like where your keys went, do you conclude there isn’t one? Why not?
If things could happen for no reason at all, how could you be sure your present beliefs weren’t among them?
When an argument convinces you, do you think its being a good argument is *why* you believe the conclusion? What does that assume?
You accept explanations everywhere in science. What principle tells you to stop asking for explanations exactly at the existence of things?
If a shelf floated in midair for no reason, would it explain why the book on it doesn’t fall?
Is a pile of three stones more dependent, less dependent, or equally dependent compared with one stone?
If nothing in a tree’s nature guaranteed its existence when it first sprouted, does anything in its nature guarantee its existence right now?
Can making a chain of borrowers longer, even infinitely long, ever produce money that nobody borrowed?
What would something have to be like for its existence to follow from what it is?
Could something that changes, or that is made of parts, depend on nothing at all? What would it depend on?
Is ‘explained by its own nature’ the same as ‘caused itself’? What would causing yourself require?
Does the sun’s gravity *entail* that the planets move in ellipses, or does it make their motion intelligible? Which does an explanation need to do?

traps.trap: Saying ‘everything has a cause’ when you mean ‘everything has an explanation.’
traps.fix: Say ‘explanation’ or ‘sufficient reason’ from the start. Point out that causes are one kind of explanation, and that something can be explained by its own nature without being caused.

traps.trap: Leaning on the Big Bang or a first moment in time.
traps.fix: Grant an infinite past up front, as Feser does. Shift to dependence *now*: what keeps this thing in existence at this moment?

traps.trap: Treating PSR as self-evident and skipping its defense.
traps.fix: Give the reductio. Denying PSR undermines perception, reasoning, and scientific explanation. Then give Della Rocca’s line-drawing challenge.

traps.trap: Stopping at ‘there’s a necessary being’ and announcing ‘that’s God.’
traps.fix: Do Stage 2: necessity requires pure act, simplicity, and essence identical with existence. Then uniqueness, being the cause of all else, and the classical attributes. This is also what rules out the universe.

traps.trap: Getting bogged down in the big-conjunction argument before the listener understands the basic idea.
traps.fix: Hold it until asked. Then give the two-part reply briefly: explanation means intelligibility, not entailment; propositions aren’t free-floating objects needing explanation.

traps.trap: Framing the question as ‘why is there something rather than nothing?’
traps.fix: Ask instead ‘why are there any contingent things at all?’ The ‘nothing’ framing implies nothingness was possible, which the argument denies, and it invites detours into physics’ so-called nothing.

Explain metaphysical necessity: God cannot fail to exist because he has no potentials, parts, or received existence, not because of the meaning of a word. This keeps the ontological argument out of the discussion.

traps.trap: Overclaiming that the argument proves a particular religion.
traps.fix: State exactly what it concludes — one necessary, simple, purely actual, intelligent, good cause of all — and note that questions about revelation come later (ch7a).

connections.note: The introduction presents the five proofs as attempted demonstrations, not probabilistic hypotheses. The rationalist proof fits that pattern: PSR is defended by reductio, and the step from PSR to a necessary being is an elimination argument, not a ‘best guess.’

Chapter 1’s principle of causality is the contrast case for PSR: a cause must be distinct from its effect, while a sufficient reason need not be. Chapter 5’s inductive argument for PSR copies chapter 1’s empirical argument for causality. Chapter 1’s replies to Hume’s conceivability argument and to quantum objections are reused here. Its hand–stick–stone hierarchical series is the model for Feser’s claim that a regress of laws must end in something that transmits power without borrowing it. And pure actuality, the first requirement of Stage 2, is chapter 1’s Unmoved Mover.

Stage 2 argues that a necessary being must be absolutely simple, because a composite thing depends on whatever combines its parts. That is the Neo-Platonic proof’s central insight, and chapter 2’s argument that there can be only one absolutely simple being supports step 20.

Chapter 3’s Scholastic realism — abstract objects exist only in minds, ultimately the divine intellect — is the key to Feser’s reply to the big-conjunction (modal-collapse) objection: propositions are not Platonic objects needing their own explanation. It also underwrites footnote 16: numbers and propositions have only derivative necessity, dependent on an infinite mind.

The closest relative. Chapter 4 answered the fallacy-of-composition charge with the red Lego wall, which chapter 5 reuses, and it reasoned from one thing’s present existence (Fido) rather than from the universe as a whole — the same strategy as chapter 5’s here-and-now route. Stage 2’s requirement that the necessary being’s essence be identical with its existence is chapter 4’s Subsistent Existence Itself. Chapter 5 explicitly treats the proofs as complementary: essence–existence composition is the *deep reason* things are contingent.

Chapter 6 opens its section on Necessity by noting that the rationalist proof argues directly for a necessary being. It then answers objections to the very idea of one: the claim that necessity is only linguistic convention, and Schrader’s ‘imagine a world with nothing in it.’ Its sections on unity, simplicity, immutability, and eternity develop the attributes Stage 2 relies on.

Chapter 6’s treatment of divine will explains how God can freely create lions rather than unicorns, with nothing internal or external compelling him. Combined with chapter 5’s point that explanation need not be entailment, this is the resource for answering modal-collapse worries. Its account of conservation fills in the here-and-now route: God sustains each contingent thing at every moment.

Chapter 7’s first half revisits chapter 5 at several points. It traces ‘What caused God?’ to Hume’s confusion of cause with sufficient reason (via Descartes’ and Spinoza’s causa sui language). It rebuts ‘Maybe the universe itself is the necessary being’ (adding that the result would be pantheism, not atheism). It reuses Leibniz’s geometry books against Grayling’s fallacy-of-composition charge. And it answers Kant’s claim that the argument secretly relies on the ontological argument, by distinguishing metaphysical necessity (pure act, simplicity, essence = existence) from logical and merely conditional necessity.

Chapter 7’s second half answers the objection that the fundamental laws are just brute facts (Mackie, Russell) by pointing back to chapter 5: PSR is true, the brute-fact view is ad hoc, and a regress of laws ending in a brute fact is like a shelf on brackets released in midair. It also notes that the principle of causality can be seen as following from PSR.

The rationalist proof has the most general starting point of the five — the intelligibility of anything at all — so it works well as a hub for connecting the others. Pure actuality, simplicity, and subsistent existence turn out to be what *necessity in the strictest sense* amounts to, which shows how the five routes converge on one reality.

quiz.q: How does Feser state the principle of sufficient reason (PSR)?
options: Everything that begins to exist has a cause of its beginning.
Whatever exists has an explanation of its existence and of the attributes it has.
Every event is fully determined by prior physical conditions.
Every potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual.
quiz.explanation: PSR concerns explanation, and it covers existence and attributes. Option A is the kalam’s causal premise, and option D is the principle of causality from chapter 1, which Feser takes care to distinguish from PSR.

quiz.q: Which of these is a difference between PSR and the principle of causality, according to Feser?
options: PSR applies only to material things, while causality applies to everything.
The principle of causality allows self-caused things, while PSR forbids them.
PSR is purely empirical, while causality is known a priori.
A sufficient reason need not be distinct from what it explains, but a cause must be distinct from its effect.
quiz.explanation: Nothing can cause itself, but something can be self-explanatory. The principle of causality also doesn’t say everything has a cause, while PSR does say everything has a sufficient reason. Option B reverses the truth: neither principle allows self-causation.

quiz.q: Whose argument that denying PSR leads to skepticism about perception does Feser adopt and then push further?
options: Alexander Pruss, developing a point from Robert Koons
J. L. Mackie, developing a point from Bertrand Russell
Michael Della Rocca, developing a point from David Hume
Reginald Garrigou-Lagrange, developing a point from Leibniz
quiz.explanation: Pruss, building on Koons, argues that without PSR our experiences might be unconnected to external objects. Della Rocca supplies the separate explicability-argument dilemma, and Garrigou-Lagrange supplies the idea that PSR is proved indirectly, by reductio.

quiz.q: Why, if PSR were false, could we not even say that a total disconnect between our perceptions and reality is improbable?
options: Because probability is only a subjective feeling.
Because perception is known to be infallible.
Because objective probabilities rest on the objective tendencies of things, and without PSR events might occur without regard to any tendencies.
Because quantum mechanics shows probabilities are undefined.
quiz.explanation: Feser’s point is that probability assessments assume events flow from the natures and tendencies of things. Deny PSR and that assumption has no basis, so we can’t even estimate the likelihood of deception.

quiz.q: Feser’s extension of the Pruss/Koons argument is meant to show that…
options: science is unreliable even if PSR is true.
a priori knowledge is the only secure knowledge.
denying PSR undermines even a priori reasoning, including the reasoning used to deny PSR.
perceptual skepticism is in fact true.
quiz.explanation: The critic might accept perceptual skepticism and retreat to a priori knowledge. Feser argues there is no refuge there: without PSR, nothing guarantees that our beliefs are caused by our reasons or that our faculties track truth. So denying PSR is self-undermining.

quiz.q: A physicist says, ‘Everything is explained by the fundamental laws, which are themselves brute facts.’ Feser’s book-and-shelf example is designed to show that…
options: if the base level is brute, the higher-level ‘explanations’ are illusory as well.
laws of nature are physical objects, like shelves.
the fundamental laws must be deterministic.
brute facts are acceptable at the bottom level but not at higher levels.
quiz.explanation: A shelf that stays up for no reason has no tendency to stay aloft, so it has none to pass to the book. Likewise, a brute fundamental law has nothing to give the laws it supposedly explains. Option D is the physicist’s own view, which Feser rejects.

quiz.q: According to Della Rocca, an ‘explicability argument’ is one that…
options: explains a phenomenon by citing a law of nature.
derives a conclusion from self-evident axioms.
shows that a claim is conceivable and therefore possible.
denies that some state of affairs obtains on the grounds that it would otherwise be inexplicable.
quiz.explanation: Examples include arguing that consciousness must be physical because otherwise it would be inexplicable, and inductive reasoning’s refusal to treat the future as unlike the past.

quiz.q: Why can’t the critic defend Della Rocca’s option 1 by saying it is simply a brute fact that some explicability arguments are legitimate and others are not?
options: Because brute facts cannot be observed.
Because that begs the question against PSR, which denies that there are any brute facts.
Because Della Rocca proved that option 1 is a formal contradiction.
Because explicability arguments about existence are the only legitimate ones.
quiz.explanation: The debate is about whether brute facts exist, so appealing to a brute fact to draw the line assumes the critic’s conclusion. An appeal to intuition fails for a related reason: the critic’s use of explicability arguments elsewhere undercuts that intuition.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think Della Rocca concedes too much in allowing that option 2 (reject all explicability arguments) may not be strictly incoherent?
options: Because giving up all explicability arguments amounts to giving up argumentation, since logic embodies standards of intelligibility and explanatory adequacy.
Because option 2 turns out to be identical to option 3.
Because option 2 requires believing in innate ideas.
Because option 2 is what most working scientists already accept.
quiz.explanation: Many arguments are explanations: explanatory demonstrations, inference to the best explanation, induction. Rejecting all of them while arguing against PSR is incoherent. Keeping argument in general while rejecting particular explicability arguments collapses back into option 1.

quiz.q: On Feser’s definitions, a contingent thing is one that…
options: exists only for a finite period of time.
might exist without any cause at all.
has its explanation in something outside itself.
has no explanation whatsoever.
quiz.explanation: A contingent thing depends on outside circumstances and would not exist if they failed. A thing could be everlasting and still be contingent; duration is not the issue.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say there is no third option besides being contingent and being necessary?
options: Because everything that exists is material.
Because a thing explained neither by its own nature nor by anything else would be explained by nothing, which PSR rules out.
Because infinite regresses are impossible.
Because Leibniz defined the terms that way.
quiz.explanation: The dichotomy follows from PSR. An explanation lies either inside or outside the thing, and ‘neither’ means ‘no explanation.’ Option C is wrong because Feser grants infinite regresses for argument’s sake.

quiz.q: An objector says, ‘Each member of the infinite series is contingent, but the series as a whole needn’t be — just as bricks weighing a pound each don’t make a one-pound wall.’ What is the best reply from the chapter?
options: Weight is a merely subjective property.
Infinite series can’t exist, so the objection is moot.
Every whole has every property of its parts.
Contingency, like color and unlike weight, carries over from parts to whole — collections are, if anything, doubly contingent.
quiz.explanation: Feser does not claim that all part-to-whole inferences are valid (option C). He says validity depends on the property. Contingency behaves like color (red Lego bricks make a red wall), and a collection depends on both its members and their arrangement.

quiz.q: Which example of Leibniz’s does Feser use against Hume’s claim that explaining each member explains the whole series?
options: A watch found lying on a heath
A hand moving a stick that moves a stone
A series of mirrors reflecting a face
An infinite series of geometry books, each copied from an earlier copy
quiz.explanation: The geometry books come from Leibniz’s ‘On the Ultimate Origination of Things.’ The hand and stick come from Feser’s earlier chapters, and the watch is Paley’s design argument, which Feser does not use.

quiz.q: What is the main point of the geometry-books example?
options: Infinite series are impossible.
Giving each member its immediate cause still leaves unexplained why the series has the character it has — its content, kinds, and laws.
Books require authors, so the universe requires a designer.
Geometry consists of necessary truths.
quiz.explanation: The example grants the infinite series. What it shows is that immediate causes don’t explain why the series is about geometry and not Shakespeare, or, applied to the universe, why it contains these kinds of things governed by these laws. Option C misreads it as a design argument.

quiz.q: Why doesn’t positing a contingent cause outside the series of contingent things solve the problem?
options: Because causes outside the universe are inconceivable.
Because it would violate the conservation of energy.
Because it only produces a higher-order series needing the same explanation, which passes the explanatory buck.
Because every cause must be simultaneous with its effect.
quiz.explanation: A contingent outside cause needs its own cause, and whatever made the first series insufficient applies to a second, a third, and even to an infinite series of infinite series.

quiz.q: What is distinctive about Feser’s ‘here-and-now’ route to a necessary being?
options: It reaches a necessary being from one contingent thing’s present existence, without any premise about the universe as a whole.
It requires that the universe began at the Big Bang.
It depends on the ontological argument.
It works only if time is unreal.
quiz.explanation: The route asks what keeps a particular thing in existence at this moment, which leads to a regress of simultaneous causes. Because it makes no claim about the whole, the composition charge has nothing to attack, and it grants an infinite past.

quiz.q: A friend says, ‘My dog exists because her parents produced her — that’s the whole explanation.’ What does Feser’s second route add?
options: Nothing, because past causes fully explain present existence.
Nothing in the dog’s nature guarantees her existence at this moment any more than at her first moment, so a present sustaining cause is needed.
The dog’s parents must still be alive for her to exist.
Dogs are necessary beings in Aquinas’ broad sense.
quiz.explanation: Past production explains how the dog came to be, not why she continues to exist now. Because she is contingent, her present existence needs a simultaneous cause. Option D confuses the broad sense of ‘necessary,’ which applies to naturally incorruptible beings such as angels.

quiz.q: Why must a necessary being be purely actual?
options: Because if it had potentials needing actualization, its existence would depend on an actualizer, so it would not really be necessary.
Because only purely actual things can be observed.
Because pure actuality is part of the dictionary definition of ‘being.’
Because Leibniz stipulated it.
quiz.explanation: The same pattern applies to parts (which would depend on a combiner) and to an essence distinct from existence (which would depend on a giver of existence). Any such dependence is incompatible with necessity in the strictest sense.

quiz.q: Why does Feser specify ‘necessary in the strictest sense’ in a footnote to Stage 2?
options: To separate God from numbers.
To separate metaphysical necessity from Kant’s logical necessity.
To concede that God might not exist in some possible worlds.
Because Aquinas also uses ‘necessary’ loosely for things with no natural tendency to corrupt, such as angels, whose necessity is only derivative.
quiz.explanation: Angels are naturally immortal and so ‘necessary’ in the broad sense, but they mix act and potency, have parts, and have an essence distinct from their existence, so they need a cause. Only God is necessary in the strictest sense.

quiz.q: The ‘big conjunction of contingent truths’ objection relies on which assumptions that Thomists reject?
options: That God is simple and that the universe is finite.
That induction is reliable and that perception is trustworthy.
That propositions need explaining the way concrete objects do, and that an explanans must logically entail its explanandum.
That infinite regresses are impossible and that time had a beginning.
quiz.explanation: Feser’s two replies target exactly these: propositions exist only in minds (Scholastic realism), so explaining concrete things and minds leaves nothing over; and explanation requires intelligibility, not entailment.

quiz.q: Which example does Feser, following Pruss, use to show that an explanation need not entail what it explains?
options: A dropped glass shattering on the floor
A fair coin landing heads
The sun’s gravity explaining the planets’ elliptical orbits, although other gravitational influences could have prevented them
Two plus two equaling four
quiz.explanation: Even non-statistical scientific explanations don’t strictly entail their explananda. The sun’s gravity makes the orbits intelligible without guaranteeing them. Statistical cases like the coin make the same point, but they are not the example Feser gives.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think quantum-mechanical objections are even weaker against PSR than against the principle of causality?
options: Because quantum mechanics has been refuted.
Because quantum events turn out to be deterministic.
Because PSR applies only to macroscopic objects.
Because whether or not quantum events have causes, they have explanations: they presuppose, and are made intelligible by, the laws of quantum mechanics.
quiz.explanation: Indeterminism is not unintelligibility. Feser adds, following Della Rocca, that the quantum critic still owes an account of where to draw the line between legitimate and illegitimate explicability arguments.

quiz.q: Why can’t the universe be the necessary being?
options: It changes, so it has potentials, and it has parts, so it is neither purely actual nor simple.
It is too large to exist necessarily.
It had a beginning at the Big Bang.
Scientists have not yet discovered what caused it.
quiz.explanation: Stage 2 shows that a strictly necessary being must be purely actual and simple. Option C is not Feser’s reason, since he grants a possibly infinite past, and option D is a god-of-the-gaps framing he rejects.

quiz.q: What is the correct reply to ‘If God doesn’t need an explanation, neither does the universe’?
options: God is the one exception to PSR.
God does have an explanation, his own nature, so the contrast is self-explanatory versus explained by another, and it rests on act/potency, simplicity, and essence/existence.
God is self-caused, whereas the universe is uncaused.
The universe needs a cause because it began to exist.
quiz.explanation: The proof makes no exception for God. Option C is a classic confusion: self-explanatory is not self-caused, because having a cause means having a potential actualized. Option D brings in kalam reasoning the proof doesn’t rely on.

quiz.q: Which step of the formal argument rules out a thing whose existence is explained by nothing at all?
options: Step 10
Step 13
Step 9
Step 19
quiz.explanation: Step 9 builds PSR into the division: explanation lies either in another (contingent) or in the thing’s own nature (necessary), and PSR excludes ‘by nothing.’ Step 13 applies the division to series. Step 19 concerns what a necessary being must be like.

quiz.q: Which steps make up the ‘here-and-now’ route to a necessary being?
options: Steps 15–17
Steps 2–3
Steps 11–14
Steps 19–21
quiz.explanation: Steps 15–17 ask why a particular contingent thing persists at any moment and show that a regress of simultaneous contingent causes fails. Steps 11–14 are the Leibniz–Clarke series route.

quiz.q: How are steps 2–3, 4–5, and 6–7 best described?
options: As a single chain in which each pair depends on the one before it
As three objections that Feser goes on to rebut
As premises about the attributes of the necessary being
As three independent supports for PSR, each pairing a conditional with a fact
quiz.explanation: Each pair gives its own route to step 8 (inductive, reductio, Della Rocca-style), so PSR survives even if one pair is doubted. They are not dependent on each other.

quiz.q: Which step secures that there is only one necessary being?
options: Step 18, because it says there is at least one
Step 21, drawing on step 20’s claim that only one thing can be purely actual, simple, and subsistent existence
Step 23, because the being causes everything else
Step 26, because God is one by definition
quiz.explanation: Step 18 says only ‘at least one.’ Uniqueness comes from combining 19 (every necessary being has these features) with 20 (at most one thing can have them). Step 23 depends on uniqueness rather than establishing it.

quiz.q: What would Feser reply to: ‘God’s nature doesn’t entail that this universe exists, so God can’t be its sufficient reason’?
options: He would agree and exempt creation from PSR.
An explanation needs to make its explanandum intelligible, not logically entail it — the sun’s gravity explains orbits without entailing them.
He would say the universe exists necessarily after all.
He would say propositions about creation need no explanation.
quiz.explanation: The Thomist PSR rejects the entailment requirement. Option C is the modal collapse that entailment would produce. Option D misapplies his point about propositions: the concrete universe does need explaining.

quiz.q: An objector says, ‘Each stone is contingent — so what? The heap needn’t be.’ Which distinction does the objection ignore?
options: Cause versus sufficient reason
Strict versus derivative necessity
Temporal versus simultaneous causes
Weight-like versus color-like properties in part-to-whole reasoning
quiz.explanation: Feser grants that part-to-whole inference fails for weight but insists it works for color, and contingency is color-like. A heap is in fact doubly contingent.

quiz.q: A critic says, ‘Theists claim everything needs a cause except God — special pleading!’ Which distinction does this ignore?
options: Cause versus sufficient reason: God has an explanation (his nature) but no cause
Weight-like versus color-like properties
The series route versus the here-and-now route
Inductive versus a priori support for PSR
quiz.explanation: The rationalist proof never says everything has a cause, and it makes no exception to ‘everything has an explanation.’ God is self-explanatory, not uncaused-and-unexplained, and self-explanatory is not self-caused.

quiz.q: A neuroscientist argues that consciousness must be a brain process because otherwise it would be inexplicable. In Della Rocca’s terms, she is…
options: committing the fallacy of composition.
denying PSR outright.
using an explicability argument, which makes it hard for her to reject such arguments about existence without arbitrariness.
giving an explanatory demonstration.
quiz.explanation: This is one of Della Rocca’s own examples of an EA. If she later says existence can be a brute fact, she owes a non-question-begging reason for drawing the line there.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say the rationalist proof complements the Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, and Thomistic proofs?
options: Because all four rely on the Big Bang.
Because the rationalist proof replaces their premises with PSR.
Because the earlier proofs quietly assumed PSR without admitting it.
Because act/potency, composition, and essence/existence are the deep reason things are contingent, while PSR is the deep reason such things need causes.
quiz.explanation: Feser presents the proofs as mutually illuminating. The earlier proofs explain *why* things are contingent, and PSR explains *why* contingent things must be caused.

quiz.q: Which three philosophers does the chapter cite as sources of the big-conjunction objection to PSR?
options: Hume, Russell, and Mackie
Leibniz, Clarke, and Pruss
James Ross, Peter van Inwagen, and William Rowe
Della Rocca, Koons, and Gerson
quiz.explanation: Ross, van Inwagen, and Rowe are cited for the objection. Gerson and Pruss are cited for critical discussion of it, and Mackie and Russell for the brute-fact view of laws.

quiz.q: According to Feser, in what sense alone is the argument ‘rationalist’?
options: It relies on innate ideas.
It is committed to PSR — reality is intelligible through and through, with no brute facts.
It holds that all knowledge rests on truths known a priori.
It originates in Descartes’ Meditations.
quiz.explanation: Feser disowns the historical rationalists’ epistemology (innate ideas, a priori foundationalism). The label refers only to the commitment to PSR.

quiz.q: What would Feser reply to: ‘Triangularity exists necessarily, so there is a necessary being that isn’t God’?
options: Abstract objects exist only in minds, so any necessity they have is derivative, flowing from an infinite mind that thinks them.
Triangularity is contingent, because triangles can be erased.
Triangularity is identical with God.
Abstract objects are brute facts exempt from PSR.
quiz.explanation: Footnote 16 draws on chapter 3: abstracta can’t exist apart from minds, so their necessity is not absolute. Option D would contradict PSR.

quiz.q: Which thinker does Feser credit with saying that PSR cannot be demonstrated directly but can be demonstrated indirectly, by reductio?
options: Reginald Garrigou-Lagrange
Bernard Wuellner
Samuel Clarke
Michael Della Rocca
quiz.explanation: Garrigou-Lagrange is quoted to this effect. Wuellner supplies a formulation of PSR, Clarke is Leibniz’s ally on the series argument, and Della Rocca supplies the EA dilemma.

quiz.q: Why does Feser call the question ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’ potentially misleading?
options: Because ‘nothing’ really means a quantum vacuum.
Because it suggests absolute nothingness was possible, whereas the proofs imply that a necessary being could not have failed to exist.
Because the question has no answer.
Because Leibniz never asked it.
quiz.explanation: He proposes instead: why are there any contingent things at all? That framing doesn’t presuppose that nothing could have existed.

quiz.q: A student says, ‘The universe could be infinitely old, so the argument collapses.’ What is the best response from this chapter?
options: Prove that an actual infinite is impossible.
Concede that the argument fails.
Grant the infinite past: the series as a whole, its specific kinds and laws, and each thing’s present existence still need explaining.
Point out that the Big Bang proves a beginning.
quiz.explanation: Feser explicitly allows a beginningless universe, cycles, or a multiverse. The argument doesn’t rest on a beginning, so options A and D change the subject.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say a collection of stones is ‘doubly contingent’?
options: Because it has twice the mass of a single stone.
Because it exists in two places at once.
Because contingency is weight-like.
Because it depends both on each stone’s existence and on the stones being gathered together as they are.
quiz.explanation: Each stone depends on conditions like physical laws holding its atoms together, and the collection depends on those conditions *and* on its assembly. So it is more contingent, not less.

quiz.q: What role do the objective tendencies of things play in the Pruss/Koons argument?
options: They show that quantum events are really determined.
They prove that substantial forms exist.
They ground objective probabilities, so without PSR we couldn’t even judge wholesale perceptual error improbable.
They are brute facts needing no explanation.
quiz.explanation: If events can occur without regard to things’ tendencies, probability assessments lose their basis. That is why denying PSR leaves perceptual skepticism not even improbable.

quiz.q: What would Feser say to a critic who insists that the burden of proof lies on PSR’s defender because PSR is a sweeping universal claim?
options: He would accept the burden and concede that PSR is unproven.
He would say PSR is self-evident and needs no argument.
He would switch to the ontological argument.
He would say the burden lies on the critic to show PSR can be coherently rejected, though the defender can also meet a burden with the arguments given.
quiz.explanation: Feser places the burden on the critic but has also offered positive arguments (induction, reductio, Della Rocca). Option B is wrong because he does argue for PSR, indirectly.

quiz.q: Why can’t the fallacy-of-composition charge even get started against the here-and-now route?
options: Because the route assumes the universe had a beginning.
Because it reasons only from one particular thing’s present existence and makes no claim about the whole.
Because it relies on quantum mechanics.
Because it concerns abstract propositions.
quiz.explanation: The charge targets inferences from parts to whole, and the here-and-now route has none. This parallels chapter 4’s Fido-based reasoning.

quiz.q: Why can’t a contingent sustaining cause, backed by an infinite chain of further contingent sustainers, explain why a stone exists now?
options: Because the whole simultaneous series is itself contingent and needs an outside explanation, just as the stone did.
Because simultaneous causes are impossible.
Because infinite chains are self-contradictory.
Because stones are necessary beings.
quiz.explanation: Feser grants the regress could be infinite. Its problem is the same as the temporal series: a series of borrowers explains no one’s having what was borrowed.

shortAnswer.q: Explain the difference between the principle of sufficient reason and the principle of causality, and show why the difference matters for the objection ‘What caused God?’
shortAnswer.model:
The principle of causality says that any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual. A cause is always distinct from its effect, and the principle does not claim that everything has a cause. PSR says everything has a sufficient reason — an explanation of its existence and attributes. A sufficient reason may lie outside the thing (a cause) or in the thing’s own nature (self-explanation). So every cause is a reason, but not every reason is a cause.

This defuses ‘What caused God?’ in two ways. The argument never says everything has a cause, and although it does say everything has an explanation, it makes no exception for God: God is explained by his nature as pure act and subsistent existence. Being self-explanatory is not being self-caused, since causation involves actualizing a potential and pure act has none.
rubric: States both principles accurately
Notes that a cause must be distinct from its effect but a reason need not be
Notes that PSR is universal while the causal principle is not ‘everything has a cause’
Explains that God is self-explanatory, not self-caused
Shows that no exception to PSR is made for God

shortAnswer.q: Reconstruct Feser’s argument that rejecting PSR is self-undermining. Include the Pruss/Koons step and Feser’s extension.
shortAnswer.model:
Step 1 (Pruss/Koons): if PSR is false, our perceptual experiences might occur for no reason, with no connection to external objects. We couldn’t even call this improbable, since objective probabilities rest on the objective tendencies of things, which events could then ignore. So denying PSR leaves no justification for trusting perception or empirical science.

Step 2 (Feser): the critic might accept this and retreat to a priori knowledge. But any justified belief assumes that we have a reason for it and that the reason is *why* we believe, and also that our faculties track truth and logic. Without PSR we have no grounds for these assumptions. Our assent might be caused by something unrelated to our reasons, and it might only seem, for no reason, that we reason well. This applies equally to the reasoning behind rejecting PSR. So rejecting PSR removes the grounds for rejecting it; it undermines rational inquiry as such.
rubric: Presents the perceptual-skepticism step and the point about objective probability
Presents the retreat to the a priori
Explains the dual role of reasons (justification and cause of assent)
Notes the assumption that faculties track truth and logic
Concludes that the denial undercuts itself

shortAnswer.q: State Della Rocca’s explicability-argument dilemma and explain how Feser pushes it further.
shortAnswer.model:
Explicability arguments (EAs) deny that some state of affairs obtains because it would be inexplicable. Philosophers and scientists use them all the time: in reductive accounts of consciousness, in the early moderns’ rejection of substantial forms, in induction. Applied to the existence of things, an EA amounts to PSR. The critic of PSR must choose: (1) some EAs are legitimate but not those about existence; (2) none are legitimate; (3) all are legitimate. Option 3 is PSR. Option 2 is unavailable to anyone who uses EAs. Option 1 is arbitrary: saying it is a brute fact that the line falls there begs the question, and intuition is undermined by the critic’s own practice. So nothing is explicable unless everything is.

Feser adds that option 2 is not merely problematic but incoherent. Even a critic who drops the specific examples still relies on valid and inductively strong reasoning and rejects fallacies, because logic embodies standards of intelligibility. Many arguments are explanations (explanatory demonstrations, inference to the best explanation, induction). Giving them all up means giving up argument, and keeping argument while rejecting particular EAs is just option 1 again.
rubric: Defines an explicability argument with at least one example
States all three options correctly
Explains why options 2 and 3 fail for the critic
Explains why option 1 is question-begging (brute fact or intuition)
Presents Feser’s extension that option 2 abandons argumentation

shortAnswer.q: Why, according to Feser, does a regress of laws of nature that ends in a brute fact fail to explain anything?
shortAnswer.model: If law C is explained by B and B by A, but A has no explanation — nothing in A and nothing beyond A accounts for its holding — then A has nothing to pass on to B or C. The book-and-shelf example makes this vivid: a shelf that stays up for no reason has no tendency to stay aloft, so it can give none to the book. Giving the book a brute tendency of its own just relocates the problem. A regress of laws is a hierarchical series, in which lower members transmit what they derive from higher ones. A hierarchical series with an ungrounded first member is like an instrument that is not the instrument of anything. So the brute-fact view held by Mackie and Russell undermines the very scientific explanations it means to protect.
rubric: Describes the structure of a nomological regress
Uses or explains the book-and-shelf example
Explains the point about imparting or transmitting
Links it to hierarchical series and instruments
Notes the implication for scientific explanation

shortAnswer.q: Hume claimed that in an infinite series of contingent things, each explained by its predecessor, everything is explained. Give three things Feser says remain unexplained.
shortAnswer.model: First, why the series exists at all. The series is just as contingent as its members and could have failed to exist (Leibniz and Clarke). Second, why the series has the particular character it has. As with Leibniz’s infinitely copied geometry books — why geometry and not Shakespeare? — we can ask why the world contains these kinds of things (stones, dogs, galaxies) and is governed by these laws rather than others. Third, why any particular member exists *now*. What produced it in the past doesn’t explain its continued existence, since nothing in its nature guarantees its existence at this moment. Appealing to further contingent causes, including higher-order series, only passes the buck.
rubric: Identifies the contingency of the series as a whole
Gives the geometry-books point about the series’ content, kinds, and laws
Identifies present existence (the here-and-now question)
Notes that further contingent causes merely relocate the problem

shortAnswer.q: Answer the charge that asking for an explanation of the whole series of contingent things commits the fallacy of composition.
shortAnswer.model: Reasoning from parts to whole is fallacious only for some properties. It fails for weight (stones under an ounce each don’t make a pile under an ounce), but it holds for color (a structure of red Lego bricks is red). Contingency behaves like color. Three contingent stones are no less contingent than one, and three million no less than three. In fact a collection is doubly contingent, depending on each member and on the members being assembled as they are. So the collection of all contingent things is contingent. Moreover, the here-and-now route makes no claim about the whole, reasoning only from one thing’s present existence, so the charge doesn’t even apply to it. (Chapter 7 adds that it is Hume who reasons fallaciously, inferring that explaining each member explains why there is anything in the series at all.)
rubric: Distinguishes properties that transfer from parts to whole from those that don’t
Places contingency correctly with the color-like properties
Explains double contingency
Notes that the here-and-now route avoids part-to-whole reasoning

shortAnswer.q: Explain Feser’s ‘here-and-now’ route to a necessary being and why it strengthens the argument.
shortAnswer.model:
Grant an infinite past. Take any particular contingent thing and ask why it continues to exist at this moment rather than being annihilated. Its past producer doesn’t answer that. Because the thing is contingent, nothing in its nature entails its existence, now any more than at its first moment. By PSR, something must cause it to exist right now. If that cause is contingent, the same question arises, producing a regress of simultaneous causes. That series as a whole needs outside explanation just as the original thing did, so only a cause that exists necessarily can end the regress.

It strengthens the argument because it needs no premise about the universe as a whole, so the composition charge has nothing to attack. It is indifferent to whether time had a beginning. And it connects the rationalist proof to the hierarchical-series reasoning of the Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, and Thomistic proofs.
rubric: Poses the question of continued existence at this moment
Explains why past causes don’t answer it
Describes the regress of simultaneous causes and its failure
Concludes to a necessary sustaining cause
Gives at least two reasons the route is stronger

shortAnswer.q: Why must a necessary being be purely actual, absolutely simple, and subsistent existence itself? And why can there be only one?
shortAnswer.model: A necessary being in the strictest sense depends on nothing outside itself. If it had potentials needing actualization, it would depend on an actualizer. If it had parts, it would depend on something combining them. If its essence were distinct from its existence, it would depend on a cause giving existence to that essence. Each case makes it contingent, so a strictly necessary being must be purely actual, simple, and subsistent existence. (Naturally immortal angels are ‘necessary’ only in Aquinas’ broad, derivative sense.) Earlier chapters showed there can be only one such being: distinguishing two would require some differentiating potential, part, or limiting essence, which none of these can have. So there is exactly one necessary being, and since everything else is contingent and depends on it, it is the cause of everything else.
rubric: Derives each of the three attributes from the absence of dependence
Distinguishes strict from broad necessity
Gives the uniqueness argument (no differentiating feature possible)
Draws the conclusion that it is the cause of all other things

shortAnswer.q: State the ‘big conjunction of contingent truths’ objection to PSR and give Feser’s two-part reply.
shortAnswer.model:
Objection (Ross, van Inwagen, Rowe): conjoin all true contingent propositions. The Big Conjunction is contingent. A necessary proposition can’t explain it, because whatever a necessary proposition entails is necessary (modal collapse). A contingent proposition can’t either, because it would be one of the conjuncts, so the conjunction would explain itself, which nothing contingent can do. So something lacks an explanation, and PSR is false.

Reply 1: the objection treats propositions as Platonic objects that need explaining like stones. For the Scholastic realist, abstract objects exist only in the minds that entertain them. What needs explaining are concrete things and their attributes, and once those and the relevant minds (including the divine mind) are explained, nothing is left over. Reply 2: the objection assumes an explanans must entail its explanandum. It needn’t. Scientific explanations generally don’t entail — the sun’s gravity explains elliptical orbits although interference could have prevented them. PSR requires intelligibility, not entailment.
rubric: States the objection with both horns
Links the necessary-explanation horn to modal collapse or entailment
Gives the reply about propositions and Scholastic realism
Gives the reply that explanation is not entailment, with an example
Notes that the Thomist PSR differs from the targeted versions

shortAnswer.q: In what ways does Feser’s rationalist proof differ from Leibniz’s and Clarke’s versions?
shortAnswer.model: (1) **Which PSR.** Feser’s PSR is Thomistic. It asks explanations only to make things intelligible, not to entail them, and it treats only concrete things and their attributes as needing explanation, which lets it escape the big-conjunction objection. (2) **Defense of PSR.** He defends it not merely as intuitive or inductive but by reductio (Pruss/Koons, extended) and by Della Rocca’s dilemma (also extended). (3) **Routes.** Alongside the Leibniz–Clarke whole-series route, he adds a here-and-now route from one thing’s present existence, which sidesteps composition worries. (4) **Stage 2.** He grounds necessity in the Aristotelian-Thomistic metaphysics of pure act, simplicity, and essence identical with existence, which supplies uniqueness and the divine attributes and rules out the universe. (5) **Minimal rationalism.** He takes on no doctrine of innate ideas or a priori foundationalism. (6) **Framing.** He prefers ‘why are there any contingent things?’ to ‘why is there something rather than nothing?’
rubric: Explains the Thomist PSR (intelligibility, not entailment; no Platonic propositions)
Describes the stronger defense of PSR
Mentions the here-and-now route
Describes the Stage 2 grounding of necessity in act/potency, simplicity, and essence/existence
Mentions at least one of: minimal rationalism, the reframed question

shortAnswer.q: A critic grants PSR but says the necessary being might be the universe, or perhaps numbers and propositions. How does the chapter respond?
shortAnswer.model: On the universe: a strictly necessary being must be purely actual and simple. The universe changes, so it has potentials being actualized, and it has diverse parts. It is not subsistent existence either, being as contingent as its parts. So it cannot explain itself, and its explanation lies outside it. (Chapter 7 adds that a self-explanatory, purely actual universe would have divine attributes, so the view would be pantheism, not atheism.) On abstract objects: chapter 3 argues independently that numbers, universals, and propositions cannot exist apart from minds that entertain them. If they are necessary, their necessity is derivative, flowing from an infinite mind. So neither the universe nor abstracta is a non-divine absolutely necessary being.
rubric: Applies Stage 2’s criteria of pure act and simplicity to the universe
Identifies change and parts as the disqualifying features
Explains that abstract objects exist in minds (chapter 3)
Distinguishes derivative from absolute necessity

shortAnswer.q: A critic accepts PSR ‘within the universe’ but says it doesn’t apply to the existence of the universe itself. How would Feser respond?
shortAnswer.model: This is Della Rocca’s option 1: explicability arguments are legitimate in general but not for the sheer existence of things. The critic owes a non-arbitrary reason for drawing the line exactly there. Saying it is a brute fact that some EAs work and others don’t begs the question against PSR, which denies brute facts. Appealing to intuition fails because the critic’s own reliance on EAs elsewhere undermines that intuition. And, echoing chapter 1’s reply to Kant, learning a principle from experience does not limit it to experience; geometry learned from ink drawings applies to figures of any color. So the restricted PSR is special pleading.
rubric: Identifies this as Della Rocca’s option 1
Explains why ‘brute fact’ begs the question
Explains why an appeal to intuition fails
Notes that a principle learned from experience isn’t limited to experience, or otherwise shows the line is arbitrary

shortAnswer.q: Distinguish necessity in the strictest sense from derivative necessity, and show how the distinction answers two different challenges.
shortAnswer.model: Strict necessity means depending on nothing whatsoever for existence, which requires pure actuality, simplicity, and identity of essence and existence. Derivative necessity belongs to things that cannot naturally cease to exist but still receive their existence from another. Aquinas calls naturally immortal angels ‘necessary’ in this sense (Third Way). The distinction answers (1) the worry that angels or other incorruptible creatures would count as the necessary being, since they are caused and composite, and (2) the claim that numbers or propositions are non-divine necessary beings, since per chapter 3 they exist only in minds and have a necessity derived from an infinite mind.
rubric: Defines strict necessity with its three requirements
Defines derivative necessity with the angel example
Applies the distinction to angels or incorruptible creatures
Applies it to abstract objects via chapter 3

shortAnswer.q: Explain why appealing to a contingent cause outside the series of contingent things only ‘passes the explanatory buck.’
shortAnswer.model: Suppose the entire infinite series of contingent things is caused by something outside it that is itself contingent. Being contingent, that cause needs a cause, and if that cause is contingent it needs another, and so on. We now have a second, higher-order series of contingent causes, and every reason that made the first series insufficient (it could have failed to exist, it has a specific character, its members borrow their existence) applies equally to the second. So we would need a third series, a fourth, and so on, and even an infinite series of infinite series would be just as contingent as the first. Each move relocates the need for explanation without meeting it. Only a cause whose existence is explained by its own nature, a necessary being, ends the regress.
rubric: States that a contingent outside cause needs its own cause
Describes the higher-order series
