Explains why the same reasons apply at every level
Mentions the infinite series of infinite series
Concludes that only a necessary being ends the regress

shortAnswer.q: Compare how quantum-mechanical objections fare against PSR and against the principle of causality.
shortAnswer.model: Against the principle of causality, a critic might argue that some quantum events lack a deterministic cause (chapter 1 answered this by noting that indeterminism is not the absence of causation). Against PSR the objection is weaker still. Whether or not odd quantum events have a *cause*, they have an *explanation*: they presuppose, and are made intelligible by, the laws of quantum mechanics. PSR asks for intelligibility, not deterministic entailment. And, as Della Rocca notes, the critic who invokes quantum mechanics still owes an account of where to draw the line between legitimate and illegitimate explicability arguments, and why there.
rubric: Distinguishes a cause from an explanation
Explains that quantum laws make quantum events intelligible
Notes that PSR doesn’t require determinism or entailment
Mentions Della Rocca’s line-drawing challenge

shortAnswer.q: Explain Feser’s claim that the rationalist proof and the earlier proofs ‘complement one another.’
shortAnswer.model: The here-and-now route resembles the Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, and Thomistic proofs: each reasons from a thing’s present dependence to a sustaining first cause. The proofs also supply each other’s ‘deep reasons.’ The earlier proofs explain *why* things are contingent: they mix act and potency, are composite, and have an essence distinct from their existence, so they need causes both to begin and to continue existing. PSR explains *why* anything like that must have a cause at all: otherwise it would be unintelligible, and everything is intelligible. Stage 2 then shows the convergence: necessity in the strictest sense is pure act, simplicity, and subsistent existence, so the rationalist proof lands on the same one reality as the earlier proofs, with the same attributes.
rubric: Notes the structural parallel (present dependence, hierarchical series)
Gives the earlier proofs’ account of why things are contingent
Gives PSR’s account of why contingent things need causes
Explains Stage 2’s convergence on one reality

shortAnswer.q: Some reject the argument because it is ‘rationalist.’ Explain what Feser’s argument does and does not commit him to regarding rationalism and PSR.
shortAnswer.model: Feser’s argument does not assume innate ideas or that all knowledge rests on truths known independently of experience, doctrines associated with Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz. It is ‘rationalist’ only in denying that there are, or could be, inexplicable brute facts, holding that reality is intelligible through and through. Nor does it take on every thesis defended under PSR’s name. Unlike some contemporary formulations, it doesn’t count propositions among the things needing explanation (only concrete things and their attributes), and it doesn’t require an explanans to logically entail its explanandum. That is why objections aimed at those stronger versions, such as the big-conjunction argument, miss the Thomist PSR.
rubric: States the rationalist doctrines Feser does not assume
Defines his minimal rationalism as PSR
Mentions that propositions are not explananda
Mentions that explanation need not be entailment
Connects this to why some objections miss

flashcards.back: Whatever exists has an explanation of its existence and of its attributes, whether or not we find it.

flashcards.front: Two differences between PSR and the principle of causality
flashcards.back: (1) A cause must be distinct from its effect, while a sufficient reason can be the thing’s own nature. (2) The causal principle doesn’t say everything has a cause; PSR says everything has a sufficient reason.
…not all reasons are causes. Something can be self-explanatory without being self-caused.
Sunglasses left by a friend, a rash from poison oak, scratching from raccoons or a cat, and an unsolved murder (we even explain why it remains unsolved).
We find explanations when we look, or know why we can’t. If PSR were false, brute events would be common and the world wouldn’t be so intelligible; its order would be a miracle.
It can’t be demonstrated directly, but it can be demonstrated indirectly, by reductio ad absurdum.
Denying PSR leads to perceptual skepticism: experiences might have no link to external objects, and we couldn’t even call that improbable, since objective probabilities depend on things’ tendencies.
Without PSR we can’t trust that our reasons cause our beliefs or that our faculties track truth. That includes a priori reasoning and the case against PSR, so denial is self-undermining.
They are brute facts: we explain phenomena by laws and laws by deeper laws, but the deepest laws have no explanation.
A shelf that stays up for no reason has no tendency to stay aloft to give the book. Likewise, a brute fundamental law has nothing to give the laws above it, so the explanation is illusory.
Della Rocca: arguing that a state of affairs doesn’t obtain because it would be inexplicable. Used in philosophy of mind, in the critique of substantial forms, and in induction.
(1) Some EAs are legitimate, but not about existence — arbitrary. (2) No EAs are legitimate — self-defeating. (3) All EAs are legitimate — this is PSR.
It is incoherent, not merely problematic. Logic embodies standards of intelligibility, and many arguments are explanations, so rejecting all EAs means rejecting argument.
All rational animals can use language; all humans are rational animals; so all humans can use language. The premises give the reason why the conclusion is true.
Explained by something outside itself; depends on outside circumstances and wouldn’t exist without them.
Explained by its own nature; cannot fail to exist; depends on nothing else.
A thing explained neither by its nature nor by anything else would be explained by nothing, which PSR rules out.
A beginningless universe; an endless series of Big Bang/Big Crunch universes; a beginningless branching multiverse.
If each contingent thing is caused by an earlier one, everything is explained and no necessary being is needed.
The series itself is contingent and could have failed to exist — so why does it exist?
Part-to-whole reasoning fails for weight but works for color (red Lego bricks make a red wall). Contingency is like color, and collections are doubly contingent.
A collection depends both on each member’s existence and on the members being gathered and arranged as they are.

An infinite chain of copies gives each book a cause but doesn’t explain why the content is geometry rather than Shakespeare, a coloring book, or a repair manual. Likewise, it doesn’t explain why the world has these kinds and laws.

flashcards.front: Why not a contingent cause of the series?
flashcards.back: It needs a cause too. Higher-order contingent series, even infinitely many, only pass the explanatory buck.

What keeps this contingent thing existing now? Its past cause doesn’t. A regress of simultaneous contingent sustainers must end in a necessary being. No premise about the universe as a whole is needed.

flashcards.front: Deep reason things are contingent (per ch5)
flashcards.back: They mix actuality and potentiality, are composite, and have an essence distinct from their existence. They need causes because otherwise they would be unintelligible.

flashcards.front: Stage 2: three marks of a strictly necessary being
flashcards.back: Purely actual (no dependence on an actualizer), absolutely simple (no dependence on a combiner), subsistent existence (no dependence on a giver of existence).
Aquinas calls naturally incorruptible things like angels ‘necessary,’ but their necessity is derivative, since they are caused. Only God is necessary in the strictest sense.
There can be only one purely actual, simple, self-subsistent being (from earlier chapters), so the necessary being is unique and causes everything else.
Only the commitment to PSR — no brute facts, reality intelligible through and through. No innate ideas and no a priori foundationalism.
(1) That propositions need explaining like concrete things. (2) That an explanans must logically entail its explanandum.
Ross, van Inwagen, Rowe: the conjunction of all contingent truths can be explained neither by a necessary truth (modal collapse) nor by a contingent one (self-explanation), so PSR fails.
Propositions exist only in minds, so explaining concrete things and minds leaves nothing over. And explanation needs intelligibility, not entailment (sun’s gravity and elliptical orbits).
Whether or not quantum events have causes, they have explanations: they are made intelligible by quantum laws. The critic still owes an answer on where to draw the EA line.
It rests on the critic, who must show how PSR can be coherently rejected. Puzzles about particular formulations don’t answer the positive arguments.

flashcards.front: Why the universe isn’t the necessary being
flashcards.back: It changes (has potentials) and has parts, so it is neither purely actual nor simple; it is as contingent as its parts.

flashcards.front: Numbers and propositions as necessary beings?
flashcards.back: Their necessity is derivative: per chapter 3 they exist only in minds, ultimately an infinite mind.

flashcards.front: God vs. the world, in one line
flashcards.back: The difference is not explained vs. unexplained but self-explanatory vs. explained by another, grounded in act/potency, simple/composite, and essence/existence.

flashcards.front: Better framing than ‘something rather than nothing’
flashcards.back: ‘Why are there any contingent things at all?’ The proofs imply that there could not have been absolutely nothing.

flashcards.front: Step 2–3: what do they claim, and why?
flashcards.back: If PSR were false, unexplained things would be everywhere, yet common sense and science find the opposite. So PSR is supported by modus tollens.

flashcards.front: Step 4–5: what do they claim, and why?
flashcards.back: If PSR were false, we couldn’t trust our cognitive faculties, but we can. Denying PSR undercuts perception and reasoning, including the reasoning behind the denial.

flashcards.front: Step 6–7: what do they claim, and why?
flashcards.back: PSR can’t be denied in a principled way while science and philosophy are credited with genuine explanations, and they have many (Della Rocca; brute-fact laws explain nothing).
PSR is true. It follows from any of the three independent pairs of premises.

flashcards.front: Step 9: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: Everything is explained by another (contingent) or by its own nature (necessary). PSR rules out ‘by nothing.’

flashcards.front: Step 11: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: Even an infinite series of contingent causes leaves the series’ own existence unexplained, because the series is itself contingent (Leibniz and Clarke).

flashcards.front: Step 12: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: A contingent cause outside the series only creates a higher-order series with the same problem. This is passing the buck.
No contingent thing or series explains why there are contingent things, so by PSR and elimination a necessary being is their cause.

flashcards.front: Step 15: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: A contingent thing’s continued existence at any moment needs a simultaneous cause distinct from it. Its past cause doesn’t explain its present existence.
An infinite regress of contingent simultaneous causes is still an unexplained contingent series, so a necessary being must be the sustaining cause.
At least one necessary being exists, explaining both why there are contingent things and how each persists.

flashcards.front: Step 19: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: A necessary being must be purely actual, simple, and subsistent existence. Potentials, parts, or received existence would make it dependent.
Only one thing can be purely actual, simple, and subsistent existence (earlier chapters), so there is only one necessary being.
That one being explains all contingent existence and sustains every contingent thing, so it is the cause of everything other than itself.
Such a being is also immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent, good, intelligent, and omniscient. That is God, so God exists.
Retreating to the a priori doesn’t help. Without PSR there are no grounds for thinking reasons cause beliefs or faculties track truth, and that includes logic.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Explanation is fine except for existence’ — reply
flashcards.back: That is Della Rocca’s option 1, which is arbitrary. Appealing to a brute fact to draw the line begs the question, and intuition is undercut by the critic’s own practice.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Then I reject all explicability arguments’ — reply
flashcards.back: That abandons argument itself, since logic embodies standards of intelligibility, and explanatory demonstrations, IBE, and induction are explanations.
Its only rationalism is PSR (no brute facts). It assumes no innate ideas and no a priori foundationalism.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Hume showed we can conceive of uncaused events’ — reply
flashcards.back: Conceiving of A without conceiving of its cause is not conceiving of A as uncaused (trilateral and triangle). This was answered in chapter 1.
Puzzles aimed at some formulations don’t touch others, or the positive arguments. The burden is on the critic to show PSR can be coherently rejected.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘A necessary being is incoherent’ — reply
flashcards.back: The necessity is metaphysical (pure act, simplicity, essence = existence), not definitional. Imagining empty scenes doesn’t test it (ch6a, ch7a).

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘God’s explaining creation means modal collapse’ — reply
flashcards.back: Explanation is intelligibility, not entailment. God freely creates, compelled by nothing internal or external (ch6b).
The result that every truth is necessary. Critics say entailment-based PSR leads to it, and the Thomist PSR avoids it.
A mystery has an explanation we don’t know. A brute fact has no explanation at all. PSR allows mysteries and denies brute facts.

flashcards.front: Hierarchical series and laws of nature
flashcards.back: Deeper laws ‘transmit’ explanatory power the way a hand moves a stick that moves a stone. The chain needs a first member with power of its own, not a brute fact.

teachBack:
**Your challenge:** Explain the rationalist proof out loud, in about **six minutes**, to a friend who is intelligent, skeptical, and has never studied philosophy. Imagine someone who says, ‘Maybe the universe is just there.’

**Constraints:**
- Never say ‘everything has a cause.’ Say ‘everything has an explanation.’
- Grant an infinite past in the first two minutes, and make the argument work anyway.
- Use exactly two images: the book on the floating shelf (for PSR and brute-fact laws) and one image of your choice for the regress (the IOU chain, the geometry books, or the lamp that is on *now*).
- Spend at least one minute on Stage 2: why ‘necessary’ means pure act, no parts, and essence = existence, and why that rules out the universe.
- End by answering ‘What caused God?’ in under 30 seconds.

**Then check yourself.** Record yourself, or have the friend repeat back what they understood. Could you:
1. Say *why* denying PSR is self-undermining, not just that it is?
2. Explain why there’s no third option beyond contingent and necessary?
3. Give the color-versus-weight reply to the composition charge?
4. Explain the here-and-now route without mentioning ‘the universe as a whole’?
5. Explain the difference between self-explanatory and self-caused?
6. Say what makes Feser’s PSR different from the version van Inwagen attacks (intelligibility vs. entailment; no Platonic propositions)?

If you stumbled on any of these, reread that summary section, then try again with a *different* audience — a twelve-year-old, then a philosophy major — to see whether you can adjust the depth without losing accuracy.

readingGuide.beforeYouRead:
This chapter asks one of the oldest questions there is: **why does anything exist that didn’t have to?** Stones, trees, people, planets, even the whole universe — all of them depend on other things. Feser argues that if you follow that dependence all the way down, you can’t stop at anything that also depends on something else. You have to reach something that exists simply because of what it is. And when you work out what such a thing must be like, it turns out to be God.

The argument has one big assumption, and Feser spends almost half the chapter defending it: **everything has an explanation**, even if we never find it. Philosophers call this the principle of sufficient reason. You already live by it — you’d never think your car stopped working ‘for no reason at all.’ Feser’s striking claim is that you *can’t* coherently deny it. If things could happen for no reason, you couldn’t trust your eyes, your memory, or even your own reasoning, including any reasoning against the principle.

Here is what you will be asked to accept along the way:

- that ‘explained by something else’ and ‘explained by its own nature’ are the only two options once brute, unexplained facts are ruled out;
- that a chain of dependent things, even an endlessly long one, is still dependent;
- that anything which can change or is made of parts depends on something else.

Why care? Because the most common atheist response to arguments for God is ‘maybe the universe is just there, and that’s all.’ This chapter is aimed squarely at that response. It is also the chapter that best answers the question ‘Then what caused God?’

Some reassurance. The hardest stretch is pages 148–153, where Feser defends the principle using arguments from other philosophers (Pruss, Koons, Della Rocca). Read them slowly and don’t worry if the names blur; the idea underneath each one is simple. The rest of the chapter moves faster, and the numbered summary on pages 161–163 lets you check your understanding step by step. Unlike some other arguments for God, this one does *not* need the universe to have had a beginning. Feser happily grants that it might be infinitely old.

map.what: Contingent versus necessary, with no third option. Then Feser grants an infinite past (a beginningless universe, Big Bang/Big Crunch cycles, a multiverse) and states Hume’s view.
map.tip: Memorize the two definitions on p. 154. The cosmology scenarios can be read quickly; the details deliberately don’t matter.

map.section: Informal statement of the argument: Stage 1
map.what: The Leibniz–Clarke point: why does the series itself exist? Footnote 8 reframes ‘something rather than nothing,’ and the fallacy-of-composition charge is answered with stones and red Lego blocks.
map.tip: Don’t skip footnote 8. Pause on why contingency is ‘like color’ and why collections are ‘doubly contingent.’

map.section: Informal statement of the argument: Stage 1
map.what: Leibniz’s infinite geometry books; why a contingent cause outside the series only passes the explanatory buck; the conclusion to a necessary being.
map.tip: Trace the ‘second series, third series…’ argument on paper with boxes and arrows.

map.section: Informal statement of the argument: Stage 1
map.what: The second route: what keeps a particular thing in existence right now? Then how this proof complements the earlier ones, and the three ways to develop it.
map.tip: This is the most important page for a modern reader, because it needs no claim about the universe as a whole. Compare it with chapter 4’s Fido example.

map.section: Informal statement of the argument: Stage 2
map.what: Why the necessary being must be purely actual, simple, and existence itself; footnote 10 on Aquinas’ looser use of ‘necessary’ (angels); uniqueness; cause of everything; the divine attributes.
map.tip: If chapters 1–4 feel hazy, review their conclusions first. Footnote 10 is short and worth reading.

map.section: A more formal statement of the argument
map.what: The whole proof in 27 numbered steps.
map.tip: Use it as a self-test: for each step, can you say which earlier pages support it? Mark steps 11, 12, 15, and 19, where most objections land.

map.what: Why ‘rationalist’ doesn’t mean innate ideas, and which version of the principle Feser defends: no Platonic propositions, and no requirement that explanations entail what they explain.
map.tip: Note the two things Thomists reject. They are the key to the next objection.

map.what: The ‘big conjunction of contingent truths’ objection (Ross, van Inwagen, Rowe) and Feser’s two replies: propositions exist in minds, and explanation needn’t be entailment (gravity and elliptical orbits).
map.tip: The hardest objection. Try the toy version with just two facts (see the module), and read the orbit example slowly.

map.what: Humean conceivability and quantum mechanics dismissed; puzzles don’t answer arguments; the burden of proof lies with the critic.
map.tip: If Hume’s conceivability point is unclear, glance back at chapter 1’s trilateral/triangle reply.

map.what: Why the universe can’t be the necessary being; why numbers aren’t either (footnote 16); ‘What caused God?’ — God is self-explanatory, not self-caused (footnote 17).
map.tip: Read footnotes 16 and 17; they are brief and important. End by explaining the God/universe asymmetry out loud.

afterReading: Without looking, state the principle of sufficient reason and give two ways it differs from ‘everything has a cause.’
Explain in three sentences why denying the principle is self-undermining.
Draw the two routes to a necessary being (the whole series; a single thing existing right now) and say why each needs no beginning of time.
Give Feser’s reply to the fallacy-of-composition charge using the stones and the red Lego blocks.
List the three things a necessary being can’t have, and say why each would make it dependent.
Answer ‘Why not the universe?’ and ‘What caused God?’ in under 30 seconds each.
State the big-conjunction objection and Feser’s two replies to it.
Take the module’s section checks and quiz, and reread the pages for any question you miss.
